This preserves local scalar-\(-6\) Koiso geometry while reducing volume by \(N^{-2}\) [Step 69]. A one-direction peripheral cover of a hyperbolic cusp has lattice type \((N,1,1)\); truncating at depth \(\log N\) produces type \((1,N^{-1},N^{-1})\), matching the quotient scale without homothetic curvature rescaling [Step 69]. The remaining problem was to evolve from \(S=0\) to an almost-cusp state while controlling all Einstein components [Step 69].

Step 73 converted a discarded approximate-anisotropy obstruction into a construction tool. For
\[
g=dr^2+e^{2r}\left[
dz^2+N^{-2}e^v dx^2+N^{-2}e^{-v}dy^2
\right]
\]
and base \(B=dr^2+e^{2r}dz^2\), direct computation gives
\[
E|_B=-\frac12\,dv\otimes dv,
\]
\[
E_x=-\frac12\left(v_{rr}+3v_r+e^{-2r}v_{zz}\right),\qquad E_y=-E_x,
\]
with vanishing base–fiber mixed components [Step 73]. Hence
\[
\|E\|_{\rm op}
=\frac12\max\left\{
v_r^2+e^{-2r}v_z^2,\,
\left|v_{rr}+3v_r+e^{-2r}v_{zz}\right|
\right\}.
\]
For
\[
v(r,z)=\chi\!\left(\frac{r-r_0}{K}\right)v_0(z),
\]
one obtains
\[
\|\operatorname{Ric}+3g\|_\infty
\le C(K^{-1}+K^{-2}+e^{-2r_0}),
\]
uniformly in the lattice parameter \(N\) [Step 73]. Symbolic verification and numerical scaling were stored in `step73_expanding_tail_verify.py` and `step73_expanding_tail.json` [Step 73]. This solved only the exterior flattening module. The interface became: construct a core reaching a large slice with \(S\approx I\), small scaled intrinsic curvature, low orbit-map energy, and enough jet control to attach the adiabatic tail [Step 73].

## Exact PE-end obstructions, anisotropy rigidity, and early core-entry failures [Steps 70–78]

For \(B=S-I\), \(b=H-3\), and \(E=\operatorname{Ric}+3g\), the exact normal equation is
\[
b'+2b+|B|^2=-E_{00}.
\]
Thus
\[
e^{2R}b(R)-b(0)+\int_0^R e^{2t}|B|^2\,dt
=-\int_0^R e^{2t}E_{00}\,dt.
\]
At a reflected center \(b(0)=-3\), this records the weighted residual and shear needed to approach a cusp [Steps 70–71]. It supplies a necessary logarithmic lower length scale under small pointwise defect, not an existence mechanism or upper length bound [Steps 70–73].

A false flat benchmark was removed. The warped metric \(dt^2+\cosh^2(t)q_{\rm flat}\) solves the normal ODE but not the tangential Einstein equation; its tangential defect is \(2\operatorname{sech}^2(t)I\). A totally geodesic Einstein center must have scalar curvature \(-6\), not zero [Step 71]. The Gaussian Cauchy system is elliptic in tangential variables, so numerical forward blow-up reflects Hadamard ill-posedness rather than necessarily geometric singularity [Steps 70–71].

An exact global reflected core with a flat \(T^3\) Poincaré–Einstein end was excluded. Doubling would give a two-ended complete Einstein manifold with nonnegative-Yamabe ends, contradicting the Witten–Yau/Cai–Galloway one-endedness alternative as used by Li–Liu; the exceptional warped product has no reflected totally geodesic slice [Step 71]. The PE expansion gives the same obstruction in center-normalized gauge [Step 71]. This excludes exact flat-PE reflection cores, not finite forced connectors or negative-Yamabe ends.

A five-field Einstein–DeTurck boundary framework was repaired for
\[
g=A\,dt^2+2D\,dt\,d\theta+C\,d\theta^2+P\,dx^2+Q\,dy^2.
\]
Reflection requires \(A,C,P,Q\) even and \(D\) odd. The center metric must be allowed to emerge rather than prescribed together with all reflection data [Step 71]. The correct gauge-fixed operator is
\[
\operatorname{Ric}+3g-\frac12\mathcal L_Vg.
\]
The outer conformal-class/mean-curvature/gauge conditions and center parity passed a nonzero-frequency complementing-symbol check, but this established neither nonlinear solvability nor uniform invertibility as length grows [Step 71].

Step 72 introduced the conformal gauge
\[
g=e^{2\phi}(dt^2+dz^2)+e^{2b}dx^2+e^{2c}dy^2,
\]
whose selected three-equation subsystem has elliptic principal determinant
\[
2(\tau^2+\xi^2)^3.
\]
This explained why earlier Gaussian-gauge experiments left large omitted constraints, but the three equations were explicitly retained only as a subsystem; all five Einstein equations still had to be solved or propagated [Steps 72–73].

For \(\delta=b-c\) and \(\sigma=b+c\), exact Einstein metrics in the diagonal orthogonally transitive class satisfy
\[
\operatorname{div}(e^\sigma\nabla\delta)=0.
\]
This yields exact finite-cylinder rigidity: reflection Neumann data and constant outer anisotropy force constant anisotropy throughout [Step 72]. Combined with the impossibility of scalar \(-6\) in the flat conformal class, it obstructed an exact reflected core with flat constant-anisotropy exit. The Step 72 extrapolation to approximate cores was later withdrawn because the sourced equation
\[
\operatorname{div}(e^\sigma\nabla\delta)
=-e^{\sigma+2\phi}(E_x-E_y)
\]
has inverse constants depending on geometry and boundary conditions, while the normal identity gives only a lower length scale [Steps 72–73].

Step 74 briefly proposed a fixed-length nonlinear boundary problem after finding that the linearized anisotropy equation
\[
\psi''+3\psi'-k^2e^{-2t}\psi=0
\]
has two bounded radial basis branches. This was overinterpreted. The reflection-normalized solution satisfies
\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}\psi(t)=\frac{\sinh k}{k},
\]
so transfer grows exponentially with frequency; fixed-mode Neumann–Dirichlet uniqueness is not frequency-uniform stability of the nonlinear Einstein map [Steps 74–75]. A prescribed CMC ODE model also assumed favorable curvature decay rather than evolving an intrinsic metric satisfying Hamilton and momentum constraints. The normal identity showed that defect and \(3-H(R)\) cannot both tend to zero at fixed physical Gaussian length [Step 75].

Step 75 extracted an exact center theorem for every periodic
\[
q=ds^2+G(s)
\]
with flat \(T^2\) orbits. Writing
\[
A=\frac12G^{-1}G',\qquad h=\operatorname{tr}A,
\]
one has
\[
R_q=-2h'-|A|^2-h^2.
\]
Since \(h=(\log\sqrt{\det G})'\) is periodic with mean zero, at a downward zero of \(h\), scalar curvature \(-6\) forces the orbit sectional curvature
\[
K_{\rm orb}=-\det A=\frac{|A|^2}{2}\ge3.
\]
The orbit-normal direction then has a \(\operatorname{Ric}_q+3I\) eigenvalue at most \(-3\), so an exact reflected Einstein core has an initially contracting principal direction [Step 75]. The small-defect estimate was corrected in Step 76 to
\[
\lambda_{\min}S'(0)\le-3+3\delta
\]
by keeping the cancellation
\[
(R_q+6)-E_{vv}=E_{11}+E_{22}-E_{nn}
\]
in a fixed orthonormal frame [Steps 75–76].

Step 76 strengthened the pointwise center theorem to a normalized integrated identity. With
\[
\rho=\sqrt{\det G},\qquad A_0=A-\frac h2I,
\]
periodicity and \(R_q=-6+e\) give
\[
\int\rho|A_0|^2\,ds
=
6\int\rho\,ds
+\frac12\int\rho h^2\,ds
-\int\rho e\,ds.
\]
For diagonal anisotropy \(d=b-c\),
\[
\int\rho\,d_s^2\,ds
=
12\int\rho\,ds
+\int\rho h^2\,ds
-2\int\rho e\,ds.
\]
At a reflected four-dimensional \(\delta\)-defect center this yields a normalized floor \(12-8\delta\) [Step 76]. Lattice quotients multiply energy and volume equally, so they do not dilute the normalized center burden [Step 76].

The transport variable was also corrected. For
\[
\operatorname{div}(\rho\nabla d)=-\rho X,\qquad X=E_x-E_y,
\]
the exact total signed flux
\[
Q=\int\rho d_n
\]
may vanish, while the relevant energy is the covariance pairing
\[
F_c=\int(d-c)\rho d_n.
\]
Its balance is
\[
F_c(r_1)-F_c(r_0)
=
\int_{\rm core}\rho|\nabla d|^2
-\int_{\rm core}(d-c)\rho X
\]
[Step 76]. The center energy fixes the initial slope of this pairing but gives no thickness estimate from Ricci pinching alone. Expanding modes can have \(d_n\to0\) while weighted stress remains finite, so the center identity alone cannot prove a uniform residual gap [Step 76].

Li–Liu’s Type-I PE/cusp family was reread as an exact outer-end and matrix-shape laboratory. Its off-diagonal \(dy+A\,dx\) term belongs to the orbit metric rather than quotient-connection curvature [Step 76]. Step 77 separated the physical reflection-center metric \(q_0\), the conformal-infinity representative \(\gamma\), and the filling-dependent coefficient \(\gamma_3\). In geodesic defining-function gauge,
\[
g=dr^2+e^{2r}
\left[\gamma+e^{-2r}\gamma_2+e^{-3r}\gamma_3+\cdots\right],
\qquad
\gamma_2=-\operatorname{Sch}(\gamma).
\]
The leading limit
\[
e^{2r}(S-I)^\circ
\to \operatorname{Sch}(\gamma)^\circ{}^\sharp
\]
is locally determined by \(\gamma\), while the nonlocal filling datum appears only after subtraction:
\[
e^{3r}\left[(S-I)^\circ
-e^{-2r}\operatorname{Sch}(\gamma)^\circ{}^\sharp\right]
\to-\frac32\gamma^{-1}\gamma_3
\]
[Step 77]. This prevented boundary-determined leading stress from being mistaken for evidence that two fillings intersect.

Under a smooth global normal foliation from a reflected center to a PE end, Riccati comparison gives
\[
H\le3\tanh r
\]
and hence
\[
R_\gamma\le-24
\]
for the center-normalized boundary representative [Steps 77–78]. Step 78 corrected the scope: equality along one ray controls that ray, while Preissmann excludes equality everywhere; one obtains strictness somewhere, not automatically at every boundary point. With
\[
u_H=3-H,\qquad w=3(1-\tanh r),\qquad z=u_H-w,\qquad Z=e^{2r}z,
\]
the consistent equation is
\[
Z'=\frac{u_H+w}{3}Z+e^{2r}|P|^2,
\qquad
-\frac{R_\gamma}{4}=6+\lim Z.
\]
These are necessary relations under the foliation assumption, not obstructions to finite forced connectors [Step 78].

The ASD/reflection obstruction was retained with proper hypotheses. An Einstein even extension across a totally geodesic hypersurface reverses orientation. If one Weyl chirality vanishes, reflection forces the other to vanish locally as well, giving constant negative sectional curvature and contradicting a compact totally geodesic \(T^3\) [Steps 68,71,77]. Li–Liu’s ASD metrics therefore cannot themselves be reflected cores, though they remain useful end models [Step 77].

Step 78 tested a rotating-eigenframe escape through the globally periodic Bianchi VII\(_0\) family
\[
\omega_1=\cos(kz)dx+\sin(kz)dy,\qquad
\omega_2=-\sin(kz)dx+\cos(kz)dy,
\]
\[
g=dr^2+a(r)^2dz^2+b(r)^2\omega_1^2+c(r)^2\omega_2^2.
\]
Writing
\[
u=a'/a,\qquad d=\log(b/c),\qquad K=2k^2a^{-2}\sinh^2d,
\]
direct curvature calculation gives slice scalar curvature \(-K\) and equations
\[
u'+Hu=3-K-E_z,
\]
\[
d''+Hd'=2K\coth d-(E_1-E_2),
\]
\[
(\log K)'=-2u+2\coth(d)d'.
\]
At a reflected center,
\[
K(0)\ge6-4\delta.
\]
For \(\delta\le3/5\), a protected-region argument gives
\[
u<0,\qquad d'>0,\qquad K>K(0)
\]
at every positive radius [Step 78]. Step 81 later strengthened this specific ODE barrier to finite-time collapse [Step 81]. This remains symmetry-specific and does not control the full two-variable orthogonally transitive system.

## Orthogonally transitive \(T^2\) reduction, Bochner obstruction, and forced complete-end theorem [Steps 79–88]

Step 79 derived the full orthogonally transitive \(T^2\)-invariant reduction. For a two-dimensional quotient metric
\[
\gamma_B=e^{2\lambda}(dr^2+dz^2)
\]
and orbit metric
\[
G=e^\sigma M,\qquad \det M=1,
\]
the exact \(\operatorname{Ric}=-3g\) equations split into:
\[
\Delta(e^\sigma)=6e^{2\lambda+\sigma},
\]
equivalently
\[
\Delta\sigma+|\nabla\sigma|^2=6e^{2\lambda},
\]
for orbit area;
\[
\operatorname{div}\!\left(e^\sigma M^{-1}dM\right)=0
\]
for the unimodular orbit shape, a weighted harmonic map into
\[
SL(2,\mathbb R)/SO(2)\cong\mathbb H^2;
\]
and
\[
\Delta\lambda
=\frac14\left(|\nabla\sigma|^2-e_{\mathbb H^2}\right)
\]
together with remaining cross and trace-free base constraints [Step 79]. Scripts under `workspace/scripts/step79_*` checked determinant, trace, energy normalization, the round cusp, and recovery of earlier scalar anisotropy equations [Step 79].

In hyperbolic polar coordinates \((d,\psi)\) on orbit-shape space,
\[
\operatorname{div}(e^\sigma\nabla d)
=e^\sigma\sinh d\cosh d\,|\nabla\psi|^2,
\]
\[
\operatorname{div}(e^\sigma\sinh^2d\,\nabla\psi)=0.
\]
The VII\(_0\) family is the helicoidal map \((d(r),kz)\); its frozen angular gradient gives the positive source that drives \(d\) outward. A general two-variable map can redistribute angular gradient in both quotient directions, so VII\(_0\) monotonicity does not automatically extend [Steps 79,81]. An Iwasawa-coordinate sign was corrected:
\[
\operatorname{div}(e^\sigma\nabla\alpha)
=-e^{\sigma-2\alpha}|\nabla\beta|^2
\]
[Step 79].

A convex-distance maximum principle gave an exact obstruction. For a fixed \(P\in\mathbb H^2\),
\[
F(U)=\frac12d_{\mathbb H^2}(U,P)^2
\]
has \(\operatorname{Hess}F\ge h_{\mathbb H^2}\). On an exact reflected cylinder with constant outer orbit map, center Neumann data and outer Dirichlet data force \(U\equiv P\) [Step 79]. Thus exact connectors cannot erase nontrivial center orbit shape to a constant exit. This did not exclude exact cores with nonconstant exit followed by a forced tail [Step 79].

The full matrix Noether current
\[
Q(r)=\int e^\sigma M^{-1}M_r\,dz
\]
is conserved and vanishes under reflection, strengthening scalar angular-flux relations [Step 79]. The same step separated quotient-connection twist from off-diagonal orbit shape. For commuting Killing fields, rank-two twist scalars are constant on a connected Einstein region; a reflection fixing the center reverses orientation and forces them to vanish. Hence exact reflected Einstein regions are locally orthogonally transitive, although \(M\) may remain fully off-diagonal [Step 79]. In approximate cores, sourced twist identities remain geometry-weighted, so small operator defect does not automatically imply a uniform twist estimate over long collapsing or expanding regions [Steps 79,88–90].

Step 80 corrected several proposed computations before executing them. A zero-mode transition on a fixed cusp begins with \(S=I\), not a reflected center \(S=0\), and its central torus is flat rather than scalar \(-6\); it merely reproduces the solved tail [Step 80]. The physical cusp coordinate \(r\) differs from conformal coordinate \(t=-e^{-r}\). The invariant forcing measure is
\[
e^\sigma d\operatorname{vol}(\gamma_B),
\]
which equals \(e^{3r}dr\,dz\) on the round cusp, not \(e^{4r}dr\,dz\) [Step 80]. Common \(N^{-2}\) scaling of both orbit directions shifts \(\sigma\) by a constant but leaves \(M\) unchanged, so the graph quotient does not by itself create orbit-shape distance \(2\log N\) [Step 80].

The load-bearing base identity was verified:
\[
E_B
=
\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma_B)
-\operatorname{Hess}\sigma
-\frac12d\sigma\otimes d\sigma
-\frac12U^*h_{\mathbb H^2}
+3\gamma_B.
\]
On the fixed cusp, \(\gamma_B=dr^2+e^{2r}dz^2\) and \(\sigma=2r+\text{const}\), so
\[
E_B=-\frac12U^*h_{\mathbb H^2}.
\]
Thus every orbit-map direction contributes positive-semidefinite stress; adding an angular orbit component cannot cancel the base defect on a frozen cusp. The unresolved mechanism must use the response of base curvature, \(\operatorname{Hess}\sigma\), and area growth to the center’s order-one orbit energy [Step 80].

A joint finite-mode experiment used
\[
g=dr^2+e^{2a}dz^2+e^{\sigma+v}dx^2+e^{\sigma-v}dy^2
\]
with the Step 69 Yamabe center, reflection data, and a Fourier-projected Koiso second jet. All five orthonormal components \(E_{rr},E_{rz},E_{zz},E_x,E_y\) were evaluated [Step 80]. Joint variation of \(a,\sigma,v\) lowered RMS and much of the residual profile relative to shape-only variation, but sampled operator suprema remained near \(15\), concentrated around physical radius \(r\approx0.2\), essentially independent of total lengths \(R=4,6\). The exits were already near umbilic with very small scaled intrinsic curvature; increasing \(R\) improved the exterior without resolving the first physical layer [Step 80]. These runs were not treated as lower-bound evidence because the nonlinear solves exhausted function evaluations, optimized averaged \(L^2\) rather than operator supremum, used finite Fourier projection and modest grids, and retained only diagonal orbit shape [Step 80].

A likely cause of the inner peak was incomplete Einstein jet matching. If
\[
l_i=l_i^0+\frac12p_ir^2+\frac1{24}w_ir^4+O(r^6),
\]
then exact reflection evolution gives
\[
p_i=\operatorname{Ric}_i(q_0)+3,\qquad
w_i=D\operatorname{Ric}_{q_0}[2p^\flat]_i-6p_i,
\qquad
\sum_iw_i=-2\sum_ip_i^2.
\]
Numerical differentiation on the projected center gave \(\|w\|_\infty\approx149.161\). Directly cutting this fourth-order germ into a cosh exterior produced still larger cutoff-layer residuals, showing that the exact inner germ must be solved on its own domain with free outgoing data rather than spliced by a prescribed cutoff [Step 80].

Step 81 adopted a more geometric center representation. For constant orbit area,
\[
q_0=dz^2+\rho_0U_0(z),
\]
where \(U_0:S^1\to\mathbb H^2\), the scalar identity is
\[
R(q_0)=-\frac12|U_{0,z}|_{\mathbb H^2}^2.
\]
Hence any analytic closed loop parametrized at constant speed \(\sqrt{12}\) is an exact scalar-\(-6\) reflected center; on a \(2\pi\)-periodic base its target length is \(2\pi\sqrt{12}\) [Step 81]. For the standard winding loop, an exact formula was derived for reflected Einstein acceleration:
\[
\operatorname{Spec}S'(0)
=
\left\{
-3,\,
3\pm\sqrt{3(k^2+12)}
\right\}.
\]
The \(z\)-direction eigenvalue \(-3\) is universal for every constant-area scalar-\(-6\) center, while orbit splitting grows with winding [Step 81]. A stronger averaged contraction theorem was obtained for arbitrary orbit-area profile:
\[
\left\langle u'(0)\right\rangle_\rho=-3,
\]
where the average uses the natural orbit-volume weight [Step 81]. Step 81 also strengthened the Step 78 VII\(_0\) barrier from persistent contraction to finite-time collapse via a cascade \(K\ge6\Rightarrow H\le\sqrt3\Rightarrow -u\) grows \(\Rightarrow K>10\Rightarrow H'\le-1-H^2\) [Step 81].

Step 82 derived physical Gaussian OT slice balances. With
\[
g=dr^2+e^{2a}dz^2+G_{ab}dx^adx^b,\quad
\rho=\sqrt{\det G},\quad
u=a_r,\quad B=\tfrac12G^{-1}G_r,\quad v=\operatorname{tr}B,
\]
and \(d\mu=e^a\rho\,dz\), the exact corrected balances are
\[
J'=6V-\int \operatorname{tr}_{\rm orbit}E\,d\mu,
\]
\[
I'=\int\left[-3+2uv+\frac12v^2-|B_0|^2
+\operatorname{tr}_{\rm orbit}E-E_{rr}\right]d\mu
\]
[Step 82]. At a first return from \(I<0\) to \(I=0\), \(\|E\|_{\rm op}\le\delta\) requires
\[
2\operatorname{Cov}_\mu(u,v)+\frac12\langle v^2\rangle_\mu-\langle|B_0|^2\rangle_\mu
\ge3-3\delta
\]
[Step 82]. Writing
\[
K=\langle |U_s|^2-h^2\rangle_\mu
\]
gives
\[
\langle R(q_r)\rangle_\mu=-K/2
\]
and
\[
x'=3-K/2-\langle E_{zz}\rangle-x(x+y),
\qquad x=I/V.
\]
A reflected scalar-\(-6\) center has \(K=12\), whereas first return requires \(K\le6+2\delta\) [Step 82]. TTCS-derived and independently checked center jets gave
\[
K'(0)=0,\qquad
K''(0)=72+2\langle|\tau|^2\rangle+\frac38\operatorname{Var}(k)\ge72,
\]
so exact reflected OT germs initially move in the wrong direction [Step 82].

Step 83 corrected sign analysis of this \(K\)-production framework and found that it does not close the connector problem by itself. After eliminating \(\tau\) and expanding \(vc\), only one group was proven nonnegative; the remaining covariance, tension, and forcing terms are indefinite [Step 83]. A systematic TTCS generator search through orbit energy, squared distance, Noether current, finite-moment combinations, and Bochner/Bakry–Émery routes found no monotone quantity excluding the \(K\)-drop [Step 83]. Step 84 reversed the Bochner assessment because the relevant drift curvature is
\[
\operatorname{Ric}_B-\operatorname{Hess}\sigma,
\]
not \(\operatorname{Ric}_B+\operatorname{Hess}\sigma\) [Step 84]. Substituting the exact base equation gives
\[
\operatorname{Ric}_B-\operatorname{Hess}\sigma
=-3\gamma_B+\frac12d\sigma\otimes d\sigma+\frac12U^*h_{\mathbb H^2}+E_B.
\]
Thus orbit stress contributes positively inside the Bochner curvature term; Step 83’s negative-eigenvalue argument did not test this coupled structure [Step 84].

Step 85 turned the corrected Bochner convention into a clean exact obstruction theorem for the orthogonally transitive free-\(T^2\) connector class. With
\[
e=|dU|^2
\]
for the orbit map \(U:B\to\mathbb H^2\), the corrected exact weighted Bochner formula is
\[
\frac12Le
=
|DdU|^2+\frac12|dU(\nabla\sigma)|^2+Q(A)-3e,
\]
where \(A=U^*h_{\mathbb H^2}\) and
\[
Q(A)=\frac12\operatorname{tr}(A^2)+2\det A\ge\frac12e^2
\]
[Steps 84–85]. Hence
\[
\frac12Le\ge\frac12e(e-6)
\]
[Step 85]. On a compact reflected exact connector, the maximum principle gives
\[
\sup e\le \max\{6,\sup_{\rm exit}e\}
\]
[Step 85]. TTCS corrected the center identity: the tangential orbit-area log-derivative \(h=(\log\rho)_s\) is not the radial mean curvature, so the correct center identity is
\[
\langle e(0,\cdot)\rangle_\mu=12+\langle h^2\rangle_\mu\ge12
\]
[Step 85]. Therefore an exact reflected free-\(T^2\) OT Einstein connector with exit orbit energy below \(12\), in particular compatible with the Step 73 expanding tail where \(e\to0\), cannot exist [Step 85]. Its scope was exact, reflected, free-\(T^2\), orthogonally transitive geometry [Step 85].

The forced superlevel weak equation and localization were then corrected. A lower bound for \(\operatorname{Ric}_B-\operatorname{Hess}\sigma\) alone is an infinite-dimensional Bakry–Émery bound and does not justify unnormalized Sobolev constants [Step 86]. The coupled Einstein equation gives the stronger finite-dimensional structure
\[
\operatorname{Ric}^{(4)}_\sigma
:=\operatorname{Ric}_B-\operatorname{Hess}\sigma-\frac12d\sigma\otimes d\sigma
=-3\gamma_B+\frac12U^*h_{\mathbb H^2}+E_B
\ge-(3+\delta)\gamma_B,
\]
corresponding to effective dimension four on the two-dimensional weighted base [Step 86]. This supports normalized local doubling, Poincaré, and Sobolev estimates on buffered balls, not absolute volume-free constants [Step 86]. The forced superlevel calculation was repaired to include both the main drift-source and cutoff-source terms, with natural root
\[
k_*=3+b_0+\sqrt{(3+b_0)^2+2f_0^2},
\]
so for \(b_0=\delta\), \(f_0=2\delta\),
\[
k_*=6+2\delta+\frac43\delta^2+O(\delta^3)
\]
[Step 86]. This gives coercivity but not a length-independent ceiling without localization of excess [Step 86].

The user proposed a shorter global route: extend controlled outer faces by exact expanding cusp ends and use a massive resolvent on the complete weighted base [Step 87]. Step 87 developed this into a reflection-dependent forced-OT obstruction. Starting from the forced Bochner inequality, with
\[
\kappa=6+2\delta,\qquad f=2\delta,
\]
one obtains
\[
(-L+\kappa)e\le \kappa^2+8\delta^2-2\operatorname{div}_\sigma V
\]
[Step 87]. Under \(CD(-(3+\delta),4)\), the TTCS-corrected Riccati Fisher information bound
\[
I(t)\le \frac{NK}{1-e^{-2Kt}}
\]
replaced a naive long-time estimate that failed on the round cusp [Step 87]. Heat-kernel gradient control and a Duhamel semigroup comparison gave a resolvent constant bounded by
\[
C_\kappa\le \frac{2}{\sqrt{3+\delta}}
\]
[Steps 87–88]. This led to the self-consistent ceiling
\[
B=\sup e
\le
\left[
\frac{4\delta}{\sqrt{3+\delta}}
+\sqrt{2(3+\delta)+\frac{20\delta^2}{3+\delta}}
\right]^2
\]
[Step 87]. Combined with the reflected center floor \(12-8\delta\), this obstructs reflected free-\(T^2\) OT connectors with complete cusp-type extensions for
\[
\delta<\delta_*\approx0.24625
\]
[Step 87]. The result was stored in `workspace/notes/step87_resolvent_obstruction_theorem.md`, with verification scripts and TTCS integration [Step 87]. Its scope was restricted: reflected, free-\(T^2\), orthogonally transitive connectors whose outer faces have the full exact-cusp attachment data needed for complete extension [Step 87].

Step 88 removed reflection using a variational minimal separator in the free-OT two-ended geometry. On a quotient cylinder \(B\) with orbit area \(\rho=e^\sigma\), the volume of an invariant hypersurface over a closed base curve \(C\) is the length of \(C\) in the auxiliary metric \(\rho^2\gamma_B\) [Step 88]. If both ends are exact outward-expanding cusp ends, this auxiliary metric is complete and proper, and lengths in the primitive essential loop class diverge at either end. A shortest primitive representative is therefore a smooth embedded geodesic, whose lift \(\Sigma\) is an invariant minimal \(T^3\) [Step 88]. The outward orientation on both ends is essential; a contracting end lets primitive lengths tend to zero and the infimum escape [Step 88].

For \(E=\operatorname{Ric}+3g\),
\[
D=\operatorname{tr}E-2E(\nu,\nu),
\]
tangential orbit energy \(e_s=|U_s|^2\), and \(h=\sigma_s\), minimality and contracted Gauss give
\[
R_\Sigma=-6+D-|II|^2
\]
[Step 88]. The intrinsic scalar formula for \(ds^2+G(s)\) is
\[
R_\Sigma=-2h_s-\frac32h^2-\frac12e_s.
\]
Periodic weighted integration gives
\[
\langle e_s\rangle
=12-2\langle D\rangle+2\langle|II|^2\rangle+\langle h^2\rangle
\ge12-8\delta
\]
[Step 88]. Since full base energy \(e\) dominates \(e_s\), every such separator forces \(\sup e\ge12-8\delta\) [Step 88]. The Step 87 ceiling uses no reflection input, so the same \(\delta_*\) obstruction applies to complete two-ended free-OT geometries with exact outward cusp ends [Step 88]. Files include `workspace/notes/step88_reflection_free_minimal_separator.md`, `workspace/scripts/step88_minimal_separator_verify.py`, and `workspace/data/step88_minimal_separator_verify.json` [Step 88].

## Twist, variable charge, separator stability, and the collapse of scalar closure attempts [Steps 88–96]

Step 88 observed that the minimal-separator floor survives a free \(T^2\) connection with twist, because restricting a free invariant connection to a one-dimensional base curve is locally gauge-trivial; translation holonomy does not alter the intrinsic scalar formula or reduced measure [Step 88]. Therefore twist can evade the theorem only by changing the upper Bochner/resolvent comparison, not by removing the geometric energy floor [Step 88]. A source-backed note from Liu’s toric Einstein analysis gave a mixed Ricci formula and constant exact twist scalars
\[
\alpha_a=\rho\langle[X,Y/\mu],V_a\rangle
\]
for exact Einstein regions [Step 88]. An exact orthogonally transitive open end forces exact twist to vanish throughout a connected exact Einstein free region, but approximate or merely asymptotic ends retain a weighted twist problem [Steps 88–90].

Step 89 derived the variable-fibre Abelian reduction for a free \(T^2\)-invariant metric
\[
g=\gamma_B+G_{ab}(d\xi^a+A^a)(d\xi^b+A^b),\qquad
G=e^\sigma M,\quad \det M=1.
\]
Using symbolic SymPy computation for
\[
g=e^{2\lambda}(dr^2+dz^2)+e^{\sigma+\alpha}(d\xi_1+Pdz)^2+e^{\sigma-\alpha}d\xi_2^2,
\]
the twist modifications were fixed in the diagonal one-charge model: orbit twist Ricci has factor \(\frac12G_{ac}G_{bd}f^cf^d\), direct base twist Ricci is \(-Q\gamma_B\), the area equation becomes
\[
L\sigma=6+Q,
\]
and the orbit traceless twist forcing satisfies \(|S_F|^2=Q^2\) in the checked normalization [Step 89]. Scripts were saved as `workspace/scripts/step89_symbolic_twist_ricci.py` and `workspace/data/step89_symbolic_twist_ricci.json` [Step 89].

Step 89 initially made a sign-propagation error, concluding that drift curvature worsens to \(-(3+Q)\gamma_B\). TTCS corrected this. The horizontal Einstein equation is
\[
\operatorname{Ric}_B-\operatorname{Hess}\sigma-\frac12d\sigma^2-\frac12A-Q\gamma_B
=-3\gamma_B,
\]
so solving for drift curvature gives
\[
\operatorname{Ric}_B-\operatorname{Hess}\sigma
=(-3+Q)\gamma_B+\frac12d\sigma^2+\frac12A
\]
[Step 89]. A constant-\(Q\) extension of the resolvent calculation suggested a favorable threshold, but Step 90 narrowed it sharply: in the forced variable-charge problem, \(Q_-=\inf Q\), \(Q_+=\sup Q\), and separator average \(Q_C\) govern different estimates and cannot be merged into a constant-\(Q\) parameter [Step 90]. With exact OT ends, \(Q_-=0\), so the available uniform curvature-dimension bound remains \(CD(-(3+\delta),4)\), not an improved one [Step 90]. A spatially varying mass cannot be inserted into the constant-mass Fisher/Beta resolvent calculation without a new variable-potential estimate [Step 90].

Step 90 corrected the treatment of twist as an arbitrary source. For fixed charge \(q\),
\[
Q=\frac12e^{-3\sigma}q^TM^{-1}q
\]
is a positive horospherical function on \(\mathbb H^2\) satisfying
\[
\operatorname{Hess}_{\mathbb H^2}Q=Qh,\qquad |\nabla_{\mathbb H^2}Q|^2=Q^2
\]
[Step 90]. Symbolic calculation established that the vertical traceless equation gives
\[
S_F=-\nabla_{\mathbb H^2}Q
\]
[Step 90]. Consequently
\[
\langle dU,DS_F\rangle=-Qe+3X+R_q,
\]
with
\[
|X|\le|\nabla\sigma|\,Q\sqrt e,\qquad
|R_q|\le\sqrt{2Qe}\,|b|
\]
after a TTCS correction [Step 90]. The \(-Qe\) term cancels pointwise with the \(+Qe\) supplied by the Einstein-solved horizontal drift curvature. Thus twist is not simply favorable; after expansion, its leading linear reaction disappears, leaving area-charge exchange, charge variation, and defect terms as the real difficulty [Step 90].

The mixed Ricci normalization was fixed as
\[
dq=\pm2\rho\,*E_{\rm mix},
\qquad |b|^2=4|E_{\rm mix}|^2_{\rm HS},
\]
so \(\|E\|_{\rm op}\le\delta\) gives \(|b|\le2\sqrt2\,\delta\) [Step 90]. On a round expanding cusp, the physical amplitude
\[
w=e^{-(3\sigma+\alpha)/2}q
\]
obeys
\[
w'+3w=b.
\]
Coordinate charge may change at order \(\delta e^{3r}\), while sustained small forcing can maintain physical twist of order \(\delta\); the earlier statement that accumulated charge necessarily decays like \(e^{-r}\) was corrected [Step 90].

Combining orbit, charge, and area equations without differentiating \(E\) singled out
\[
W=e+2Q+3|\nabla\sigma|^2.
\]
Its first-order exchanges cancel and its flux is \(O(\delta\sqrt W)\), but its zero-order part is not coercive for large \(Q\): at a common critical point compatible with exact second jets, the nonflux contribution is \(54-2Q^2\) [Step 90]. This superseded the Step 89 overclaim that the free-\(T^2\) obstruction theory was substantially complete; approximate twist with sourced charge remained unresolved even with exact cusp ends [Step 90].

Step 90 exposed a concrete local mechanism through a radial charged reduction. In the radial ansatz
\[
\gamma=dr^2+\psi^2d\theta^2,\qquad
M=\operatorname{diag}(e^\alpha,e^{-\alpha}),\qquad q=(q_0,0),
\]
the exact constant-charge equations are
\[
u'=6+Q-u^2-Hu,\qquad
v'=Q-Hv-uv,
\]
\[
K=-3+Q+Hu,\qquad
H'=-K-H^2
\]
[Step 90]. Smooth-center data have
\[
u=\frac{6+Q_0}{2}r+O(r^3),\qquad
v=\frac{Q_0}{2}r+O(r^3),
\]
\[
H=r^{-1}-\frac{Q_0}{2}r+O(r^3),\qquad
K(0)=\frac32Q_0
\]
[Step 90]. Numerical continuations for \(Q_0=0.1,1,3,10,30,100\) all reached \(r=4\), redshifted \(Q\) rapidly, and approached the expanding state
\[
u=2,\qquad v=0,\qquad H=1,\qquad K=-1,\qquad Q=0
\]
[Step 90]. A forced taper experiment with \(|b|=O(\delta)\) succeeded in many radial disk-cap runs with \(\|\operatorname{Ric}+3g\|_{\rm op}<0.925\delta\) [Step 90]. The user then clarified that this radial cylindrical control search should stop: cylindrical \(r\)-levels have intrinsically flat \(T^3\) metrics, so the flat-slice theorem forces \(\delta\ge3/2\) for a passage from \(\mathcal H\to-3\) to \(\mathcal H\to+3\); disk caps avoid the obstruction only because an angular circle collapses [Step 91]. The toral black-hole coordinate change
\[
\phi=\theta+kx
\]
reproduces the charged radial ansatz from \(dr^2+f^2d\phi^2+a^2(dx^2+dy^2)\), showing that large radial \(Q\) partly reflects choice of free torus subgroup rather than a new ambient curvature mechanism [Step 91].

Step 91 established twist-sensitive separator stability. For a stable invariant minimal separator, O’Neill/Koszul formulas show twist contributes exactly \(Q\) to \(|II|^2\), independent of orientation sign [Step 91]. The full invariant second variation later took the form
\[
\int\rho\left(\kappa^2+\tfrac12h_\nu^2+\tfrac12e_\nu+Q\right)\phi^2\,ds
\le
\int\rho\left((\partial_s\phi)^2+(3-E_{\nu\nu})\phi^2\right)\,ds
\]
for every invariant normal speed \(\phi(s)\) [Steps 91–92]. The constant test gives \(Q_C\le3+\delta\), and combining with the scalar identity gives the raised separator floor
\[
\langle e_s\rangle\ge12-8\delta+2Q_C
\]
[Step 91]. An initial Step 91 interpretation that a turning point required positive slice curvature was corrected by the user and Step 92: with
\[
D=\operatorname{tr}E-2E(\nu,\nu),
\]
the correct contracted Gauss identity is
\[
R_\Sigma=-6+D+\mathcal H^2-|II|^2.
\]
At \(\mathcal H=0\), this gives \(R_\Sigma\le -6+4\delta\), not \(R_\Sigma\ge6-4\delta\); \(\mathcal H=0\) must also be kept distinct from \(\partial_r\mathcal H=0\) [Step 92]. The flat-slice barrier survives because \(R_\Sigma=0\) in the flat radial case [Steps 91–92].

Step 92 fused the separator stability form with scalar curvature. Conjugating by \(\phi=\rho^{-1/2}y\) removes the uncontrolled weight and gives an unweighted Schrödinger form with
\[
\mathcal W=\frac34|II|^2+\frac18(h^2+e_s),\qquad
a_\delta=\frac92+\frac32\delta
\]
[Step 92]. Exact square-well models show that stability controls concentrated mass but not pointwise height or a universal length scale [Step 92]. Tangential Maxwell transport combined with this capacity control yields a finite but enormous bound on separator \(\sup_C Q\), independent of separator length and \(\rho\)-oscillation, but it is not \(\delta\)-small and does not control global \(Q_+=\sup_B Q\) [Step 92].

Most importantly, Step 92 converted normal-energy concentration from formal data into exact local geometry. For any positive analytic periodic \(P\), choose a closed immersed curve \(U\subset\mathbb H^2\) with \(|U_s|^2=12+2P\). With \(q=ds^2+M(U(s))\) on \(T^3\), a target unit normal \(N\), and vertical trace-free Weingarten block \(B=\sqrt{P/2}\,M^{-1}dM(N)\), the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints for Einstein constant \(-3\) hold exactly; \(e_\nu=2P\) can spike arbitrarily high while full strict stability remains true for sufficiently concentrated fixed-mass bumps [Step 92]. Koiso’s analytic Cauchy theorem then gives genuine local analytic Einstein germs realizing these data [Step 92]. A charged version in Step 94 chose \(0<S<3\), a periodic hyperbolic target curve with \(|U_s|^2=12+2S\), fixed nonzero charge scaled so \(Q<S\), \(P=S-Q\), vertical block \(B=\sqrt{P/2}M^{-1}dM(N)\), and mixed Weingarten covector \(m=-q/2\) at \(\rho=1\). The complete block has \(\operatorname{tr}W=0\), \(\operatorname{tr}(W^2)=S\), scalar curvature \(-6-S\), all Hamiltonian and momentum constraints, and full Jacobi form \(\int(|\nabla\phi|^2+(3-S)\phi^2)\); Koiso gives local analytic Ricci \(-3g\) germs with nonzero conserved twist and stable minimal \(T^3\) for \(0<S<3\) [Step 94]. This proved that no separator-local argument, even using full stability and exact local Einstein constraints, can bound normal orbit energy or separator charge pointwise; any obstruction must use a collar or both ends [Steps 92–94].

Step 93 derived the exact fixed-charge diagonal identity
\[
LQ=\frac{|\nabla Q|^2}{Q}-18Q-4Q^2,
\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
L\log Q=-18-4Q
\]
in the charge-aligned diagonal model [Step 93]. It was initially overinterpreted as a maximum-principle obstruction. The user corrected this in Step 94: for \(L=\Delta+\nabla\sigma\cdot\nabla\), \(LQ<0\) at an interior maximum is compatible with the maximum principle, and scalar ODE solutions \(y''=-18-4e^y\) with \(Q=e^y\) have positive interior maxima and decay to zero at both infinities [Step 94]. The Step 93 boundary-maximum inference, \(Q=O(\delta^2)\) prediction, and purported independent recovery of the OT obstruction were withdrawn [Step 94]. Exact OT open ends still force zero charge in a connected exact Einstein region by the separate conservation law \(dq=0\), not by \(Q\to0\), since physical \(Q\) can decay by redshift with nonzero coordinate charge [Step 94].

Step 94 extended the fixed-charge calculation invariantly. For
\[
F(U)=\frac12q^TM(U)^{-1}q,\qquad \beta=\log F,
\]
one has
\[
\operatorname{Hess}_{\mathbb H^2}\beta=h-d\beta\otimes d\beta,\qquad |\nabla\beta|=1
\]
[Step 94]. Combining \(\tau_\sigma(U)=-Q\nabla\beta\), \(L\sigma=6+Q\), and \(Q=e^{-3\sigma}F(U)\) yields
\[
L\log Q=-18-4Q+e-|d(\beta\circ U)|^2.
\]
The final term is nonnegative transverse orbit energy and vanishes only in the charge-aligned diagonal reduction [Step 94]. Thus even the sign of \(L\log Q\) at a critical point is not controlled in general fixed-charge geometry [Step 94]. Variable-charge logarithmic formulas are singular at charge zeros and require care at exact OT ends [Step 94].

Step 94 also constructed a smooth two-ended redshift-taper family that satisfies the Maxwell and area equations and both exact OT charge end values while keeping separator \(Q=1/2\). Delaying a fixed-width charge taper to distance \(R\) makes the physical source \(\|b\|_\infty\) decay like \(e^{-3\sqrt6 R/2}\), while the weighted charge/source ratio grows like \(e^{2\sqrt6 R}\) [Step 94]. The exact first integral
\[
(\rho')^2=6\rho^2-\rho^{-1}-5
\]
explains the rates [Step 94]. This family is not a reduced Einstein connector because freezing \(M\) violates the orbit equation and the horizontal equation is omitted; it isolates precisely which equations must carry any remaining cost [Step 94].

The invariant horizontal compatibility identity was then derived:
\[
2\operatorname{div}_\sigma H-d\operatorname{tr}H
=
-dT-Td\sigma-\langle Z,dU\rangle-m_q
\]
[Step 94]. Its radial specialization recovers
\[
C'=-2(u+h)C-wb,
\]
so the Step 90 second terminal moment is the invariant charge-work term, not a radial accident [Step 94]. For \(A=e^{-3\sigma}M^{-1}\), \(Q=\frac12q^TAq\), and \(m_q=q^TAdq\), Step 95 incorporated the user’s charge-work quadratic identity:
\[
\int m_q(X)\,d\mu_\sigma
=-\frac12\int q^TK_Xq\,d\mu_\sigma,\qquad
K_X=X(A)+(\operatorname{div}_\sigma X)A
\]
for end-supported vector fields \(X\) with \(q=0\) on outer collars [Step 95]. This separates source freedom from geometric freedom: changing the sign of the mixed source does not by itself cancel a signed \(K_X\) contribution. However, Step 96 clarified that for compactly supported \(X\) and fixed coordinate charge,
\[
\frac12c^TK_Xc=\operatorname{div}_\sigma(QX),
\]
so its integral vanishes algebraically by charge conservation; compactly supported \(X\) gives a null diagnostic, not an independent obstruction [Step 96]. A useful field must arise from an adjoint problem spanning the center and both ends, with coefficient growth measured on the same degenerating geometry [Step 96].

Step 95 also briefly claimed that the OT resolvent ceiling applied unchanged to charged connectors because \(+Qe\) in drift curvature was favorable. TTCS refuted this: the twist tension derivative contributes
\[
\langle dU,D(-Q\nabla\beta)\rangle=-Qe+3Q\langle\nabla\sigma,d(\beta\circ U)\rangle,
\]
cancelling the \(+Qe\) from drift curvature. The net twist Bochner contribution is
\[
3Q\langle\nabla\sigma,d(\beta\circ U)\rangle,
\]
which in the diagonal constant-charge case is \(-3Q\langle\nabla\alpha,\nabla\sigma\rangle\) and has no fixed sign [Step 95]. The charged obstruction theorem and any import of the Step 87 ceiling to variable-charge geometry were withdrawn [Step 95].

Step 96 rejected another proposed radial cylindrical BVP: curving only the two-dimensional base \(dr^2+\phi(r)^2dz^2\) leaves radial level \(T^3\) metrics intrinsically flat when all coefficients depend only on \(r\), so the \(\delta\ge3/2\) flat-slice barrier already excludes that model [Step 96]. It also removed unsupported premises that a general minimal separator has \(\nabla\sigma=0\), that \(L\sigma\ge6\) bounds transition diameter, or that an exterior subdomain inherits the complete-base resolvent ceiling despite entrance data [Step 96].

The correct object became the spatially varying charged Koiso center. In Gaussian form \(g=dn^2+q(n,s)\), with \(K=q_n/2\), \(W=q^{-1}K\), and \(H=\operatorname{tr}W\), the exact Einstein Cauchy system is
\[
q_n=2K,\qquad
K_n=\operatorname{Ric}(q)+3q-HK+2Kq^{-1}K,
\]
with constraints
\[
R(q)-H^2+|W|^2=-6,\qquad \operatorname{div}K-dH=0
\]
[Step 96]. Symbolic matrix calculations recovered the momentum equations and cancellation of vertical connection terms [Step 96]. From exact center data \(H=0\), \(|W|^2=S\), \(R(q_\Sigma)=-6-S\), one obtains the Taylor structure
\[
H_n=3-S,\qquad
a_{nn}=-3-S-Q(s),\qquad
\sigma_{nn}=6+Q(s)
\]
[Step 96]. Thus for \(0<S<3\) the strictly stable charged separator initially expands in both outward directions while separating base-circle contraction and orbit-area expansion; this is how true two-variable geometry evades the radial flat-slice model [Step 96]. A short Fourier method-of-lines evolution to \(n=0.02\) matched these Taylor formulas but was explicitly only local analytic evidence; Gaussian Einstein evolution is elliptically ill-posed and gives no complete collar [Step 96].

Step 96 formulated the gauge-fixed global residual map on a two-ended quotient cylinder in conformal base coordinates:
\[
\mathcal E=(H,T,Z,B_{\rm mix}),
\]
where \(H\) is the horizontal tensor residual, \(T=L\sigma-6-Q\) the area residual, \(Z=\tau_\sigma(U)+\nabla_UQ\) the orbit-map residual, and \(B_{\rm mix}=e^{-3\sigma/2}M^{-1/2}dq\) the first-order charge block [Step 96]. The scalar/map principal block has determinant \(-2|\xi|^8\); with the two first-order charge blocks, the overdetermined Gram determinant is \(4|\xi|^{20}\) and the generic symbol has full rank six [Step 96]. This injective Douglis–Nirenberg principal symbol does not by itself establish Fredholmness or a finite cokernel; boundary conditions, weights, Bianchi redundancy, and compatibility spaces remain to be determined [Steps 96–97]. A first round-cusp indicial calculation for \(\gamma=y^{-2}(dy^2+ds^2)\), \(\sigma=-2\log y\), constant \(U\), and zero background charge found scalar roots \(-1,0,3\), orbit roots \(0,3\), and a constant-coordinate-charge mode whose mixed Ricci norm is redshifted by three powers of \(y\) while horizontal contribution \(Q\) is quadratic and redshifted by six powers [Step 96]. This identified a possible end-escaping near-kernel but not its compatibility with the charged center or both ends [Step 96].

## Full-matrix matching, exterior benchmarks, and finite-length floors [Steps 97–99]

Step 97 attempted to develop the two-ended matching problem through trial metrics and initially presented an “orbit-shape conformal dilution mechanism” as a breakthrough. Several trial phases were explored: a sigmoid interpolation from Koiso center fields to an expanding round cusp; a radial backbone ODE for area/base variables; a Taylor-center trial using Koiso jets; and a Gaussian-cusp orbit equation analysis [Step 97]. The useful observation was that for a warped exterior
\[
g=dn^2+\cosh^2(n)q_\Sigma,
\]
the exact warped-product formulas give
\[
E_{nn}=0,\qquad E_{nT}=0,\qquad
E_T^\sharp=\operatorname{sech}^2(n)\bigl(\operatorname{Ric}(q_\Sigma)^\sharp+2I\bigr)
\]
[Steps 97–98]. Thus tangential defect from fixed slice geometry decays like \(e^{-2n}\) in the expanding exterior [Steps 97–98]. This is a useful exterior benchmark, related to the earlier Step 73 expanding-tail mechanism, but it is not a connector construction [Step 98].

The user and Step 98 corrected the Step 97 interpretation. The supremum of the cosh trial occurs at \(n=0\) and is unchanged by extending the ends; \(K(0)=0\) irrespective of off-diagonal entries in \(q_\Sigma\), so it cannot retain the charged Koiso Weingarten data [Step 98]. Inserting the correct \(q_\Sigma\) does not insert charge [Step 98]. Even the pure cosh class cannot approach zero defect on \(T^3\): if
\[
\|\operatorname{Ric}(q_\Sigma)^\sharp+2I\|<2/3,
\]
the three-dimensional Ricci-to-sectional formula makes every sectional curvature negative, contradicting Preissmann [Step 98]. The Step 97 principal script also replaced the full orbit matrix by a diagonal matrix extracted from its entries, removing genuine orbit-shape geometry; it omitted normal–tangential Ricci components and used a coordinate Euclidean symmetrization instead of the invariant generalized eigenvalue/operator norm [Step 98]. Its orbit roots \(0,-2\), conjugate-point interpretation, and coordinate-repair conclusion were withdrawn. The correct round-cusp orbit equation is
\[
\alpha_{nn}+3\alpha_n+e^{-2n}\alpha_{ss}=0
\]
with radial roots \(0\) and \(-3\) [Step 98]. Minimality does not imply \(U_n=0\) for the charged center, and loss of positivity of a quadratic Taylor truncation near \(0.47\) proves neither a conjugate point nor smooth continuation of the exact Einstein germ [Step 98].

Step 98 then built the full-matrix representation needed for meaningful matching. With charged Koiso center data \(q_0(s),K_0(s)\),
\[
S_0=q_0^{1/2},\qquad A=S_0^{-1}K_0S_0^{-1},\qquad \widehat R=S_0^{-1}\operatorname{Ric}(q_0)S_0^{-1},
\]
each half-cylinder is represented by
\[
q=S_0\exp(X)S_0.
\]
The center conditions
\[
X=0,\qquad X_r=\pm2A,\qquad X_{rr}=2(\widehat R+3I)
\]
give
\[
q_r=\pm2K_0,\qquad
q_{rr}=2(\operatorname{Ric}(q_0)+3q_0+2K_0q_0^{-1}K_0),
\]
because \(d^2\exp(X)/dr^2|_{X=0}=X_{rr}+X_r^2\); no commutativity assumption is used and the sign disappears in \(X_r^2\) [Step 98]. Matrix exponentiation preserves positive definiteness and retains all orbit and mixed directions [Step 98]. Analytic center jet residuals were below \(8.6\times10^{-14}\) [Step 98].

All ten components of
\[
E=\operatorname{Ric}+3g
\]
were assembled in Gaussian coordinates:
\[
E_{rr}=3-\operatorname{tr}(q^{-1}K_r)+\operatorname{tr}(W^2),
\]
\[
E_{ri}=q^{jk}\nabla_jK_{ki}-\partial_iH,
\]
\[
E_{ij}=\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{ij}+3q_{ij}-(K_r)_{ij}-HK_{ij}+2(Kq^{-1}K)_{ij}
\]
[Step 98]. Cholesky conjugation \(E_{\rm orth}=L^{-1}EL^{-T}\), where \(g=LL^T\), computes generalized eigenvalues \(Ev=\lambda gv\) and hence the invariant pinching norm [Step 98]. A flat-slice hyperbolic test \(q=e^{2r}I\) had residual below \(4.2\times10^{-12}\) in the principal run [Step 98]. The constrained center residual test showed that normal and tangential center blocks are at roundoff, while the mixed Codazzi block decreases rapidly with Fourier resolution, from \(1.3634\) at \(N_s=16\) to \(6.76\times10^{-6}\) at \(N_s=128\); coarse center maxima are Fourier underresolution, not geometric lower bounds [Step 98].

A single quintic joining exact center jets to an expanding attachment stayed positive but created a large inner tangential residual: at \(N_s=64\), \(n_r=35\), \(R=2.5\), the positive and negative halves had suprema \(970.66\) and \(99.57\) [Step 98]. A more flexible direct nodal experiment at \(n_r=11\), \(N_s=16\), \(R=1\) reduced two interior packed residual norms from \(260.21\) to \(8.90\) and from \(137.10\) to \(8.22\), with joint norm \(294.12\) to \(12.12\) [Step 98]. This demonstrated discrete compensability by genuine full-matrix directions, but not a continuous connector: endpoint derivative arrays were overwritten rather than produced by the represented field, coefficients were not saved for refinement, nonlinear products were not dealiased, the regularizer was non-negligible, and the final coarse maximum \(1.3634\) matched the \(N_s=16\) center Codazzi resolution error [Step 98]. The current matching standard became: build a resolution-continuable analytic jet-preserving representation, evaluate derivatives from the field itself, save coefficients, refine on independent grids, and track every Ricci block and residual projection [Step 98].

Step 99 applied the normal focusing balance as a quantitative control on these matching experiments. On either outward Gaussian half, with
\[
\mathcal H=\operatorname{tr}W,\qquad W^\circ=W-\frac{\mathcal H}{3}I,
\]
every represented metric satisfies
\[
\mathcal H'=3-\frac{\mathcal H^2}{3}-|W^\circ|^2-E_{rr}.
\]
With a prescribed minimal center \(\mathcal H(0)=0\) and exact expanding attachment \(\mathcal H(R)=3\), a trial with \(\|E\|_{\rm op}\le\delta\) must obey
\[
1\le k\tanh(kR),\qquad k=\sqrt{1+\delta/3}.
\]
At \(R=1\) this already forces \(\delta\gtrsim1.318\), and for large \(R\) the necessary floor is asymptotic to \(12e^{-2R}\) [Step 99]. Thus fixed-\(R\) refinement cannot drive defect to zero; radius continuation is mathematically necessary, not merely a numerical convenience [Step 99].

Step 99 also derived the exact weighted normal-block projection. With
\[
u=\mathcal H-3\tanh r,
\]
\[
\int_0^R\cosh^2r\,(-E_{rr})\,dr
=
3\cosh^2R(1-\tanh R)
+
\int_0^R\cosh^2r\left(|W^\circ|^2+\frac{u^2}{3}\right)dr
\]
[Step 99]. The first term is the endpoint cost and the second measures additional shear and mean-curvature mismatch generated by the actual transition [Step 99]. This is an adjoint-weighted projection with known meaning; it should be evaluated on the same continuous fields as the full residual to distinguish compulsory normal cost from tangential/mixed failure or node-hiding [Step 99].

Tangential residual then emerged as the dominant inner cost in the current trial family. For the quintic transition on \([0,1]\), the \(E_T\) decomposition showed spatial curvature \(\operatorname{Ric}(q)\) peaking around \(21.4\), followed by \(-K_r\), \(-HK\), and \(2Kq^{-1}K\); total \(E_T\) peak was about \(28.7\), roughly three times the normal block \(E_{rr}\approx10.7\) [Step 99]. Optimization of one intermediate \(X(r_t)\) and added radial modes gave only about \(1.2\times\) improvement [Step 99]. Segmented inner-quintic plus exact exterior trials confirmed that the inner transition dominates and may worsen with longer transition length, while exterior terms decay as expected [Step 99]. TTCS confirmed there is no tangential Raychaudhuri analogue with a positive-definite integrand, but if \(E_T\equiv0\) then contracted Bianchi and constraint propagation imply full \(E\equiv0\); any finite-\(R\) connector must have tangential residual somewhere [Step 99].

The largest Step 99 route change came from a Chern–Gauss–Bonnet Ricci pinching floor for closed four-manifolds with \(\chi=0\). On any closed oriented four-manifold with \(\chi=0\), the Chern–Gauss–Bonnet identity gives
\[
\int|\operatorname{Ric}^\circ|^2
=
2\int|W|^2+\frac1{12}\int s^2.
\]
If
\[
\|\operatorname{Ric}-\Lambda g\|_{\rm op}\le\delta,
\]
then \(|\operatorname{Ric}^\circ|^2\le4\delta^2\) and \(|s|\ge4(|\Lambda|-\delta)\). Since \(|W|^2\ge0\), one obtains
\[
\delta\ge \frac{|\Lambda|}{1+\sqrt3}.
\]
For \(\Lambda=-3\),
\[
\delta\ge \frac{3}{1+\sqrt3}=\frac{3(\sqrt3-1)}2\approx1.098.
\]
[Step 99]. For a connector inside a closed \(\chi=0\) graph-type manifold, a volume absorption calculation gives
\[
\left(4\delta^2-\frac43(3-\delta)^2\right)\operatorname{Vol}_{\rm conn}
\ge12\operatorname{Vol}_{\rm cusps},
\]
so the connector defect must be strictly above the same \(1.098\) threshold when cusp regions are present [Step 99]. This floor is sharp at \(|W|=0\) and is the same Chern–Weil structure as the early \(2\chi>3|\tau|\) filter, now used as a universal pointwise lower bound on \(\chi=0\) targets [Step 99]. For \(\chi<0\) the bound strengthens; for \(\chi>0\) it weakens or disappears [Step 99].

This changed the graph-manifold connector subproblem: on \(\chi=0\) closed targets, the goal is not \(\delta\to0\) near \(\operatorname{Ric}=-3g\), which CGB forbids, but whether one can construct metrics approaching the finite CGB-compatible threshold \(\delta\approx1.098\) or enough pinching for the original interval analysis [Step 99]. The current full-matrix quintic residual around \(28.7\) remains far above that target, and the cosh exterior benchmark reaches \(1.098\) only after sufficient expansion; the difficult interval is still the inner transition from charged Koiso center toward an expanded region [Step 99]. For \(\chi>0\) alternatives such as surface bundles or hyperbolic connected sums, the CGB floor is less restrictive, but those routes lack graph-manifold all-sign Einstein nonexistence or lack a construction [Steps 84–85,99].

## Hyperbolic connected sums, graph topology, and other negative-side candidates [Steps 84–99]

The \(N\#N\) route remains complementary to graph-manifold \(T^2\)-neck work. Reading Besson–Courtois–Gallot/Bessières, Kotschick, LeBrun, and Sambusetti sources led to a provisional quantitative calculation for a hyperbolic four-manifold \(N\). If \(M=N\#N\), \(\chi=\chi(N)\), \(V_N=4\pi^2\chi/3\), and \(\|\operatorname{Ric}+3g\|_{\rm op}\le\delta\), then BCG plus Chern–Gauss–Bonnet compatibility gives
\[
\chi(8\delta+2\delta^2)\ge6+4\delta+\frac23\delta^2,
\]
so \(\delta\) is asymptotically at least \(3/(4\chi)\) [Step 84]. This explains a natural scale but does not construct a sequence; increasing cover volume alone cannot dilute an operator-norm defect in a surgery region [Steps 84–85]. The connected-sum interface is \(S^3\), not \(T^3\), so free-\(T^2\) periodic identities do not transfer directly [Step 85].

A02’s warped waist barrier \(\delta\ge3/2\) for warped-product turnarounds with nonnegative fiber curvature was absorbed as an independent obstruction to a large subclass [Steps 85–87]. Orbifold+ALE candidates were narrowed by Chern–Weil neutrality, and A02’s later high-dimensional comments confirmed that known negative-Einstein obstructions currently rely on four-dimensional Chern–Gauss–Bonnet/\(\Lambda^2\)-splitting mechanisms rather than transferable higher-dimensional tools [Steps 87–89]. The active free-\(T^2\) frontier after Step 99 is no longer a local regularity or scalar maximum-principle question. Exact local charged Koiso germs, stable separators, redshift tapers, and exterior conformal decay all show substantial local flexibility, while flat-slice, exact OT, complete-end Bochner, and CGB floors show substantial global restrictions [Steps 88–99]. The decisive object is a shared-parameter, two-variable, full-matrix matching problem: can one preserve a charged Koiso center, pass through an inner transition with all ten Ricci blocks controlled in invariant norm, discharge/attach to both ends, and satisfy horizontal charge-work and Bianchi compatibility; or does a genuine adjoint projection or topological identity impose a nonzero lower cost beyond the known Raychaudhuri and CGB floors [Steps 94–99]?

The positive branch has remained independent and unresolved. Tight positive Ricci pinching plus noncollapse gives strong compactness and finiteness tools, but collapse is compatible with Einstein manifolds, as lens spaces illustrate [Steps 4–9]. No closed manifold is currently established in this session to carry positive Ricci while provably carrying no Einstein metric [Steps 64,67,90,99]. Sha–Yang gives positive Ricci on \(\#_k(S^2\times S^2)\), while arbitrary Einstein existence is already open for small \(k\), including \(k=2,3\) [Step 67].

Peer sessions investigated positive orbifold desingularization, mixed chirality, Green responses, Ozuch/Biquard coefficients, and higher obstruction maps [Steps 77–99]. Same-chirality constructions were checked against known Kähler–Einstein results, but the mixed-chirality topology \(\#_3(S^2\times S^2)\) has \(b_+=3\) and cannot admit a positive Kähler–Einstein metric; any Einstein construction there must be genuinely non-Kähler [Steps 77–78]. A01 withdrew a proposed positive-side Green-response positivity after identifying a negative TT mode and singular self-pairings; later peer updates reframed the positive target as tensor-sector \(Q\)-channel responses \(q_{\rm diag}\) and \(q_{\rm adj}\) with pole-dependent weights and determinant degeneracy, not the earlier scalar mixed-chirality interpretation [Steps 82,90].

These positive-side threads currently prove neither a counterexample nor a universal positive-branch theorem [Steps 73–99].

Higher dimensions remain much less developed. Four-dimensional Chern–Weil, Seiberg–Witten, graph-manifold, \(T^2\to\mathbb H^2\), and Step 99 CGB floor mechanisms do not directly transfer [Steps 2–99]. Kaluza–Klein collapse and product examples show that collapse alone is not decisive, while corrected slice-cascade arguments do not identify a universal first open dimension [Steps 2–67]. ### Research Line

The session began by protecting the exact logical form of Yau Problem 26. The agents split the problem into positive and negative normalized branches, recorded the same-smooth-manifold output quantifier as the central trap, and treated \(n=2,3\) as separate baselines rather than templates for \(n\ge4\) [Steps 1, 10]. The first sustained negative route used four-dimensional gauge/topological obstructions. Ishida–LeBrun manifolds were attractive because they are known to exclude all Einstein metrics under appropriate topological hypotheses. After the user corrected the missing gradient term in a pure \(W^+\) idea, the line shifted to the mixed scalar–Weyl inequality and near-critical Chern–Weil profiles [Steps 2-3, 29-30]. This turned the problem from a straightforward compactness theorem into a collapse/extraction problem [Steps 3-6].

Collapse model work then served mainly to remove false assumptions. Abelian, nil, Taub–NUT–AdS, Pontryagin, static, and toric calculations revealed local mechanisms and pitfalls, but all relied on symmetry or cover assumptions absent from arbitrary pinched metrics. The research line moved to a smoothing/extraction mechanism on the original manifold [Steps 7-13]. The transported-cutoff Ricci flow was selected after the user’s small-radius \(r^4\) correction because it preserves the closed manifold and fixes exact negative Einstein metrics [Steps 13-15].

From Steps 15-61, the cutoff-flow program grew through repeated corrections. Localized Li estimates and fixed-cutoff formulations failed, so the architecture became transported cutoffs, weighted moments, shifted curvature \(T=\mathrm{Rm}+G\), \(U=aT\), signed Hessian integration by parts, exact defect bookkeeping, and first-exit estimates [Steps 15-46]. By Step 61 the Ishida–LeBrun module was coherent but restricted. The session then reassessed quantifier-level routes. Anderson’s sectional-pinching theorem, provisionally accepted with caveats, suggested that sufficiently tight negative sectional pinching already gives negative Einstein metrics, so the hard regime is Ricci-only pinching with unbounded Weyl/sectional curvature and collapse [Steps 62-64]. Several four-dimensional torus and Chern–Weil detours sharpened the landscape. The positive branch stayed separate throughout this period. Product arguments, Kähler obstructions, and local Ozuch calculations were repeatedly prevented from being overread as same-manifold Einstein nonexistence. Recent peer messages shifted the positive-side target toward tensor-sector \(Q\)-channel responses with pole-dependent weights and determinant degeneracy, requiring the actual ALE source structure rather than scalar mixed-chirality heuristics [Steps 73, 77-81, 87-90]. No positive-branch proof or disproof has been obtained.

The current state of the full project is open. The restricted Ishida–LeBrun flow module remains a deep possible theorem but not a global answer. The graph-manifold negative route has produced strong reusable infrastructure: tail construction, Koiso-center and center-energy identities, exact and forced OT Bochner formulas, effective weighted geometry, minimal-separator lower bounds, and refined twist/Maxwell equations [Steps 63-90]. Within free-OT complete extensions, exact and small-forced low-energy connectors are obstructed; within forced twist, a two-ended charged-throat matching problem remains unresolved [Steps 85-90]. Outside that class, approximate twist with full matching, singular \(T^2\) orbits, diffuse non-OT graph metrics, and \(S^3\)-neck \(N\#N\) constructions remain live negative routes. The positive branch and higher-dimensional no-Einstein/topological obstruction questions also remain unresolved. No final proof, disproof, dimension-only constants, fixed-dimensional two-sign counterexample, or Lean formalization has been reached [Steps 1-90].
