This corrected an earlier overstrong disproof criterion and became the standing guardrail against local or metric-nearby arguments: proving that a particular input metric has no nearby Einstein metric cannot refute the problem if the same smooth manifold has an unrelated Einstein metric elsewhere in metric space [Steps 1–2]. The desingularized football orbifold yielding \(S^2\times S^2\), which does carry a product Einstein metric, remained the canonical warning example [Step 1].

Early local-flexibility and gluing routes were filtered by this quantifier discipline. A high-frequency Ricci-flexibility idea on a flat background was abandoned after computing

## Four-dimensional Chern–Weil, Ishida–LeBrun near-saturation, and the calibrated germ obstruction [Steps 2–6, 29–30, 43, 61, 65]

The research moved early to dimension four because Chern–Weil formulas, Hitchin–Thorpe, Seiberg–Witten theory, and LeBrun/Ishida–LeBrun inequalities link Ricci pinching to topology [Step 2]. Scripts and notes such as `verify_chern_weil_pinching.py`, `critical_compatibility_model.py`, and `step2_quantitative_4d_analysis.tex` checked constants and candidate families [Step 2].

A stable basic result was established: if
\[
\|\operatorname{Ric}-\Lambda g\|_{\rm op}\le\delta|\Lambda|,
\qquad
\delta<(\sqrt3-1)/2,
\]
then Chern–Gauss–Bonnet and signature identities force \(2\chi>3|\tau|\) [Step 2]. This gives a cheap absolute exclusion class for tight pinching of either sign, including every closed four-manifold with \(2\chi\le3|\tau|\), but does not address all no-Einstein manifolds or dimension-only constants [Steps 2,65]. A Step 64 suggestion that a \(\mu_4\) slice invariant was unknown was corrected in Step 65 by exactly this Chern–Weil estimate: at nonzero normalization, flat four-torus type slices have a positive lower bound, and the Weyl term appears on the forced-positive side rather than absorbing the discrepancy [Steps 64–65]. Step 67 later clarified that this is a nonzero-normalization lower bound, not a Ricci-flat coercivity statement [Step 67].

For LeBrun no-Einstein families \(X\#k\overline{\mathbb{CP}}^{\,2}\), an initial uniform negative-branch gap claim was withdrawn after rereading Ishida–LeBrun and a user correction: the derivation had illegally dropped a negative gradient term in the self-dual Weitzenböck formula, and \(F_A^+\) is not generally harmonic [Steps 2–3]. The valid interface became Ishida–LeBrun Theorem 7 for
\[
M=(\#_{j=1}^m X_j)\#N,\qquad m=2\text{ or }3,
\]
with
\[
A=\sum c_1^2(X_j),\qquad D=4m-(2\chi+3\tau)(N),
\]
excluding Einstein metrics when \(D\ge A/3\) under the relevant Bauer–Furuta/SW and \(b_+(N)=0\) hypotheses [Step 3]. Step 61’s source review confirmed Theorem D excludes every Einstein metric, not just metrics with a prescribed Einstein constant, under those hypotheses [Step 61].

The equality case \(D=A/3\) became the critical testbed. Assuming a hypothetical sequence on a fixed critical Ishida–LeBrun manifold with \(\delta_i=\|\operatorname{Ric}_{g_i}+g_i\|_\infty\to0\), Chern–Weil analysis gave \(|s_i+4|\le4\delta_i\), \(\operatorname{Ric}^\circ_i=O(\delta_i)\), fixed-topology volume convergence, and \(\int|\operatorname{Ric}^\circ_i|^2\to0\) [Step 3]. Completing squares in the genuine mixed scalar–Weyl inequality produced the calibrated Weyl profile
\[
\int\left(|W_i^+|-\frac1{2\sqrt6}\right)^2\,d\mu_i
=O(A\delta_i^2)
\]
[Steps 3–4]. This showed ordinary negative Kähler–Einstein regions, with \(|W^+|=2/\sqrt6\), and scalar-flat connectors are both far from the calibrated value and cannot occupy positive-volume bulk in a near-saturating critical sequence [Step 4].

The local obstruction then became the central reusable endpoint. If a near-saturating sequence contains a regular noncollapsed local limit, elliptic regularity forces a smooth Einstein-scale patch with
\[
\operatorname{Ric}=-g,\qquad s=-4,\qquad
\operatorname{Spec}(W^+)=(-1/6,1/12,1/12)
\]
[Step 5]. A sign-sensitive Derdziński shortcut was replaced by a direct projector computation: on an oriented Einstein four-manifold with \(W^+\) having one simple and one double constant eigenvalue, \(\delta W^+=0\) forces the corresponding two-form line to be parallel and hence \(\nabla W^+=0\); the Einstein–Weyl identity
\[
\Delta|W^+|^2=2|\nabla W^+|^2+s|W^+|^2-36\det W^+
\]
then gives a contradiction for the calibrated spectrum [Step 6]. This established that any argument extracting a smooth calibrated Einstein germ kills the near-saturating sequence [Steps 5–6].

Step 29 extended the algebra beyond exact criticality by retaining \(\sigma=D-A/3\ge0\), producing defect identities \(D_a\le R-\sigma\le R\) and an unconditional lower bound \(\delta\gtrsim\sqrt{\sigma/A}\) for strictly supercritical families [Step 29]. Step 30 clarified that escaping families must have \(\sigma_i/A_i\to0\); near-critical but strictly supercritical families still require the analytic machinery [Step 30]. Step 43 later supplied a terminal LeBrun spectral density bound,
\[
\int G_{\rm spec}\le6Q+48\pi^2(-q_{\rm top})_+,
\]
and for
\[
\mathfrak D=|E|^2+(s+4)^2+(s+8\sqrt6|W^+|)^2+G_{\rm spec},
\]
\[
\int\mathfrak D\le119Q+912\pi^2(-q_{\rm top})_+
\]
[Step 43]. This became the terminal chart density input for the restricted Ishida–LeBrun module.

## Collapse, covers, Taub–NUT, and reduced symmetry lessons [Steps 6–16]

Once noncollapsed calibrated patches were excluded, the work shifted to collapse: Naber–Zhang, Huang–Wang, Rong, Jiang–Kong–Xu, and Lott’s reduced Einstein equations were examined to see whether local covers in maximal nilpotency-rank regions could unwrap collapse and recover the forbidden germ [Steps 6–8]. A key correction was that defect transfer to covers is a normalized-local-average problem, not an absolute-integral problem [Steps 6–8]. Step 8 proved a normal-cover mean-transport lemma,
\[
\fint_{B_r(\hat p)}\pi^*\phi
\le
\frac{V_{-K}^{(n)}(3r)}{V_{-K}^{(n)}(r)}
\fint_{B_r(p)}\phi,
\]
using a Borel section, disjoint deck translates, and Bishop–Gromov comparison [Step 8]. The resulting theorem was conditional: low-dimensional GH models, maximal nilpotency rank, a nondegenerate model noncollapse radius, and small normalized local deficit on the base would force the forbidden germ on a lifted chart; it remained open whether near-saturation supplies such geometry or whether rank-drop regions carry most volume [Step 8].

Exact abelian and nilpotent symmetry models clarified what can and cannot be excluded. Lott’s orbit-volume equation
\[
\Delta_Bv=\left(\frac{|F|^2}{4}-\lambda N\right)v,\qquad \lambda=-1,
\]
gives a positive zero-order term excluding some pure collapsed regular models by maximum principle [Steps 6–8]. In the nil\(^3\)/Heisenberg cohomogeneity-one case, a sign was corrected:

## Return to the full quantifiers: graph manifolds, entropy, and the neck problem [Steps 62–66]

Step 62 reopened the full quantifier-level question after recognizing that the Ishida–LeBrun route succeeds, if it succeeds, because its topological density is localizable: a retained chart forces a calibrated Einstein germ and contradiction. A general Einstein obstruction may instead evacuate topology into shrinking regions while every regular chart has admissible Einstein geometry [Step 62]. The counterexample quantifiers were sharpened: refuting a sign branch in fixed dimension requires no-Einstein manifolds with normalized \(\|\operatorname{Ric}\mp g\|_\infty\to0\); full disproof requires both signs in one dimension, possibly on different manifolds [Step 62].

Literature review found Brendle–Kapouleas compact ancient-flow examples on a fixed Eguchi–Hanson desingularization with \(\sup|\operatorname{Ric}|\to0\) and \(\sup|\operatorname{Rm}|\to\infty\), illustrating topology/curvature concentration but without Einstein exclusion [Step 62]. Kapovitch–Lott’s noncollapsed almost Ricci-flat topology results showed the complementary phenomenon: if the regular noncollapsed geometry is controlled, the manifold often reconstructs Ricci-flat topology, so uncontrolled information lives in collapse [Step 62]. Anderson’s 2003 preprint, later supported in part by Hamenstädt–Jäckel for Gromov–Thurston manifolds, was internally assessed as closing sectionally pinched counterexample routes, but its preprint status and hypotheses remained flagged as non-load-bearing until independently certified [Steps 62–64].

Extended graph four-manifolds became the most concrete negative counterexample candidates because Di Cerbo excludes all Einstein metrics and the pieces are assembled from hyperbolic cusp geometries [Step 62]. A scalar warped double-cusp model \(dr^2+f(r)^2g_{T^3}\) with \(u=f'/f\) showed
\[
\operatorname{Ric}_{rr}=-3(u'+u^2),\qquad
\operatorname{Ric}_{\tan}=-(u'+3u^2),
\]
so \(\|\operatorname{Ric}+3g\|_{\rm op}\le\delta\) forces \(|u^2-1|\le2\delta/3\), preventing cusp orientation reversal for \(\delta<3/2\) [Step 62]. Step 63 generalized this to every \(g=dr^2+G(r)\) with intrinsically flat \(T^3\) slices. With \(S=\frac12G^{-1}G'\), \(H=\operatorname{tr}S\), the traced Gauss equation gives
\[
H^2-\operatorname{tr}(S^2)=-(R_g-2\operatorname{Ric}(\partial_r,\partial_r)),
\]
and pinching near \(-3g\) plus \(\operatorname{tr}(S^2)\ge H^2/3\) yields
\[
H^2\ge9-6\delta.
\]
Thus any flat-slice collar requiring \(H\) to pass through zero is impossible for small \(\delta\), including diagonal, anisotropic, off-diagonal, and noncommuting \(G(r)\) models [Steps 63,67]. Step 67 later clarified that this covers all matrix collars with constant-coefficient \(T^3\) slices, because such slices are intrinsically flat and \(S\) is self-adjoint; it does not cover general Gaussian collars \(dr^2+\gamma_r(x)\) with curved induced \(T^3\) metrics [Step 67].

Step 64 tested whether Di Cerbo’s entropy exclusion had a stable \(O(1)\) margin. Decomposing the proof through Connell–Suárez–Serrato minimal Ricci volume, Gauss–Bonnet, LeBrun Lemma 7, and Preissmann, the agents found each step saturated: approximate \(\|\operatorname{Ric}+3g\|\le\delta\) relaxes the entropy bound from \(h\le3\) to \(h\le3+\delta\), so CSS gives only an \(O(\delta)\) relaxation, not a quantitative gap [Step 64]. The route became an entropy-rigidity/neck-localization problem rather than a cheap margin theorem [Step 64].

Step 65 corrected Step 64’s \(\mu_4\) bifurcation claim using the Step 2 Chern–Weil estimate. The corrected cascade was: slice dimension 2 blocked by Gauss–Bonnet, slice dimension 3 blocked in sectional terms by Preissmann when \(\|\operatorname{Ric}+2g\|_{\rm op}<2/3\) forces negative sectional curvature, slice dimension 4 has a nonzero-normalization Chern–Weil lower bound, and genuinely open behavior begins in higher slice dimensions [Step 65]. Step 65 also formulated Conjecture F: near-equality in CSS entropy should force the \(O(1)\) slice defect into a JSJ collar, where the flat-slice barrier applies [Step 65]. In a double-warped model class it derived

H'=3-|S|^2-e,

and interpreted the calibrated band as the locus where \(H\) can persist without drift [Step 65]. A finite \(S^1\)-invariant \(T^3\) scalar example with \(R<0\) everywhere showed the pointwise scalar condition at an \(H=0\) slice is satisfiable; the obstruction must be integrated/topological, not just pointwise scalar [Step 65].

## Koiso local reversal, 20260912 manuscript absorption, and the graph-neck reopening [Steps 67–69]

Step 67 produced the decisive correction to the false local obstruction: Koiso’s analytic Einstein Cauchy theorem gives local exact negative Einstein bands through curved \(T^3\) data. For an analytic \(T^3\) metric \(q\) of scalar curvature \(-6\), with totally geodesic central slice, the local analytic solution of \(\operatorname{Ric}=-3g\) satisfies

## Weighted normal identity, exact flat-end obstruction, and repaired elliptic matching [Steps 70–71]

Step 70 derived a weighted normal identity for exact reflection cores, but Step 71 corrected its interpretation. For a Gaussian collar with \(S=(1/2)h_t^{-1}\partial_th_t\), \(H=\operatorname{tr}S\), \(B=S-I\), \(b=H-3\), and \(E=\operatorname{Ric}+3g\), the exact normal equation is
\[
b'+2b+|B|^2=-E_{00}.
\]
Thus
\[
e^{2R}b(R)-b(0)+\int_0^R e^{2t}|B|^2\,dt
=
-\int_0^R e^{2t}E_{00}\,dt.
\]
For a reflection center \(b(0)=-3\) and exact outgoing cusp value \(H(R)=3\), the same forcing tensor must satisfy
\[
3+\int_0^R e^{2t}|S-I|^2\,dt
=
-\int_0^R e^{2t}E_{00}\,dt.
\]
The residual must be negative in the weighted normal direction and offset both the central deficit and weighted shear [Steps 70–71]. Under \(|E_{00}|\le\delta\), this gives a logarithmic necessary length scale such as \(R\gtrsim\frac12\log(1/\delta)\), but it is not a sufficiency statement [Steps 70–71].

Step 71 withdrew the Step 70 “flat \(T^3\) exact benchmark.” The warped metric \(dt^2+\cosh^2(t)q_{\rm flat}\) solves the normal equation \(u'+u^2=1\) with \(u=\tanh t\), but the tangential equation \(u'+3u^2=3\) fails; the tangential Einstein defect is \(2\operatorname{sech}^2(t)I\) [Step 71]. Equivalently, a totally geodesic center requires scalar curvature \(-6\), not a flat \(T^3\) metric [Step 71]. This example became a model of constraint failure, not an existence baseline [Step 71]. The elliptic correction also changed the meaning of “stability”: the \(T^2\)-invariant Gaussian-gauge system has elliptic principal part, so forward Cauchy blow-up is Hadamard ill-posedness rather than a geometric singularity, and decay of intrinsic-curvature coefficients does not imply arbitrary center data approach a cusp [Steps 70–71].

A stronger global obstruction closed the exact flat-PE-end reflection route. If a complete \(\operatorname{Ric}=-3g\) half-core with smooth reflection center and flat \(T^3\) Poincaré–Einstein infinity existed, doubling would produce a connected complete Einstein manifold with two nonnegative-Yamabe PE ends [Step 71]. Li–Liu Proposition 6.6, restating Witten–Yau/Cai–Galloway in the zero-Yamabe case, permits only one end except for a rigid Ricci-flat warped product with one PE and one cusp end; that exception has no totally geodesic reflection slice [Step 71]. A local PE expansion gives the same obstruction: the weighted identity forces the center-normalized infinity representative to have scalar curvature below \(-12\), incompatible with the flat conformal class [Step 71]. ## Step 72: conformal gauge and the \(T^2\)-invariant anisotropy obstruction [Step 72]

The Step 72 user message first supplied a boundary compatibility obstruction that changed which elliptic boundary problems were worth solving. For an exact \(\operatorname{Ric}=-3g\) finite cylinder, the outer Gauss constraint with
\[
S=(H/3)I+S_{\rm tf}
\]
is
\[
R_\gamma=-6+\frac23H^2-|S_{\rm tf}|^2.
\]
If the outer conformal class is flat on \(T^3\) and \(H\) is constant with \(|H|<3\), then \(R_\gamma<0\) everywhere, impossible for \(\gamma=u^4\gamma_{\rm flat}\) because
\[
R_\gamma=-8u^{-5}\Delta_{\rm flat}u
\]
is nonnegative at a maximum of \(u\) [Step 72]. At \(H=3\), integration forces \(u\) constant and \(S_{\rm tf}=0\), recovering rigid flat umbilic cusp data [Step 72]. Therefore exact finite Einstein continuation with fixed flat conformal class and constant \(H_R<3\) should not be run; meaningful alternatives are to allow negative-Yamabe outer conformal classes and account for later flattening cost, or to solve a genuinely forced finite problem with flat outer conformal class [Step 72]. For forced metrics with \(E=\operatorname{Ric}+3g\) and \(\|E\|_{\rm op}\le\delta\),
\[
R_\gamma=-6+\frac23H^2-|S_{\rm tf}|^2+\operatorname{tr}_TE-E_{nn},
\]
so a constant-\(H\) flat-conformal boundary requires
\[
\delta\ge\frac{9-H^2}{6},
\]
approximately \(\delta\ge\varepsilon-\varepsilon^2/6\) for \(H=3-\varepsilon\) [Step 72]. This boundary Gauss balance and the interior weighted normal balance must be satisfied by the same forcing tensor [Step 72].

Step 72 then replaced the degenerate Gaussian-gauge ansatz by a conformal gauge:
\[
g=e^{2\phi}(dt^2+dz^2)+e^{2b}dx^2+e^{2c}dy^2.
\]
For the natural three-equation subsystem \((E_{tt}+E_{zz},E_{xx},E_{yy})\) in unknowns \((\phi,b,c)\), the principal symbol determinant is
\[
2(\tau^2+\xi^2)^3,
\]
nonzero for every nonzero covector [Step 72]. This explained why prior Gaussian-gauge BVP experiments produced large \(E_{00}\) and \(E_{01}\) residuals: the earlier system was degenerate, not merely stiff [Step 72]. The conformal-gauge files include `step72_conformal_gauge_einstein.py` and `step72_conformal_gauge_system.json` [Step 72].

The main Step 72 structural result is a \(T^2\)-invariant anisotropy drift-Laplacian. Subtracting the \(E_{xx}/g_{xx}\) and \(E_{yy}/g_{yy}\) equations gives
\[
\Delta\delta+\nabla\sigma\cdot\nabla\delta=0,
\qquad
\delta=b-c,\quad \sigma=b+c,
\]
equivalently
\[
\operatorname{div}(e^\sigma\nabla\delta)=0
\]
[Step 72]. TTCS independently verified this derivation and corrected an orbit-area formula to
\[
\Delta\rho=6e^{2\phi}\rho
\]
with no spurious \(-|\nabla\delta|^2\) term [Step 72]. The drift-Laplacian gives a rigidity corollary on \([0,R]\times S^1\): with Neumann at the reflection center, if \(\delta\) is nonconstant then its oscillation at the outer boundary strictly exceeds its center oscillation; if the outer \(\delta\) is constant, then \(\delta\) is constant everywhere [Step 72].

A Frobenius analysis near the cusp boundary, where the drift coefficient behaves like \(\sigma'=2/(1-t)\), found indicial roots \(p=0\) and \(p=3\); both fundamental solutions are finite at the cusp [Step 72]. Numerical integration of Fourier modes with initial amplitude 1 at the center gave finite but amplified cusp amplitudes: approximately 1.175 for mode \(n=1\), 1.813 for \(n=2\), and 3.339 for \(n=3\), with amplification increasing in mode number [Step 72]. This propagation theory is quantitative and potentially reusable for other \(T^2\)-invariant Einstein boundary-value problems [Step 72].

The Yamabe component of the obstruction is that no positive function solves
\[
\Delta_{\rm flat}u=\frac34u^5
\]
on flat \(T^3\); hence no metric of scalar curvature \(-6\) lies in the flat conformal class [Step 72]. In the \(T^2\)-invariant central ansatz
\[
h_0=d\theta^2+e^{2f(\theta)}dx^2+e^{-2f(\theta)}dy^2,
\]
the scalar curvature is
\[
R(h_0)=-2(f')^2,
\]
equal to zero only for constant \(f\) [Step 72]. Thus any \(T^2\)-invariant scalar \(-6\) Koiso center lies in a negative-Yamabe class and carries nonconstant anisotropy \(\delta=2f(\theta)\) [Step 72]. Combining this with the drift-Laplacian: a reflected \(T^2\)-invariant half-core would start with nonconstant center anisotropy, but a flat hyperbolic cusp requires constant \(T^2\) cross-section anisotropy; the drift-Laplacian amplifies rather than erases the oscillation [Step 72]. Step 72 records this as a structural obstruction to \(T^2\)-invariant reflected half-core constructions toward flat cusps [Step 72].

The obstruction is conditional in scope. It does not rule out general non-\(T^2\)-invariant graph-neck constructions, surface-bundle \(E_D\) counterexamples, positive-branch phenomena, or higher-dimensional constructions where the relevant fiber dimension and conformal/Yamabe behavior differ [Step 72]. It also does not by itself prove a graph-manifold gap theorem; it blocks the quotient-compatible \(T^2\)-invariant anisotropic core mechanism developed in Step 69 [Steps 69,72]. Step 72’s route map accordingly lists the remaining viable directions as: non-symmetric graph construction, surface-bundle Einstein nonexistence via monodromy-specific arguments, tower/global positive-branch mechanisms, or a focused certification push for the restricted Ishida–LeBrun module [Step 72].

## Positive branch and higher-dimensional context [Steps 4–72]

The positive branch has remained secondary but increasingly important. In dimension four, tight positive Ricci pinching plus noncollapse gives strong finiteness tools via Myers, Bishop–Gromov, and Cheeger–Naber; however, collapse can occur and does not itself obstruct Einstein existence, as round lens spaces illustrate [Steps 4–9]. A02 explored \(\#_k(S^2\times S^2)\), toric/rod structures, integral identities, ALF/NUT transitions, positive noncollapsed Ozuch-type obstructions, and product-quotient examples [Steps 17–57 context]. No reduction from arbitrary metrics to invariant metrics was found [Steps 17–25 context].

A key output-quantifier lesson came from A01’s BCGP \(\mathbb Z_4^2\) product-quotient work: serious near-Einstein/gluing candidates can carry unrelated exact Einstein metrics through \(\mathbb Q\)-Gorenstein smoothing, Aubin–Yau on an ample-canonical fiber, ADE simultaneous resolution, and Ehresmann arguments [Step 54 context]. This reinforced that K-instability or nearby Kähler–Einstein obstruction does not imply absence of arbitrary Einstein metrics; Page and Chen–LeBrun–Weber metrics on non-KE del Pezzos are the standard warning [Step 64].

The Strategist in Step 64 judged that no closed manifold is known to carry positive Ricci while provably lacking all Einstein metrics; the positive branch should therefore be treated primarily as an existence problem unless a first positive-Ricci/no-Einstein example is found [Step 64]. Step 67 refined this: \(\#_k(S^2\times S^2)\) has positive Ricci for every \(k\) by Sha–Yang, while Einstein existence is unknown already for \(k=2,3\); resolving this would itself be a major standalone result [Step 67]. A02’s Step 74 findings, absorbed in Step 72, report limits on positive local higher-obstruction methods: an \(\ell\)-classification, higher-obstruction subcriticality/tower issues, and product propagation making \(P_4^+\) a bottleneck for \(n\ge6\) [Step 72]. These are peer-session context, not completed A03 theorems [Step 72].

Higher dimensions remain much less developed. Early notes observed that four-dimensional Chern–Weil/SW tools do not transfer, and Kaluza–Klein positive Einstein collapse exists in codimension-one constructions such as \(L(q,1)\times N^d\) [Steps 2–63]. Sectionally pinched counterexample routes are tentatively closed by Anderson/Hamenstädt–Jäckel-type results, but only under their actual hypotheses [Steps 62–64]. The corrected slice cascade and KK rank analysis shifted viable negative counterexample territory toward ambient dimension at least six, but Step 67 withdrew any precise first-open-dimension conclusion based solely on isolated slice inequalities [Steps 64–67]. Step 72’s \(T^2\)-invariant obstruction is four-dimensional and symmetry-specific; it does not rule out higher-dimensional graph or torus-bundle mechanisms [Step 72].

### Research Line

The session began by protecting the exact logical structure of Yau Problem 26: normalized positive and negative branches were separated and the all-dimensional, dimension-only quantifiers kept visible [Steps 1, 10]. Early exploration tested flexibility, perturbative, convergence, and desingularization mechanisms; their failures established durable standards — a failed Einstein construction is not absence of all Einstein metrics, extra controls cannot be imported, and gauge perturbations are not true Ricci flexibility [Steps 1-2].

The research moved to four-dimensional negative topology for its strong independent obstructions. The user-corrected mixed Ishida–LeBrun scalar–Weyl estimate made the critical boundary \(D=A/3\) central, and near-critical analysis produced the calibrated profile plus the Step 6 projector argument ruling out a noncollapsed Einstein germ with the calibrated \(W^+\) spectrum: any tight sequence must collapse at fixed scale while carrying diffuse calibrated mass [Steps 2-6]. A period of collapse-model study (abelian, nil, Taub–NUT–AdS, Pontryagin, static, toric) produced caution and corrections rather than a proof, establishing that collapse needs an extraction mechanism, not model classification [Steps 7-12].

Smoothing became the active method after the small-radius \(r^4\) observation restored fixed-scale regularization in collapsed settings, and the normalized cutoff flow was selected [Steps 13-15]. Early localized Li arguments failed, forcing the degenerate Wang/Yang framework: weighted moments, shifted curvature \(T=\mathrm{Rm}+G\), \(U=aT\), the signed Hessian IBP principle, volume-weighted disjoint supports with the collapse-independent \(\mathcal S K_2^{1/2}\) cancellation, and the two-stage curvature/defect strategy with global \(Q\) kept separate [Steps 16-39]. Steps 35 and 39 were genuine conditional advances (the \(J_6\) mechanism and the all-\(p\) defect inequality), while repeated overpromotion (Steps 37, 39, 41, 47, 49, 51) and user/Preceptor corrections established a central methodological standard: estimates only matter on one realized exact flow with the same supports, constants, and terminal metric [Steps 37-54].

The start problem dominated Steps 49-54: coefficient regularization that treated cutoff jets as bounded was rejected; critical-energy cancellation was killed by the flat-torus test; Xu's fixed-coordinate construction clarified that the cutoff must be transported; the transported square \(\widehat\chi\) was adopted; and the first Banach contraction was withdrawn for confusing input and output derivative control [Steps 49-54].

Steps 55-56 simplified and then repaired the start. The strategist observed that the two-layer frozen-input iteration was unnecessary: solving the metric and transported cutoff as one coupled regularized system keeps top-order exchanges within one pair [Step 55]. User review then found Step 55's arbitrary-order coefficient split false; Step 56 replaced it with a genuine tame estimate and a doubly regularized \((\varepsilon,\nu)\) strongly parabolic approximation, yielding a per-datum, regularization-uniform local existence route with a smooth pullback to the exact fixed-cutoff flow — credible but not yet certified at proof level, and explicitly without uniqueness of the degenerate limit [Step 56]. The same step corrected the quantitative handoff: unweighted \(H_2\), the stationary \(Q_{\mathrm{rest}}\) remainder, and four separated notions of uniformity [Step 56].

Steps 57-58 connected the exact flow to the first-exit mechanism. The \(H_2\) derivation closed on the actual flow with \(\nabla G=0\) and signed Hessian absorption [Step 57]. The critical-to-subcritical bridge was repaired so initial cubic concentration cannot determine the observation time — the relative estimate \(Y\le C\mathcal S H_2^{1/2}(D_2+r^{-2}H_2)\) replaced the invalid \(Y(0)\) argument — and the curvature Moser ladder was derived independently of the defect ladder, reaching \(\|aF_T(t)\|_\infty\le C\Gamma/t\) conditionally [Step 58]. The \(W^{1,p}\to L^\infty\) bridge gave pointwise curvature on positive slabs, but the agents recorded that bounded curvature does not bound cutoff jets across the degenerate collar [Steps 57-58].

Steps 59-61 addressed the passage to a common observation time. Step 59 assembled a finite-threshold restart and identified the defect Moser endpoint that closes the coupled \((\Gamma,V)\) bootstrap; user review exposed the hidden overlap-uniqueness dependency and the ungauged \(L^2\) estimate was disproved by an explicit symbol example [Steps 59-60]. Step 60 replaced restart-on-overlap by all-order continuation, fixed-background \(C^\infty\) convergence, and autonomous time-jet splicing, and simplified the terminal argument to Liouville/Fubini chart selection, strong \(W^{2,q}\) convergence, \(L^1\) density passage, and the open-ball projector contradiction [Step 60]. Step 61's Preceptor review confirmed the mechanism after two corrections — the stationarity invariant \(T=0\Rightarrow E=0\) (removing phantom reaction terms) and starting the universal induction at \(m=2\) (the \(m=1\) residual argument was circular) — and verified from the original source that Ishida–LeBrun's Theorem D excludes every Einstein metric under its hypotheses [Step 61].

Step 61 then delivered a strategic reassessment that redirected the session: a completed restricted module would prove that known no-Einstein manifolds cannot approach the normalized negative Einstein equation — a positive gap — but it supplies neither the no-Einstein fixed-width pinched sequences a disproof requires nor a dimension-only existence interval [Step 61]. The session pivoted to Explore, adopting the localizable-versus-evacuable topology distinction as the shared question for existence and obstruction routes: what information about Einstein-admitting topology is lost in the regular local limit, and can it be recovered or exploited [Step 62].

Steps 62-63 mapped the counterexample landscape with concrete results. Brendle–Kapouleas and Kapovitch–Lott make the topology-loss problem precise (concentration with small Ricci versus noncollapsed reconstruction) [Step 62]. Anderson's 2003 sectional-pinching-to-Einstein theorem — reviewed in detail and found internally sound, with independent confirmation by Hamenstädt–Jäckel for Gromov–Thurston families — closes all sectionally-pinched counterexample routes [Steps 62-63]. Four-dimensional BCG rigidity identifies what a decisive negative-branch construction would require (an exotic smooth real-hyperbolic four-manifold with arbitrarily pinched metrics), but no such construction exists and Farrell–Jones starts in higher dimensions [Step 62]. Extended graph manifolds, the most concrete all-Einstein-excluded topology, were blocked as a counterexample source by the flat-slice mean curvature barrier \(H^2\ge9-6\delta\) — anisotropy, noncommuting shape operators, and removable twist cannot reverse a cusp for \(\delta<3/2\), and the proposed non-flat escape was itself topologically impossible — suggesting a gap theorem instead [Steps 62-63]. Step 63 closed with the cross-zero quantifier normalization reducing Yau 26 to two single-sign questions and five TTCS-generated candidate directions (K-stability gap and orbifold desingularization ranked highest), which Agent1 is to assess [Step 63].

The present state is therefore two-tracked. The restricted negative module is a developed candidate — per-datum start route, exact-flow first-exit estimates, all-order continuation with the Step 61 corrections, defect endpoint closing the bootstrap, and a simplified terminal chart mechanism — whose remaining burden is one connected tensor-level realization on a single flow plus persistent-center selection [Steps 56-62]. The broader inquiry has reopened at the quantifier level: both single-sign branches remain open in every dimension \(n\ge4\), the positive branch has no identified candidate mechanism in this session, \(n\ge5\) has only the collapsed-torus-bundle proposal, dimension-only constants are unaddressed, and Lean 4 formalization remains out of scope until the mathematics is complete [Steps 61-63].

## Goal, quantifier discipline, and early route filtering [Steps 1-2, correction Step 10]

The session began from the full Yau Problem 26: for each \(n\ge2\), decide whether dimension-only constants \(c_n<C_n\) exist such that any closed connected smooth \(n\)-manifold carrying a smooth metric \(g\) with
\[
c_ng\le \operatorname{Ric}_g\le C_ng
\]
(quadratic-form sense) must admit some smooth Einstein metric \(h\), unrelated to \(g\), with unrestricted Einstein constant [Step 1]. Early work normalized quantifiers by scaling and separated positive and negative normalized pinching branches. A correction fixed an overstrong disproof criterion: to refute the fixed-dimensional statement, both forcing branches must fail, but not necessarily on the same smooth manifold [Steps 1,10].

Several seductive routes were eliminated because they ignored the output-metric quantifier: local Einstein nonexistence near \(g\), perturbative obstruction, or orbifold/ALE gluing near one metric cannot disprove the statement if the same smooth manifold carries an Einstein metric elsewhere in metric space. The desingularized football orbifold yielding \(S^2\times S^2\) (which has a product Einstein metric) became the standard warning [Step 1]. A high-frequency Ricci-flexibility idea on a flat background was abandoned after the principal-symbol computation
\[
\ker\sigma_\xi(D\operatorname{Ric})=\{\xi\otimes v+v\otimes\xi\},
\]
so apparent second-order Ricci sources are only infinitesimal diffeomorphism directions [Steps 1-2]. Literature filtering corrected Min-Oo's theorem (it needs extra scale-invariant sectional/diameter hypotheses; Ye's fragment preserved unresolved issues), downgraded Lohkamp flexibility (one-sided, not closed-manifold two-sided pointwise \(\operatorname{Ric}\approx -g\)), and bounded orbifold/ALE gluing hopes [Steps 1-2].

## Four-dimensional negative branch and the corrected Ishida–LeBrun interface [Steps 2-3]

The active route moved to dimension four, where Chern–Weil formulas, Hitchin–Thorpe, Seiberg–Witten theory, and LeBrun/Ishida–LeBrun inequalities connect Ricci pinching to topology [Step 2]. Scripts `verify_chern_weil_pinching.py`, `critical_compatibility_model.py`, and note `step2_quantitative_4d_analysis.tex` checked constants and candidate families [Step 2].

A stable early result: under normalized two-sided pinching \(\|\operatorname{Ric}-\Lambda g\|_{\rm op}\le\delta|\Lambda|\) with \(\delta<(\sqrt3-1)/2\), Chern–Gauss–Bonnet and signature identities force \(2\chi>3|\tau|\), excluding Hitchin–Thorpe violators as tight-pinching counterexamples for either sign [Step 2]. Useful clarification, not a forcing-branch solution.

For LeBrun no-Einstein families \(X\#k\overline{\mathbb{CP}}^{\,2}\), an initial uniform negative-branch gap claim was withdrawn after rereading Ishida–LeBrun and a user correction: the derivation illegally dropped a negative gradient term in the self-dual Weitzenböck formula, and \(F_A^+\) is not generally harmonic [Steps 2-3]. The valid interface became Ishida–LeBrun Theorem 7 for
\[
M=(\#_{j=1}^m X_j)\#N,\quad m=2\text{ or }3,\quad A=\sum c_1^2(X_j),\quad D=4m-(2\chi+3\tau)(N),
\]
with exact Einstein metrics excluded when \(D\ge A/3\) [Step 3]. The equality boundary \(D=A/3\) became the critical laboratory: exact Einstein metrics are ruled out, but that alone gives no uniform metric gap [Step 3].

## Critical near-saturation, calibrated Weyl profile, and the local forbidden germ [Steps 3-6]

On a critical Ishida–LeBrun manifold, assuming a hypothetical sequence \(\delta_i=\|\operatorname{Ric}_{g_i}+g_i\|_\infty\to0\), the agents organized Chern–Weil variables (`step3_boundary_near_saturation.tex`, `verify_step3_boundary_constants.py`) [Step 3]. Pointwise pinching gives \(|s_i+4|\le4\delta_i\), \(\operatorname{Ric}^\circ_i=O(\delta_i)\), fixed-topology volume convergence, \(\int|\operatorname{Ric}^\circ_i|^2\to0\) [Step 3]. Completing squares in the genuine mixed scalar–Weyl inequality produced the calibrated Weyl modulus profile
\[
\int\left(|W_i^+|-\frac1{2\sqrt6}\right)^2\,d\mu_i=O(A\delta_i^2)
\]
[Steps 3-4]. Consequence: ordinary negative Kähler–Einstein regions (\(|W^+|=2/\sqrt6\)) and scalar-flat connectors are both far from the calibrated value and cannot occupy positive-volume bulk in a critical near-saturating sequence [Step 4]. Codex work decomposed the LeBrun equality chain into nonnegative deficits (`codex_loop/Research_Report.md`, `quantitative_deficit_analysis.md`) — useful for local densities but not supplying Sobolev constants, harmonic radius, or noncollapse [Steps 3-4,9].

The next question: must a near-saturated sequence contain a regular Einstein-scale patch? Cheeger–Naber regularity was used cautiously (uniform local volume lower bounds → harmonic-coordinate compactness → weak \(\operatorname{Ric}=-g\) limit upgraded by elliptic regularity) [Step 5]. A shortcut was corrected: \(L^\infty\) control of \(\operatorname{Ric}+g\) gives no derivative control, so Bianchi gives no smallness of \(\operatorname{div}W^+\) [Step 5]. Any regular local limit would need
\[
\operatorname{Ric}=-g,\qquad s=-4,\qquad \operatorname{Spec}(W^+)=(-\tfrac16,\tfrac1{12},\tfrac1{12})
\]
[Step 5]. A sign-sensitive Derdziński appeal was replaced (after user warning) by a direct projector calculation: on an oriented Einstein four-manifold with \(W^+\) having one simple and one double constant eigenvalue, expanding \(\delta W^+=0\) for \(W^+=\mu\Pi_++(\lambda-\mu)\omega\otimes\omega\) forces \(\omega\) parallel, hence \(\nabla W^+=0\); but the Einstein–Weyl identity
\[
\Delta|W^+|^2=2|\nabla W^+|^2+s|W^+|^2-36\det W^+
\]
with the calibrated spectrum gives \(|\nabla W^+|^2=1/16\), contradiction [Step 6]. This became the central reusable endpoint: any bridge extracting a smooth calibrated Einstein germ kills the near-saturating sequence [Steps 5-6]. Conditional global-local knowledge at this stage: a \(\delta_i\to0\) sequence on a fixed critical manifold cannot have noncollapsed regular unit-scale patches; with positive total volume, volume must collapse locally and diameter diverge [Step 6].

## Collapse, covers, Taub–NUT, and reduced rank-one models [Steps 6-12]

With noncollapsed patches excluded, work turned to collapsed geometry: Naber–Zhang collapse regularity, Huang–Wang bounded-Ricci covering geometry, Rong, Jiang–Kong–Xu, Lott's Einstein equations with local symmetry [Steps 6-8]. Guiding idea: unwrap collapsed fibers on local covers in maximal nilpotency-rank regions and recover the forbidden germ. Key correction: deficit transfer to covers is a normalized-average problem, not an absolute-integral one [Steps 6-8].

In exact abelian symmetry models, Lott's orbit-volume equation
\[
\Delta_B v=\left(\frac{|F|^2}{4}-\lambda N\right)v,\qquad \lambda=-1,
\]
has a positive zero-order term excluding some regular pure collapses by maximum principle [Steps 6-8]. The nil\(^3\)/Heisenberg cohomogeneity-one case corrected a sign: with \(\rho=a_3^2/(a_1^2a_2^2)\), \(v''=(3-\rho/2)v\), consistent with the complex hyperbolic cusp [Step 7]. Circle-base periodic cases excludable under an interior maximum bound; finite-interval bases subtle due to endpoint blowup of \(\rho\) [Steps 7-8].

Step 8 repaired cover-deficit transport via a normal-cover local mean-transport lemma:
\[
\fint_{B_r(\hat p)}\pi^*\phi\le\frac{V_{-K}^{(n)}(3r)}{V_{-K}^{(n)}(r)}\fint_{B_r(p)}\phi
\]

## Return to the full quantifiers: topology loss, graph manifolds, exotic hyperbolic routes [Steps 62-63]

Step 62 (Agent1, Explore) reopened the quantifier-level question, exploiting a distinction the restricted route exposed: Ishida–LeBrun theory forces a diffuse curvature density incompatible with every smooth calibrated Einstein germ — that is why one retained chart yields a contradiction. A general Einstein obstruction need not localize this way; topology may evacuate into shrinking exceptional regions while every regular chart has admissible Einstein geometry [Step 62]. The counterexample quantifiers were sharpened: refuting a branch requires a fixed dimension and manifolds carrying normalized metrics with \(\|\operatorname{Ric}\mp g\|_\infty\to0\) while every underlying manifold excludes all Einstein metrics; complete refutation needs both signs in one dimension, on possibly different manifolds; a degeneration route must control pointwise defect inside the topology-carrying region and separately establish all-sign Einstein nonexistence [Step 62].

Literature (three focused knowledge requests) clarified mechanisms: Brendle–Kapouleas give a compact ancient-flow sequence on a fixed Eguchi–Hanson desingularization with \(\sup|\operatorname{Ric}|\to0\) and \(\sup|\operatorname{Rm}|\to\infty\) — topology and curvature concentrating while Ricci becomes small, but a zero-Einstein-scale phenomenon without Einstein exclusion [Step 62]. Kapovitch–Lott show the complementary phenomenon: noncollapsed almost Ricci-flat four-manifolds with suitable topology reconstruct K3/flat topology, hence carry Ricci-flat metrics; uncontrolled information sits precisely in collapse [Step 62]. Anderson's 2003 preprint claims sufficiently tight negative sectional pinching (dimension-only threshold) produces a negative Einstein metric, explicitly covering Gromov–Thurston and Farrell–Jones manifolds; its validity could not be established by retrieval at this step [Step 62]. Farrell–Jones exotic smoothings give arbitrarily sectionally pinched metrics in high dimensions but exclude only hyperbolic metrics, not arbitrary Einstein metrics; in dimension four, Besson–Courtois–Gallot rigidity would force an Einstein metric on a homotopy-real-hyperbolic manifold to be hyperbolic (other signs excluded by fundamental group), so an exotic smooth hyperbolic four-manifold with pinched metrics would be decisive — but no four-dimensional exotic smoothing construction is known, and the Farrell–Jones mechanism starts in higher dimensions where 4D Einstein rigidity is unavailable [Step 62].

Extended graph four-manifolds emerged as the most concrete counterexample candidates (source-supported exclusion of all Einstein metrics; assembled from hyperbolic cusp pieces). A new local calculation: for the naive double-cusp metric \(g=dr^2+f(r)^2g_{T^3}\), \(u=f'/f\), the Ricci eigenvalues \(-3(u'+u^2)\) (radial) and \(-(u'+3u^2)\) (tangential) with \(\|\operatorname{Ric}+3g\|_{\rm op}\le\delta\) force \(|u^2-1|\le2\delta/3\), so for \(\delta<3/2\), \(u\) cannot change sign — scalar warping cannot reverse cusp orientation under tight pinching [Step 62]. A02's opposite-warping calculations were flagged as a possible anisotropic escape lacking global cap and all-Einstein topology argument [Step 62]. The restricted flow module was reassessed: A01's `step58_all_order_continuation_proof.md` repairs stationarity and the \(m=1\) circularity consistently with Step 61; direct reading of A03's Step 56 found the per-datum construction explicitly represented with no new concrete false cancellation identified; remaining work is verifying exact gauge-fixed generating identities and connecting derived estimates on one realized flow — dispersed exposition is not itself a defect, and scripts alone do not establish tensor identities [Step 62].

Step 63 (Agent2, Explore) executed three actions. First, the strategist's invariant test settled the flat-slice class cheaply: for \(g=dr^2+G(r)\) with intrinsically flat \(T^3\) slices, \(S=\tfrac12G^{-1}G'\), \(H=\operatorname{tr}S\), the traced Gauss equation gives
\[
H^2-\operatorname{tr}(S^2)=-(R_g-2\operatorname{Ric}(\partial_r,\partial_r)),
\]
so \(\|\operatorname{Ric}+3g\|_{\rm op}\le\delta\) implies \(|H^2-\operatorname{tr}(S^2)-6|\le4\delta\); self-adjointness gives \(\operatorname{tr}(S^2)\ge H^2/3\), hence the flat-slice mean-curvature barrier
\[
H^2\ge 9-6\delta:
\]
no contracting-to-expanding cusp reversal is possible for \(\delta<3/2\), even with anisotropy and noncommuting shape operators; shear strengthens the obstruction; \(r\)-dependent torus translations are locally removable and supply no curvature-bearing twist (`step63_torus_transition_analysis.py/json`) [Step 63]. TTCS verification then exposed a critical error in the proposed non-flat escape: an exact Einstein funnel \(dr^2+\cosh^2(r)g_N\) would need \(\operatorname{Ric}_{g_N}=-2g_N\) on \(T^3\), forcing constant sectional curvature \(-1\), impossible for \(\pi_1=\mathbb Z^3\); Lohkamp gives \(\operatorname{Ric}<0\), not Einstein; and a scaling argument for defect reduction was invalid (stretching the annulus does not remove \(O(1)\) algebraic constraints at the \(H=0\) slice) [Step 63]. Corrected conclusion: the graph-manifold counterexample route is blocked by the \(T^3\) slice topology — evidence toward a gap theorem rather than a counterexample; for general slices \(\gamma_r\) the constraint \(H^2-|S|^2=R(\gamma_r)-R_g+2\operatorname{Ric}(\partial_r,\partial_r)\) shows intrinsic negative slice curvature could in principle change the conclusion, and any new neck mechanism must explain what permits the transition [Step 63].

Second, Anderson's 2003 preprint was reviewed in detail: the proof appeared self-contained and sound on internal review (ergodic Lemma 2.2 the subtlest step), and Hamenstädt–Jäckel (2024) independently confirms the conclusion for Gromov–Thurston manifolds; on this assessment all sectionally-pinched counterexample routes are closed, though formal publication status was not independently certified [Step 63].

Third, a TTCS-generated quantifier normalization was adopted: for \(n\ge4\), any valid pinching interval \([c_n,C_n]\) must not cross zero, because any metric can be rescaled into a cross-zero interval; this reduces Yau 26 to two independent single-sign questions, and reframes the core object as precompactness vs. degeneration of sequences with trace-free Ricci \(\to0\) in \(C^0\) [Step 63]. Five candidate research directions were generated and ranked, with K-stability gap (positive branch) and orbifold desingularization (negative branch) ranked highest by feasibility (`step63_quantifier_normalization.md`, `step63_status.md`; peer messages #436-440) [Step 63].

The positive branch remained secondary but structurally informative. In dimension four, positive tight pinching plus noncollapse gives strong finiteness via Myers, Bishop–Gromov, Cheeger–Naber; infinitely many \(\#_k(S^2\times S^2)\)-type examples would have to collapse, but collapse itself does not obstruct Einstein existence (round lens spaces collapse) [Steps 4-9]. A02 explored \(\#_5\mathbb{CP}^2\), toric/rod structures, integral identities on \(\#_k(S^2\times S^2)\); no reduction from arbitrary to invariant metrics [Steps 17-25]. A02's Chern–Weil saturation result: collapse pins both chiral energies exactly, so positive-collapse obstruction must find forced energy defect, not missing budget [Step 57 context]. A01's BCGP \(\mathbb Z_4^2\) product-quotient resolution (\(T_X^0\cong(\pi_*T_Y)^G\), \(H^2(X,T_X^0)=0\), Aubin–Yau on the ample-canonical fiber, ADE simultaneous resolution plus Ehresmann) shows serious near-Einstein/gluing candidates can carry unrelated exact Einstein metrics — the strongest standing confirmation of the output-quantifier warning [Step 54]. Higher dimensions \(n\ge5\) remain largely untouched: the 4D machinery does not transfer; codimension-one positive Einstein collapse exists via Kaluza–Klein constructions (\(L(q,1)\times N^d\)); no high-dimensional no-Einstein family has been connected to two-sided pinching [Steps 2-63]. Anderson-type results (if valid) close near-hyperbolic high-dimensional counterexample routes [Steps 62-63].

Peer sessions materially shaped the work throughout: corrections to Min-Oo and scalar–Weyl overclaims, projector obstruction support, nil\(^3\) sign repair, Taub–NUT interpretation, weighted Moser alignment, the false half-power objection, tensor-energy checks, the Sobolev-convention repair [Steps 1-45]; then the flow-theorem stress testing pattern — Steps 48, 50, 52, 54, 56, 58, 60, 61 each prevented or repaired premature promotion [Steps 45-61]. Scripts and TTCS remain valuable for algebra, exponents, allocation ledgers, and stress tests, but do not by themselves certify PDE existence, source-theorem applicability, geometric convergence, or final theorem status [Steps 1-63].

# Dense Evidence: Yau Problem 26 (Steps 1–63)

## Results, Observations, and Their Meaning

### Problem quantifiers, normalization, and settled dimensions

- For fixed \(n\), the original interval-pinching statement \(Q_n\) reduces to normalized one-sign alternatives \(P_n^+\lor P_n^-\): any nondegenerate interval contains a positive- or negative-sign subinterval after constant rescaling of the metric/Ricci endomorphism. A disproof in one fixed dimension must defeat both signs, possibly on different manifolds [Step 1; corrected Step 10].

- Dimensions \(2\) and \(3\) are positive: \(n=2\) by uniformization, \(n=3\) by Hamilton's positive-Ricci theorem. The unresolved range begins at \(n=4\) [Step 1].

- Step 63 added a sharper normalization with major structural consequence. Under constant rescaling \(g\mapsto tg\), the \((0,2)\)-Ricci tensor is unchanged, so for any cross-zero interval \(c_n<0<C_n\), every closed \(n\)-manifold admits a conforming metric: any bounded Ricci tensor satisfies \(ctg\le\operatorname{Ric}\le Ctg\) for \(t\) large. Since closed no-Einstein manifolds exist in dimension \(4\) (Hitchin–Thorpe violators, Ishida–LeBrun families), the cross-zero statement is false for \(n=4\); hence any valid interval must be single-sign. Yau 26 thereby reduces to two independent single-sign questions per dimension, and the core scientific object becomes the precompactness-versus-degeneration alternative for sequences with trace-free Ricci tending to zero in \(C^0\) [Step 63]. The \(n\ge5\) side of the cross-zero exclusion depends on existence of closed no-Einstein manifolds in those dimensions; the dimension-4 ground is source-solid.

- Counterexample quantifiers were sharpened in Step 62: defeating one branch requires a fixed dimension and a sequence of smooth manifolds carrying metrics with \(\|\operatorname{Ric}\mp g\|_{L^\infty}\to0\), while every underlying manifold excludes every Einstein metric (all signs of \(\lambda\)). A single finite-width example tests mechanisms but refutes nothing. Complete refutation requires failure of both signs in one fixed dimension, though the two sequences may use different manifolds. Any degeneration construction must control the pointwise defect inside the topology-carrying regions, not only away from them, and must separately prove all-sign Einstein nonexistence [Step 62].

- The full goal remains: for every \(n\ge2\), prove or disprove existence of dimension-only \(c_n<C_n\), with same-manifold output quantifier (output \(h\) need not be near \(g\); \(\lambda\) unrestricted), plus independently checkable Lean 4 formalization [Step 1 onward].

### Orbifold/desingularization evidence

- In Morteza–Viaclovsky Einstein-orbifold desingularization, with \(g_t=t(g_{\rm cal}+th)\), the local Ricci expansion is \(\operatorname{Ric}(h_t)=t\Lambda h_t+t\lambda o+R_t\), \(|R_t|\le Ct^2\rho^2\). Constant scaling leaves the \((0,2)\)-Ricci tensor unchanged, so on fixed ALE-core sets the unweighted endomorphism defect tends to \(\lambda g_{\rm cal}^{-1}o\), whose eigenvalues are \(-1/(1+r^{2n})\) (multiplicity \(2n-2\)) and \((n-1)/(1+r^{2n})\) (radial/Hopf). If \(\lambda\ne0\), core supremum tends to \((n-1)|\lambda|\); weighted norms and ALE rescaling do not remove it. Transition-annulus residuals are \(O(t^{1/2})\); uniform pinching via this route requires vanishing first obstructions at all singular points [Step 1].

- Local nonexistence near a chosen orbifold degeneration is not evidence that the smooth resolution has no Einstein metric: the two-point football Eguchi–Hanson resolution is \(S^2\times S^2\), which is product-Einstein [Step 1]. A01's BCGP \(\mathbb Z_4^2\) product-quotient result (Step 54, below) reinforces this output-quantifier lesson. A02's Biquard-anchoring analysis reported \(O(t^{1/2})\) defect at ALE scale, confirming why gluing alone cannot reach the pinching target [Step 57 peer record].

### Perturbative Ricci-symbol route (closed)

- The flat-background principal symbol of \(D\operatorname{Ric}\) has no nongauge kernel: \(\ker\sigma_\xi(D\operatorname{Ric})=\{\xi\otimes v+v\otimes\xi\}\) for \(\xi\ne0\), checked algebraically and numerically for \(n=3,4,5\). The proposed high-frequency averaged-cone construction from nongauge linear Ricci-flat modes is unavailable; second-order terms of truncated gauge perturbations cancel after completion to an exact pullback [Steps 2–3].

### Four-dimensional Chern–Weil and gauge-theoretic constraints

- Strengthened Hitchin–Thorpe: if \(\|g^{-1}(\operatorname{Ric}-\Lambda g)\|_\infty\le\delta|\Lambda|\) with \(\delta<(\sqrt3-1)/2\approx0.366\), then \(2\chi>3|\tau|\). Hitchin–Thorpe-violating and equality-boundary manifolds cannot support sufficiently tight normalized pinching of either sign — already a direct pinching-gap mechanism for that topology class [Step 2].

- For LeBrun/Ishida–LeBrun no-Einstein families, the valid gauge input is Ishida–LeBrun Proposition 4: \((4\pi^2)^{-1}\int(s^2/24+2|W^+|^2)\ge\frac23(a^+)^2\) under the monopole hypotheses. The claimed stronger pure \(W^+\) bound \(\int|W^+|^2\ge(4\pi^2/3)(a^+)^2\) was withdrawn: its derivation dropped a negative gradient term in LeBrun's Weitzenböck estimate and treated \(F_A^+\) as harmonic [Steps 2–3].

### Weyl profile, bubbles, and the forbidden local germ

- Metric-by-metric calibration inequality (source-supported, computationally checked):
  \[
  \int\Bigl(|W^+|-\tfrac1{2\sqrt6}\Bigr)^2d\mu\le\tfrac7{24}\int|E|^2d\mu,\qquad E=\operatorname{Ric}+g,
  \]
  via Chern–Gauss–Bonnet, the genuine monopole inequality, and completion squares. The calibrated value \(1/(2\sqrt6)\) is one quarter of the Kähler–Einstein \(|W^+|=2/\sqrt6\); positive-volume regions cannot converge to ordinary negative Kähler–Einstein bulk [Steps 4, 15].

- Scalar-flat ASD connector regions are incompatible with pointwise defect \(<1\) since \(|s+4|=4\) there [Step 4].

- Four-dimensional Weyl energy is scale invariant. For fixed topology, any smooth noncollapsed shrinking-scale blow-up of a hypothetical pinched sequence must be Ricci-flat and \(W^+=0\), hence locally hyperkähler in the relevant orientation. For \(A_i\to\infty\), only normalized smallness is available unless \(A_i\delta_i^2\to0\); finite absolute \(W^+\)-energy bubbles are not excluded by this argument [Step 4].

- The sign dispute about Derdziński's theorem was resolved by a projector argument: for an Einstein four-metric with \(W^+\) having two distinct constant eigenvalues, writing \(W^+=\mu\Pi_++(\lambda-\mu)\omega\otimes\omega\) and using \(\delta W^+=0\) forces \(\nabla\omega=0\), hence \(\nabla W^+=0\), independent of the sign of the simple eigenvalue. But the Einstein–Weyl identity \(\Delta|W^+|^2=2|\nabla W^+|^2+s|W^+|^2-36\det W^+\) at \(s=-4\), spectrum \((-1/6,1/12,1/12)\), \(|W^+|^2=1/24\), \(\det=-1/864\) forces \(|\nabla W^+|^2=1/16\): contradiction. This is the hard local obstruction the terminal route aims to manufacture. Derdziński 1983 Proposition 5 independently supports it [Steps 5–6].

- Combining regular-patch extraction with this obstruction: any hypothetical \(\delta_i\to0\) sequence on a fixed critical Ishida–LeBrun manifold must satisfy \(\sup_p\operatorname{Vol}_{g_i}B_1(p)\to0\); with total volume \(\to32\pi^2A/9>0\), Bishop–Gromov forces diameter to diverge. This reduces the question to everywhere unit-scale collapse; it is not yet a gap theorem [Step 6].

- Weitzenböck convention fixed: \(q(R)(\omega)_{ij}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ik}\omega_{kj}+\operatorname{Ric}_{jk}\omega_{ik}-2R_{ikjl}\omega_{kl}\). Under the calibrated spectrum, harmonic self-dual forms are not nearly parallel (\(\int|\nabla H|^2=\int|H|^2\) simple eigenform; \(3/2\) ratio in the double eigenspace), correcting collapse-rank attempts based on "almost parallel" monopole forms [Step 9]. Walsh polarization gives \(L^1\)-type orthogonality/phase separation but not pointwise Gram nondegeneracy [Steps 4, 9].

### Collapse models, covers, and Taub–NUT evidence

- Lott's adapted free-abelian Einstein equation \(\Delta_Bv=(|F|^2/4-\lambda N)v\) strongly restricts exact regular pure abelian negative-Einstein collapse on closed/parabolic bases, but near-Einstein application requires approximate symmetry and transition control; averaging a metric can destroy Ricci defect [Steps 6–7].

- Earlier capacity estimates were false (invalid integration-by-parts/AM–GM sign); finite volume gives \(v\in L^1\), not a bound on \(v\). Corrected nil\(^3\) equation \(v''=(3-\rho/2)v\), \(\rho=a_3^2/(a_1^2a_2^2)\), checked against the complex-hyperbolic cusp; the periodic circle-base case is excluded via \(\rho\le2/3\), but finite intervals need endpoint control. The CH\(^2\) cusp \(v(s)=Ce^{4s/\sqrt6}\) has finite volume and infinite base length — a genuine collapse model refuting any finite-volume cusp-length bound [Steps 7–8].

- Global defect smallness does not transfer to local covers: covering multiplicity amplifies lifted integrals (collapsed product \(U\times S^1(\ell_i)\): \(O(\ell_i)\) downstairs, \(O(1)\) on a fixed unwrapped patch). Corrected normal-cover mean lemma: under \(\operatorname{Ric}\ge-(n-1)K\), for a normal local cover with buffer, \(\fint_{B_r(\hat p)}\pi^*\phi\le[V_{-K}(3r)/V_{-K}(r)]\fint_{B_r(p)}\phi\), via Borel section, disjoint deck translates, Bishop–Gromov [Step 8].

- Taub–NUT–AdS (\(\nu\to0\)) is not a good-point countermodel. Exact symbolic checks verified \(\operatorname{Ric}+g=0\), NUT smoothness, corrected volume density (after a factor-of-two orbit-density error), and \(|W|^2=32\nu^2(4\nu^2-3)^2/[3(r+\nu)^6]\); script orientation has \(W^+=0\), total full-Weyl energy \(\to32\pi^2\). At fixed distance from the NUT, small domains unwrap to real hyperbolic four-space (sectional curvature \(-1/3\)) whose completed-square deficit is \(16\), not small. It demonstrates cover-choice failure, not calibrated escape [Steps 9–10].

- Under homothety, curvature endomorphism spectra scale by \(r^2\) when a radius-\(r\) ball is blown up: the forbidden spectrum becomes \((-r^2/6,r^2/12,r^2/12)\); the projector/Derdziński contradiction is homogeneous at fixed scale but degenerates if the useful scale tends to zero [Step 10].

### Uniformity taxonomy (governing discipline for all flow estimates)

- Four distinct uniformities must be separated: (i) regularization-parameter uniformity for one initial datum (achieved by the Step 56 construction); (ii) sequence-geometric uniformity for a pinched sequence (must come from first-exit estimates using only legitimate geometric inputs — never from initial high Sobolev norms or datum-dependent cutoff jets); (iii) geography-family uniformity across varying topology; (iv) dimension-only uniformity. Curvature-to-volume budgets do not bound initial high Sobolev norms or higher cutoff jets, so the local lifespan is not sequence-uniform; the intended mechanism starts each datum for whatever positive time it has, runs the first-exit chain, and excludes earlier maximal endpoints by datum-dependent positive-time continuation [Step 56].

### Positive branch, higher dimensions, and external routes

- Positive normalized pinching has structural advantages (Myers diameter control; positive scalar kills SW monopoles) but no dimension-only volume lower bound; round lens-space quotients show input collapse compatible with Einstein outputs [Steps 4–5]. A02's Cheeger–Naber-based finiteness: in dimension 4, \(|\operatorname{Ric}-g|_{\rm op}\le\delta_0<1/2\) plus volume lower bound gives finitely many diffeomorphism types; any positive-pinching sequence on pairwise distinct manifolds must be volume-collapsed — a dichotomy, not existence [Step 8].

- A02 reported codimension-one positive Einstein collapse in every \(n\ge5\) via Kaluza–Klein-type \(L(q,1)\times N^d\), dimension 4 blocked by a Bochner-type mechanism in that analysis; toric analysis on \(\#_k(S^2\times S^2)\) gave a "BREAK" verdict (integral identities insufficient); collapsed toric adversaries survive edge-cone/strut accounting (transitions are NUTs); the diagonal constant-\(K\) obstruction is only \(1.84\%\); a bi-Kähler loophole appeared in a positive noncollapsed Ozuchi route; \(E\)-type bubbles have \(W=0\) so the main positive exceptional case is \(A_1\); rank-null \(A_1\) insertions and mixed quotient rows are open targets, not settled counterexamples. A02's Chern–Weil saturation result: collapse pins both chiral energies exactly, so a positive-collapse obstruction must find forced energy defect, not missing budget. A02's Kähler exclusion/SW depletion leaves simply connected 4-manifolds with \(b_+\ge2\) and no monopole classes in the gap between existence and nonexistence machines. These peer reports are not independently developed here [Steps 22–25, 36, 41, 44, 47–52, 57–62].

- A01's BCGP \(\mathbb Z_4^2\), \(K^2=2\), six-\(A_1\) product-quotient resolution: \(T_X^0\cong(\pi_*T_Y)^G\), \(H^2(X,T_X^0)=0\) by equivariant Serre duality/Künneth/characters, globalized node smoothings, Aubin–Yau on the ample-canonical smooth fiber, ADE simultaneous resolution plus Ehresmann transfer a negative Einstein metric to the minimal resolution — evidence that serious near-Einstein candidates may already admit an unrelated exact Einstein metric, illustrating the output-metric quantifier [Step 54 peer record].

- Step 62 literature findings: Brendle–Kapouleas give a compact ancient Ricci flow on a fixed Eguchi–Hanson desingularization with \(\sup|\operatorname{Ric}|\to0\) while \(\sup|\operatorname{Rm}|\to\infty\) — topology and curvature concentrating in shrinking regions, but a zero-Einstein-scale phenomenon that does not exclude another Einstein metric on the smooth manifold. Kapovitch–Lott show that under noncollapse plus suitable spin/\(\pi_1\) information, almost Ricci-flat four-manifolds reconstruct K3 or flat topology and hence carry Ricci-flat metrics; the uncontrolled information lies precisely in collapse [Step 62].

- Anderson's 2003 preprint states that sufficiently tight sectional pinching around \(-1\), with a threshold depending only on dimension, produces a negative Einstein metric, explicitly including Gromov–Thurston and Farrell–Jones manifolds. Step 62 could not validate its status by retrieval; Step 63's detailed internal review found the proof self-contained and sound (the ergodic Lemma 2.2 is the subtlest step), and Hamenstädt–Jäckel 2024 independently confirms the conclusion for selected Gromov–Thurston families by a spectral argument. All sectional-pinching counterexample routes are therefore closed: exotic near-hyperbolic smoothings are an existence laboratory, not a no-Einstein sequence [Steps 62–63].

- Farrell–Jones exotic smoothings give arbitrarily tightly sectionally pinched metrics in high dimensions, but non-diffeomorphism to a hyperbolic manifold excludes only hyperbolic metrics. In dimension four, Besson–Courtois–Gallot rigidity appears to force any Einstein metric on a homotopy-real-hyperbolic manifold to be hyperbolic, with positive Einstein excluded by infinite \(\pi_1\) and Ricci-flat excluded by \(\pi_1\) structure; thus an exotic smooth real-hyperbolic four-manifold with pinched metrics would be a decisive negative-branch construction — but no four-dimensional exotic smoothing construction is known; the FJ mechanism starts in higher dimensions where the special 4D Einstein rigidity is unavailable [Step 62].

- Extended graph four-manifolds (Di Cerbo) have source-supported exclusion of all Einstein metrics and are assembled from hyperbolic cusp pieces — the most concrete counterexample topology candidate. Scalar cusp calculation: for \(g=dr^2+f(r)^2g_{T^3}\), \(u=f'/f\), the Ricci eigenvalues are \(-3(u'+u^2)\) radial and \(-(u'+3u^2)\) tangential; \(\|\operatorname{Ric}+3g\|_{\rm op}\le\delta\) forces \(|u^2-1|\le2\delta/3\), so for \(\delta<3/2\), \(u\) cannot change sign and a scalar-warped neck cannot reverse cusp orientation [Step 62].

- Step 63 strengthened this to a representation-invariant barrier: for \(g=dr^2+G(r)\) with intrinsically flat \(T^3\) slices, \(S=\tfrac12G^{-1}G'\), \(H=\operatorname{tr}S\), the traced Gauss equation gives \(H^2-\operatorname{tr}(S^2)=-(R_g-2\operatorname{Ric}(\partial_r,\partial_r))\); tight pinching implies \(|H^2-\operatorname{tr}(S^2)-6|\le4\delta\), and self-adjointness gives \(\operatorname{tr}(S^2)\ge H^2/3\), hence \(H^2\ge9-6\delta\). No continuous contracting-to-expanding reversal is possible for \(\delta<3/2\), even with anisotropy and noncommuting shape operators — shear strengthens the obstruction. An \(r\)-dependent torus translation over a one-dimensional base is locally removable by coordinates; it carries no curvature twist. For general slices the constraint becomes \(H^2-|S|^2=R(\gamma_r)-R_g+2\operatorname{Ric}(\partial_r,\partial_r)\); at a mean-curvature-zero slice, tight pinching requires \(R(\gamma_r)=-6-|S|^2+O(\delta)\), so intrinsic negative slice curvature is the only freedom that could change the conclusion [Step 63].

- TTCS verification then blocked the proposed escape: \(T^3\) cannot carry \(\operatorname{Ric}=-2g\) (it would force constant sectional curvature \(-1\), contradicting \(\pi_1=\mathbb Z^3\)); Lohkamp gives \(\operatorname{Ric}<0\), not Einstein; stretching the transition annulus does not remove \(O(1)\) algebraic constraints at the \(H=0\) slice. The graph-manifold counterexample route via flat torus slices is therefore blocked and instead suggests a gap theorem; A02's opposite-warping modes remain relevant only if they genuinely leave the flat-slice one-dimensional-base setting [Step 63].

- Step 63's TTCS generator produced five new research directions; the record identifies Direction 2 as a K-stability gap framework for the positive branch (ranked highest feasibility, Med-High), Direction 3 as orbifold desingularization for the negative branch (Med feasibility), and Direction 4 as collapsed torus bundles for \(n\ge5\) (the only concrete higher-dimensional proposal); Directions 1 and 5 are not specified in the available record. ### Decisions and Recorded Reasons

- The original Yau Problem 26 quantifiers remain active: for each \(n\), one dimension-dependent nondegenerate Ricci interval should force existence of some Einstein metric on the same closed connected smooth manifold. A four-dimensional negative-branch theorem on special topology cannot prove or disprove the full all-dimensional, dimension-only statement [Steps 1, 28-45, 53-54]. Low-dimensional baselines were kept separate: \(n=2\) by uniformization and \(n=3\) by Hamilton’s positive Ricci theorem are compatible with the proposition but do not guide \(n\ge4\) [Step 1].

- The problem was decomposed into positive and negative normalized branches \(P_n^+\), \(P_n^-\). The reason recorded was that any nondegenerate real Ricci interval contains a same-sign subinterval after scaling, so a disproof in a fixed dimension must defeat both normalized sign branches, not merely one [Steps 1, 10].

- Early broad counterexample routes were narrowed. ALE/orbifold desingularization was demoted from a global counterexample mechanism to a local obstruction mechanism because unweighted ALE Ricci residuals retain obstruction terms at fixed nonzero Einstein scale, and failure of one Einstein smoothing does not exclude another Einstein metric on the same smooth resolution [Step 1]. Min-Oo-type convergence and Lohkamp negative-Ricci flexibility were judged insufficient because they impose or lack the wrong controls for two-sided Ricci pinching [Step 1]. Flat high-frequency perturbations were deprioritized after the Ricci principal symbol was found to have only gauge kernel, so completed gauge perturbations cannot produce a genuine averaged Ricci cone [Step 2].

- The active laboratory moved to four-dimensional negative topology because Seiberg–Witten, Chern–Weil, and Ishida–LeBrun estimates provide strong no-Einstein obstructions. An initial pure \(W^+\) lower-bound claim was withdrawn after the user identified the missing gradient term in LeBrun’s Weitzenböck argument; the valid mixed scalar–Weyl inequality became the retained gauge-theoretic input [Steps 2-3]. This shifted the route from an immediate quantitative gap to near-critical analysis around \(D=A/3\) and \(\sigma=D-A/3\to0\) [Steps 3, 29-30].

- Near-critical pinching was reframed as a calibrated-profile problem. Hypothetical sequences with \(\delta_i=\|g_i^{-1}(\operatorname{Ric}_{g_i}+g_i)\|_\infty\to0\) force scalar/Weyl/Chern–Weil profiles close to a calibrated configuration, but the agents explicitly did not upgrade those integral facts to noncollapse, smooth convergence, or global Einstein existence [Steps 3-4]. Standard negative Kähler–Einstein bulk and scalar-flat connector pictures were rejected as positive-volume calibrated models because their Weyl-modulus profiles or Ricci defects are incompatible with the calibrated pointwise pinching [Steps 3-4].

- The calibrated noncollapsed local model was rejected. If a four-dimensional Einstein local limit has constant \(W^+\) spectrum with one simple and one double eigenvalue, \(\delta W^+=0\) forces the eigenform to be parallel and then \(\nabla W^+=0\); the calibrated spectrum \((-1/6,1/12,1/12)\) violates the Einstein–Weyl identity in that case [Step 6]. Thus any tight near-critical sequence for fixed critical topology must collapse at every fixed usable scale while preserving nontrivial calibrated volume/energy [Steps 5-6].

- Collapse-model work was kept as diagnostic, not classificatory. Lott orbit-volume equations obstruct many exact regular abelian negative-Einstein collapse models only under symmetry/adaptedness assumptions unavailable for arbitrary pinched metrics [Steps 7-8]. The nil\(^3\) sign was corrected; real nil\(^3\) cusp-ray models exist, and finite volume alone does not imply the earlier convexity exclusion [Steps 7-8]. Taub–NUT–AdS was reinterpreted from a universal-cover counterexample to a warning about cover-domain choice and bad NUT-core curvature averages [Steps 9-10].

- Pontryagin and circle-reduction ideas were refined but demoted. Pontryagin mass should be treated diffusely through the \(\Lambda^2_+\) characteristic density, not as localized NUT charge [Steps 10-11]. Static and twisted circle reductions were corrected but judged insufficient: corrected static Weyl formulas and \(H^2\times H^2\) show static classification is too narrow, and toric orthogonal transitivity does not make arbitrary Hopf circles static [Steps 11-12]. Kaluza–Klein/chiral variables remain useful collapse language but not the main proof engine [Step 12].

- Ye Li/Wang-style smoothing was restored as promising after the user emphasized the small-radius \(r^4\) factor: bounded mean \(|\mathrm{Rm}|^2\) on all scales up to one yields small scale-invariant energy at a fixed physical radius without sending the Einstein scale to zero [Step 13]. The normalized cutoff flow
  \[
  \partial_t g=-2a(\operatorname{Ric}+g),\qquad a=\chi^2
  \]
  was chosen because it stays on the original closed manifold, fixes exact negative Einstein metrics, and gives a homogeneous defect equation in \(E=\operatorname{Ric}+g\) [Steps 14-15].

- The analytic requirements were separated. Weighted \(aE\) controls metric drift; global unweighted \(Q=\int |E|^2\) is needed for terminal topological calibration; pointwise regularity is needed later only on strict \(a=1\) plateaux [Steps 15, 36]. A fixed-topology completion-square inequality
  \[

### Research Line

The session began by protecting the exact logical structure of Yau Problem 26. The agents separated normalized positive and negative branches and kept the all-dimensional, dimension-only quantifiers visible. This prevented the four-dimensional negative Ishida–LeBrun work from being mistaken for a full solution and remains the governing strategic constraint [Steps 1, 10, 28-54].

Initial explorations tested whether known flexibility, perturbative, convergence, or desingularization mechanisms could quickly resolve a branch. ALE/orbifold smoothing, Min-Oo-type convergence, Lohkamp negative flexibility, and flat high-frequency perturbations all failed to give the required same-manifold Einstein-existence or nonexistence conclusion under pure two-sided Ricci pinching. These failures established durable standards: a failed Einstein construction is not absence of all Einstein metrics, extra sectional/diameter controls cannot be imported, and gauge perturbations cannot be counted as true Ricci flexibility [Steps 1-2].

The research then moved to four-dimensional negative topology because it offered strong independent obstructions. The first topological gap attempt overclaimed a pure \(W^+\) inequality, and the user correction redirected the route to the valid mixed Ishida–LeBrun scalar–Weyl estimate. The critical boundary \(D=A/3\) became central: away from it, known inequalities can give easier quantitative separation, but near-critical \(\sigma/A\to0\) required understanding possible tight metrics rather than quoting no-Einstein theorems [Steps 2-4, 29-30].

Near-critical analysis produced the calibrated scalar/Weyl/topological profile and a key local contradiction. Standard negative Kähler–Einstein and scalar-flat connector models were incompatible with the calibrated profile, and the Step 6 projector argument ruled out a noncollapsed Einstein germ with the calibrated \(W^+\) spectrum. This was the first strong geometric obstruction: any hypothetical tight sequence must collapse at fixed scale while carrying diffuse calibrated mass [Steps 3-6].

The subsequent collapse-model period developed caution rather than a proof. Abelian, nil, Taub–NUT–AdS, Pontryagin, static, and toric reductions each revealed possible failure modes or necessary corrections, but all depended on special symmetry, cover choices, or localized-charge interpretations not available for arbitrary pinched metrics. The lasting lesson was that collapse must be handled by an extraction/smoothing mechanism, not by classifying a small set of model collapses [Steps 7-12].

Smoothing became the active method after the small-radius \(r^4\) observation restored fixed-scale regularization as plausible in collapsed settings. The normalized cutoff flow was selected because it preserves the closed manifold and fixes exact negative Einstein metrics. Early localized Li arguments failed because of domain mismatch and lack of finite propagation, forcing the more delicate degenerate Wang/Yang framework with weighted quantities and global \(Q\) kept separate from local smoothing [Steps 13-20].

The analytic framework evolved through several repairs. Weighted moments \(H_q,J_m\), shifted curvature \(T=\mathrm{Rm}+G\), and \(U=aT\) replaced raw curvature quantities because transition regions cannot be handled by dividing by \(a\). The four-dimensional Sobolev-volume cancellation survived later scrutiny: on maximal-function good supports, \(K_2(0)\) scales with local volume while the Sobolev constant carries volume\(^{-1/2}\), so \(\mathcal S K_2^{1/2}\) can be collapse-independent on matched supports [Steps 19-20, 30-34, 46-47, 54].

Steps 50-54 progressively sharpened that bottleneck. The project no longer seeks an unweighted homogeneous curvature-energy proof or a naive fixed-cutoff DeTurck flow. The precise unresolved analytic statement is now a transported-square mixed parabolic–transport start theorem with weighted dissipation, branch-oriented difference estimates, all-order \(\varepsilon\)-uniform hierarchy, smooth limit across zeros, pullback to the exact fixed-cutoff geometric flow, and restart from smooth endpoints [Steps 50-54]. The positive-time shifted \(T/U/C\) continuation mechanism remains a separate downstream tool once a start exists [Steps 50, 54].

The Step 54 scaling correction preserved the viability of the restricted IL route. A02’s claim that the global Seiberg–Witten density bound forces \(\delta_0\sim A^{-1/2}\) was rejected because the terminal construction averages over a proportional-volume family of eligible cores, not one arbitrary unit ball; \(\int\mathfrak D\le C\delta^2\operatorname{Vol}(M)\) and \(\operatorname{Vol}(P)\ge\alpha\operatorname{Vol}(M)\) give a selected core with mean \(O(\delta^2)\) uniformly [Step 54]. Thus the IL route is not strategically defeated by that scaling argument, although it remains a special four-dimensional negative mechanism and analytically incomplete [Step 54].

The exact restricted theorem statement still needs care if the analytic start closes. It must state the monopole sign-family hypothesis, source-supported sufficient cases, \(q=D-A/3\) or \(q/A\to0\) assumptions, negative-part corrections if \(q<0\), curvature-to-volume/geography bounds, small initial \(\|\operatorname{Ric}+g\|_\infty\), support parameters, and which constants are per-datum, per-topology, or geography-uniform [Steps 29-30, 43, 46-54]. It must also explicitly avoid using stationary collars, disjoint summation, or global \(Q\) cancellation before the exact flow is obtained [Steps 48, 54].

The positive branch and high-dimensional directions remain open but increasingly important. A02’s positive-branch corrections showed that some apparent exceptional bubbles are not obstruction sources, that \(A_1\)-type rank-null insertions and mixed product-quotient rows are the hard cases, and that a bi-Kähler loophole remains in noncollapsed first-order projection [Steps 41, 44, 50-54]. A01’s product-quotient result showed that at least one serious candidate actually carries a negative Einstein metric via algebraic-geometric smoothing and Aubin–Yau, reinforcing the original problem’s output-metric quantifier: local near-Einstein or gluing behavior does not determine whether the smooth manifold admits some other Einstein metric [Step 54].

The full Yau Problem 26 remains unsolved. The current restricted negative program has produced reusable analytic and geometric ideas—volume-weighted support extraction, degenerate cutoff smoothing, shifted curvature/cutoff-jet continuation, terminal spectral density, and forbidden calibrated Einstein germs—but no completed theorem yet because the exact transported-square start is still open [Steps 46-54]. Even if completed, it would address only a specified four-dimensional negative Ishida–LeBrun geography. The broader project still needs a positive-branch forcing or obstruction mechanism, arbitrary four-manifold topology analysis, \(n\ge5\) ideas, true dimension-only constants, and Lean 4 formalization only after the mathematics is complete [Steps 1, 28-54].
