\le \frac7{24}\int|E|^2,\qquad E=\operatorname{Ric}+g
\]
[Step 15]. This separated analytic demands: global \(L^2\) defect preservation for topology, weighted pointwise control of cutoff velocity for metric equivalence, and plateau regularity where \(\chi=1\) [Step 15]. But Step 15 overclaimed that localized Li bootstrap and a fixed-topology gap were resolved [Step 15]. Agent4 withdrew that gap theorem in Step 16 because Li’s bootstrap supremum involves boundary centers outside the work domain, diffusion has no finite propagation, and an interior smoothing estimate alone would not propagate curvature energy through transition regions needed for global \(Q(t)=\int|E|^2\) [Step 16]. The \(7/24\) inequality remained valid only as an ingredient conditional on later \(Q\)-control [Step 16].

Step 16 introduced the exponential-pullback alternative to broad collapse classification [Step 16]. Conditional on bounded sectional curvature on positive-volume buffered plateaux, exponential pullback to \(T_pM\) gives noncollapsed balls even if the original metric is collapsed and \(\exp_p\) is many-to-one [Step 16]. Rauch comparison and Liouville/geodesic-flow averaging yield an estimate of the form
\[
\int_P \operatorname{avg}_{B_r(0),\exp_p^*g}(F\circ\exp_p)\,d\mu(p)
\le C(n,K,r)\int_MF\,d\mu
\]
without sheet-number loss [Step 16]. The harmonic-form passage was also repaired: unique continuation alone does not prevent local mass escape, so current-metric monopole data were reconstructed using the positive part \(q^+\) of \(q=\sqrt6|W^+|-s\), gaining harmonic-amplitude and lowest-eigenline error densities without derivatives of the approximating weight [Step 16]. This harmonic/eigenline transport was later superseded by a direct LeBrun spectral density, but the exponential chart selection remained central [Steps 16,42-43].

## Weighted Wang/Yang hierarchy, support localization, and Sobolev convention repair [Steps 17-34]

The analytic program was reorganized as a simultaneous cutoff-flow bootstrap [Steps 17-23]. Step 17 derived a cleaner defect evolution under \(a=\chi^2\): inverse-metric variation cancels an explicit cubic defect reaction, leaving a schematic inequality with \(-2a|\nabla E|^2\), \(a\operatorname{Rm}(E,E)\), and cutoff-linear terms [Step 17]. TTCS corrected that pointwise defect maximum estimates need \(\|a\operatorname{Rm}(g(t))\|_\infty\), not just initial curvature mean, coupling curvature regularity and defect preservation [Step 17]. A finite-neighbor local energy system was proposed, but Step 18 downgraded it to conditional first-exit inequalities requiring smooth existence, metric comparability, Sobolev geometry, fixed overlap, cutoff control, and small neighboring energies [Steps 17-18].

Step 18 introduced the weighted defect variable \(U=aE\), showing that commuting \(a\) through the Laplacian cancels leading singular terms and that \(da\otimes da/a=4\,d\chi\otimes d\chi\) is regular [Step 18]. Fixed-\(p>2\) estimates for \(aE\) could propagate under provisional geometry, but iteration to \(p=\infty\) with one critical threshold was not automatic [Step 18]. A user sharpened derivative thresholds: metric drift requires integrability of \(\|aE\|_\infty\), while connection/cutoff-Hessian drift would need estimates like \(|\chi\nabla U|\le C\delta t^{-1/2}(r^2/t)^{2/p}\), integrable only for \(p>4\) [Step 19]. Later work kept this relevant for quantitative Hessian drift but removed it as load-bearing for zero-order first-exit closure [Steps 20-21].

Step 20 changed representation to Wang-compatible weighted moments:
\[
H_q=\int\eta^2a^{q-2}F^q,\qquad
J_m=\int\eta^2a^{m-2}|E|^m,\qquad
F=(1+|\operatorname{Rm}|^2)^{1/2}
\]
[Step 20]. Here \(H_2\) is unweighted critical curvature energy, \(H_3=\int\eta^2aF^3\) is the weighted cubic potential, and \(J_6\) preserves the initial \(\delta^6\) defect factor [Step 20]. The Yang fixed-cutoff exponent recurrence \(p_{j+1}=3p_j/2\), \(p'_{j+1}=3p'_j/2+1\), with \(p'_j=p_j-2\), exactly matches the weights \(a^{p_j-2}\) [Steps 20,25]. Thus powers of \(\chi\) became essential rather than disposable boundary suppression [Step 20].

A proposed Nash semigroup shortcut using conformal measure \(d\nu=a^{-2}d\mu\) was rejected [Steps 21-22]. The inverse-square potential stress test \(V=\kappa/|x|^2\), \(0<\kappa<1\), showed that small Hardy form bound does not prevent singular spatial weights in the heat kernel, so ordinary unweighted \(L^2\to L^\infty\) ultracontractivity fails [Step 22]. The lesson was that critical \(L^2\) form smallness is insufficient; the route must perform the critical-to-subcritical upgrade \(H_2\to H_3\), then weighted Moser iteration [Step 22].

Step 23 repaired localization by replacing a graph argument that tried to absorb outer dissipation into inner dissipation [Step 23]. The agents returned to a single-good-support construction aligned with Yang and Wang: the auxiliary cutoff \(\eta\) equals one near the whole support of the flow cutoff \(\chi\), so the unweighted \(L^2\) factor in Hölder is controlled by the same component energy while Sobolev variables retain the flow cutoff [Step 23]. The matched weak inequalities became
\[
H_q'+c_qD_q
\le C_qr^{-2}H_q+
C_q\int\eta^2a^{q-1}F^{q+1}
\]
for \(q=2,3\) under provisional first-exit geometry [Step 23]. The \(q=2\) estimate gives spacetime \(H_3\), and a separate \(q=3\) inequality propagates a good time slice to terminal time, excluding narrow spikes [Step 23]. Homogeneous defect estimates \(Q\) and \(J_6\) remained distinct [Step 23].

Step 24 found a curvature-evolution correction: under the conformal component \(h=-2ag\), the fully covariant curvature tensor has a linear term \(-2a\operatorname{Rm}\), verified by constant homothety [Step 24]. Step 25 corrected its interpretation: this term is not net damping for evolving curvature norm-energy because inverse metrics and volume variation cancel the scaling effect in dimension four [Step 25]. The route must rely on matched Sobolev absorption and homogeneous defect control, not artificial normalization coercivity [Step 25].

Step 25 made the exact Yang-weight correspondence central [Step 25]. The interpolation
\[
a^{p-1}F\Phi^p
=(aF^3)^{1/3}\big(a^{3p/2-2}\Phi^{3p/2}\big)^{2/3}
\]
followed by Sobolev and Young gives polynomial-in-\(p\) coefficients compatible with a convergent Moser product once \(H_3\) is controlled [Step 25]. Starting at \(p_0=3\) was expected to yield \(\|a\operatorname{Rm}\|_\infty\sim1/t\), while starting at \(p_0=6\) with \(J_6\) was expected to yield integrable \(\|aE\|_\infty\sim\delta(r^2/t)^{1/3}\) [Step 25]. Step 26 extended fixed-exponent derivations to a complete general-\(p\) weighted tensor inequality for \(p\ge3\), including boundary terms, Hessian-\(a\) integration by parts, regularization for \(|E|\), noninteger cutoff-power handling, and active-region energy bookkeeping [Step 26]. The notes `step26_general_p_and_sobolev_resolution.md` and `verify_step26_general_p_and_sobolev.py` became key references [Step 26].

Step 26 also resolved an initial Sobolev-input gap at source level [Step 26]. A Maheux–Saloff-Coste local Sobolev inequality supplies, under Ricci lower bounds,
\[
\|u\|_4^2\le \mathcal S\left(\|\nabla u\|_2^2+r^{-2}\|u\|_2^2\right),
\qquad \mathcal S\sim C(n,Kr^2)\frac{r^2}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Vol}(B_r)}}
\]
in the squared convention used later; compactly supported functions only add a lower-order term [Steps 25-26, notation corrected Step 34]. Step 33 temporarily misdiagnosed Sobolev absorption as carrying an extra volume factor and proposed only per-manifold conclusions using fixed-topology ball-volume lower bounds [Step 33]. Step 34 corrected both. In the squared Sobolev convention,
\[
K_3\le K_2^{1/2}\|\chi F\|_4^2
\le \mathcal S K_2^{1/2}(D_2+r^{-2}K_2).
\]
On matched good supports \(K_2\le K_0V\), so \(\gamma=\mathcal S K_2^{1/2}\le Cr^2\sqrt{K_0}\), collapse-independent [Step 34]. The fixed-manifold rescue was invalid: Ricci lower bound plus bounded total volume does not imply bounded diameter or fixed-radius ball-volume lower bounds, as degenerating products of closed hyperbolic surfaces show [Step 34]. Peer messages helped correct this misdirection [Step 34].

## Shifted curvature, topology-family extension, and support geometry [Steps 27-30]

Step 27 repaired the high-order continuation specification by shifting curvature:
\[
G=\frac{g\wedge g}{2(n-1)},\qquad T=\operatorname{Rm}+G,\qquad U=aT.
\]
Then \(\operatorname{Ric}(G)=g\), \(\operatorname{Ric}(U)=a(\operatorname{Ric}+g)\), and the normalized velocity is \(\partial_tg=-2\operatorname{Ric}(U)\) [Step 27]. This absorbs the normalization source into the same curvature-contraction structure driving Wang’s cutoff-jet induction [Step 27]. The highest cutoff term \(\chi\nabla^{m+2}\chi*U\) is real; one integration by parts lowers it only to current \(\nabla^{m+1}\chi\), so the induction must couple \(\nabla^mU\) with \(\nabla^{m+1}\chi\), not suppress the extra cutoff order [Step 27]. Step 28 reviewed the shifted-curvature report and found the architecture plausible but still source-dependent at grouped Wang integrations and finite staggered-exponent estimates [Step 28].

A user message in Step 29 pushed the algebra beyond the critical boundary by retaining \(\sigma=D-A/3\ge0\) and \(I-R=A-D\) instead of imposing equality [Step 29]. The completed-square and monopole bounds extend to the entire Ishida–LeBrun no-Einstein side: topological excess \(\sigma\) tightens calibration, producing a defect identity of the form \(D_a\le R-\sigma\le R\) [Step 29]. This gave an unconditional above-critical lower bound schematically \(\delta\gtrsim\sqrt{\sigma/A}\) for \(\sigma>0\), checked by `verify_step29_family_extension_algebra.py`, `verify_step29_corrected_family.py`, and `verify_step29_uniform_gap.py` [Step 29]. Step 30 sharpened the interpretation: any escaping family with \(\delta_i\to0\) must satisfy \(\sigma_i/A_i\to0\), but strictly supercritical near-critical families with \(\sigma_i>0\) and \(\sigma_i/A_i\to0\) remain part of the analytic problem [Step 30].

Step 29 consolidated a terminal density bridge using joint density controlling Einstein defect, calibrated modulus, harmonic-form amplitude, and lowest-eigenline error; exponential-pullback averaging would select a chart whose smooth limit has the calibrated spectrum, leading to the Step 6 contradiction [Step 29]. Step 30 corrected two details [Step 30]. For varying topology, terminal errors must be normalized by \(A_i\), and positive-weight regularization should use \(\varepsilon_i=Q_i/\operatorname{Vol}_i\), not \(\varepsilon_i=Q_i\), to avoid extensive errors [Step 30]. Lowest-eigenline density is controlled only on bounded-curvature regions \(L_i\), not globally; it must be multiplied by \(1_{L_i}\) and extended by zero outside [Step 30].

Step 30 also repaired support geometry [Step 30]. The earlier \(r/5\)-separated centers did not make supports of radius \(2r/3\) disjoint, and choosing one component could lose all useful volume under collapse [Step 30]. The corrected construction takes a maximal \(r\)-separated net in the maximal-function good set, colors the graph joining centers at distance \(\le12r\), retains a color class of maximal volume weight, and obtains disjoint \(B_{6r}\) auxiliary domains while preserving a fixed fraction of total \(B_r\)-volume [Step 30]. Later refinements used disjoint \(B_{8r}\) Sobolev domains and nested strict buffers [Steps 46,54]. Use one common cutoff
\[
a=\sum_j\chi_j^2,
\]
with strict centers, larger plateau regions, support buffers, and Sobolev domains organized so all local estimates live on the same outer domains [Steps 30,46].

Topology-uniform inputs were sharpened [Step 30]. BMY points in the wrong direction for the needed upper bound, while Noether gives \(c_2(X_j)\le5c_1^2(X_j)+36\) for minimal general-type summands [Step 30]. For the standard \(b_+(N)=0\) subfamily, the exact formula
\[
\chi(N)=A/3+\sigma+6-4m-6b_1(N)
\]
must be retained; in a near-critical band \(\sigma/A\le\kappa\), it controls \(\chi(M)/A\), recovering the earlier controlled-subclass bound at \(\sigma=0\) [Steps 18,30].

## Weighted Moser, defect estimates, and continuation corrections [Steps 31-40]

Step 31 resolved a false objection that the weighted Moser iteration had a fatal half-power mismatch [Step 31]. For
\[
Z_p=a^{(p-1)/2}\Phi^{p/2},\qquad K_p=\int a^{p-2}\Phi^p,
\]
the actual parabolic step combines a time supremum of \(K_p\) with spatial Sobolev control of \(Z_p\):
\[
K_{2p}=\|Z_p\|_4^4,\qquad K_{3p/2}\le K_p^{1/2}K_{2p}^{1/2}
\]
on the active region [Step 31]. The alleged mismatch came from considering \(\|Z_p\|_3^3\), which the iteration does not use [Step 31]. A Codex counterexample showed ordinary unweighted Moser on \(U=aT\) fails near zeros of \(\chi\), so the weighted route remained primary [Step 31]. Step 31 again over-promoted the analytic state by claiming first-exit and continuation were essentially closed; Step 32 corrected this [Steps 31-32].

Step 32 established that the valid recurrence is a direct spacetime recurrence
\[
\int_I K_{3p/2}
\le(\sup_I K_p)^{1/2}\,
\mathcal S\int_I(\|\nabla Z_p\|_2^2+r^{-2}K_p),
\]
not an unsupported \(\sup K_{2p}\) passage or false four-dimensional Ladyzhenskaya product [Step 32]. Reaction weight \(a^{p-1}\), same-support cubic potential \(Y=\int aF^3\), \(J_6\), global \(Q\), moving Sobolev constants, and metric/support first-exit quantities must be proved together [Step 32]. Step 32 also sharpened continuation: at \(m=2\), the term
\[
\int\chi|\nabla^2\chi|\,|\nabla^2U|^p
\]
cannot be directly absorbed by \(\chi^2\)-weighted dissipation without either an evolving \(\|\nabla^2\chi\|_4\) estimate or exact grouped Wang cancellation [Step 32].

A user simplification in Step 35 removed artificial regularization for the key defect seed [Step 35]. Instead of \(\Phi_\varepsilon=(|E|^2+\varepsilon^2)^{1/2}\), set \(s=|E|^2\). Then
\[
J_6=\int \eta^2a^4s^3
\]
is smooth even where \(E=0\), and
\[
(\partial_t-a\Delta)s^3
=3s^2(\partial_t-a\Delta)s-6as|\nabla s|^2
\]
allows direct fixed-exponent proof [Step 35]. `workspace/notes/step35_unregularized_J6_persistence_lemma.md` found that the defect reaction is linear in curvature, so
\[
P_6=\int Fw_6^2,\qquad w_6=\eta a^{5/2}|E|^3,
\]
is absorbed by two-factor Hölder/Sobolev using \(\|F\|_2\), not by the three-factor curvature seed \(Y\) [Step 35]. Under smooth first-exit geometry and small \(\gamma=\mathcal S K_2^{1/2}\), this gives
\[
J_6(t)\le e^{C(1+r^{-2})t}J_6(0)
\]
without relying on \(q=3\) curvature seed [Steps 35-36].

Step 36 confirmed \(J_6\) persistence as a genuine conditional advance but kept it conditional on smooth degenerate flow, moving Sobolev/support comparability, and local \(K_2\) control [Step 36]. Step 36 also clarified unresolved interfaces: a transported DeTurck/existence proposal had used the wrong gauge; cancellation by a diffeomorphism generated by \(aW\) requires
\[
\mathcal L_{aW}g=a\mathcal L_Wg+da\otimes W^\flat+W^\flat\otimes da,
\]
and the scalar cutoff is transported under pullback [Step 36]. Generic \(a+\varepsilon\) strictly parabolic approximation was not accepted because Schauder constants depend on lower ellipticity and proposed small-\(a\) estimates did not close top derivatives [Step 36]. Weighted \(J_6\) and \(\|aE\|_\infty\) cannot replace global \(Q=\int|E|^2\) in terminal calibration; \(Q\) needs its own homogeneous estimate [Step 36].

Step 37 attempted to build transported DeTurck existence, global \(Q\), and base-pair continuation notes [Step 37]. A user message at Step 38 forced a more careful reading: Step 37’s base-pair note still contained erroneous estimates and an invalid finite-\(L^p\)-to-\(L^\infty\) passage [Step 38]. The key repair was a signed Hessian integration-by-parts lemma. For
\[
J=\int\chi(\nabla_i\nabla_j\chi)B^{ij}(V),
\]
with \(|B|\le C_p|V|^p\) and \(|\nabla B|\le C_p|V|^{p-1}|\nabla V|\),
\[
|J|\le\varepsilon\int\chi^2|\nabla V|^2|V|^{p-2}
+C_{p,\varepsilon}\|d\chi\|_\infty^2\int|V|^p
\]
[Step 38]. This requires neither division by \(a=\chi^2\) nor any norm of \(\nabla^2\chi\) [Step 38]. Applied to \(V=\nabla^2U\), it removed the apparent single-\(\chi\) Hessian obstruction in the \(m=2\) current-order term \(\chi\nabla^2\chi*\nabla^2U\), but did not complete higher shifted-curvature induction [Step 38].

Step 38 consolidated the curvature smoothing module on a provisional smooth first-exit interval [Step 38]. With squared Sobolev convention and \(\gamma=\mathcal SK_2^{1/2}\), the \(q=2\) estimate gives \(\sup K_2+\int D_2\lesssim K_2(0)\) and \(\int Y\lesssim\gamma K_2(0)\); \(q=3\) propagation gives \(Y(t)\lesssim\gamma K_2(0)/t\), hence \(\mathcal S^2Y(t)\lesssim\gamma^3/t\) [Step 38]. A01’s tensor inequality supplied a provisional general curvature inequality
\[
K_p'+c[pD_p^{\rm Rm}+p(p-2)D_p^F]
\le Cp^N(r^{-2}+1+\mathcal S^2Y)K_p,
\]
leading by \(p\mapsto3p/2\) to the expected endpoint \(\|aF(t)\|_\infty\lesssim\gamma/t\) [Step 38]. The defect side still lacked the all-\(p\) engine beyond fixed \(J_6\) [Step 38].

Step 39 resolved the defect all-\(p\) gap on smooth first-exit intervals [Step 39]. In `workspace/notes/step39_general_p_defect_power_inequality.md`, the agents worked directly with \(s=|E|^2\) and \(s^{p/2}\) for real \(p\ge6\), avoiding Kato regularization, division by \(a\), \(\nabla^2\chi\), and any \(E\)-independent source [Step 39]. The theorem was
\[
(H_p^E)' + c\|\nabla z_p\|_2^2
\le Cp^4(1+r^{-2}+\mathcal S^2Y)H_p^E
\]
for every real \(p\ge6\) [Step 39]. TTCS verified the algebraic structure and `workspace/scripts/verify_step39_defect_power.py` passed [Step 39]. The structural discovery was that fixed-\(p\) two-factor absorption is unsuitable along the Moser ladder because it would require \(\gamma\lesssim1/p\); the all-\(p\) argument must use a three-factor Hölder identity
\[
R_p\le Y^{1/3}H_p^{1/3}\|z_p\|_4^{4/3}
\]
and Young \((3,3/2)\), producing \(Cp^4\mathcal S^2Y\) with only polynomial \(p\)-growth [Step 39].

Step 39 also overclaimed a finite-exponent continuation induction and self-improving first-exit theorem [Step 39]. Step 40 identified a decisive flaw: a residual
\[
\chi\,\nabla^{m+1}\chi\,\nabla U\,|\nabla^mU|^{p-1}
\]
was estimated using unknown current-level \(\|\nabla^{m+1}\chi\|_{2p}\) and then silently replaced by \(\|\nabla^{m+1}\chi\|_p\) [Step 40]. The same step corrected the false assertion that every derivative of \(a=\chi^2\) carries a \(\chi\) factor; already
\[
\nabla^2a=2\chi\nabla^2\chi+2d\chi\otimes d\chi
\]
[Step 40]. Supersession notices were inserted into Step 39 continuation, first-exit, and consolidated-status notes [Step 40].

The main new proof in `workspace/notes/step40_m2_coupled_continuation_mechanism.md` repaired the \(m=2\) hard term [Step 40]. With \(V=\nabla^2U\), \(Z=\nabla^3\chi\), \(W=\nabla U\), and \(\Theta=\nabla^2\chi\), the hard integral
\[
\int\chi\,Z*W*P(V)
\]
is not estimated directly. Write \(Z=\nabla\Theta\) and integrate one derivative off \(\Theta\). The resulting terms \(d\chi*\Theta*W*P(V)\), \(\chi\Theta*V*P(V)\), and \(\chi\Theta*W*\nabla P(V)\) are controlled by previous-level finite exponents, the Step 38 signed Hessian lemma, and weighted dissipation [Step 40]. This avoids current \(Z\) in \(L^{2p}\) and avoids \(W\in L^\infty\) [Step 40]. Step 40 extended this into a staggered all-order candidate
\[
T_0\to(U_1,C_2)\to T_1\to(U_2,C_3)\to T_2\to\cdots,\qquad C_j=\nabla^j\chi,
\]
but this remained a candidate tensor-energy mechanism, not a realized flow theorem [Step 40].

## Premature theorem assemblies, terminal density repair, and tensor-ledger development [Steps 41-45]

Step 41 tried to turn the Step 40 positive-time induction into a continuation criterion and then into an unconditional restricted gap theorem [Step 41]. TTCS corrections included multiplicative metric comparison, connection-difference induction, autonomous time jets, transported-coefficient linearization weight, and finite observation-time formulation [Step 41]. Step 41 nevertheless overclaimed that the four-dimensional negative Ishida–LeBrun gap theorem was unconditional modulo all-order induction formalization [Step 41]. Step 42 superseded this claim by independently inspecting A01’s assembled theorem and exposing hidden interfaces [Step 42].

Step 42 repaired three major interfaces [Step 42]. First, local curvature seed estimates must be homogeneous in \(K_2\); bare additive \(C_0\) or \(C_0T\) terms destroy first-exit margins on shrinking-volume supports [Step 42]. Retaining the actual curvature energy identity, stationary collars, signed Hessian integration, and \(|da|^2/a\) gives
\[
K_2'+cD_2\le CY+C(1+r^{-2})K_2.
\]
With \(Y\le C\gamma(D_2+r^{-2}K_2)\), one gets a relative estimate
\[
K_2(t)/K_2(0)\le \exp(C\theta(1+r_0^2)+C\gamma_*^3)
\]
after choosing \(\theta,\gamma_*\) small [Step 42]. Second, sequence-uniform smoothing estimates require only \(|d\chi|\le C/r\), not uniform \(\|\nabla^2\chi\|_\infty\); Ricci lower bounds and averaged curvature do not supply Hessian bounds [Step 42]. Third, terminal geometry needs strong curvature convergence; \(C^{1,\alpha}\) or weak \(W^{2,p}\) convergence is insufficient because curvature uses second derivatives [Step 42]. Buffered plateaux and finite time \(T=\theta r^2\) allow local conversion to ordinary Ricci flow and Shi estimates [Step 42].

Step 42 also simplified the terminal spectral chain [Step 42]. Instead of transporting monopole solutions and eigenlines, use a pointwise LeBrun spectral density
\[
G=f^2-(b_-)^2.
\]
For trace-free \(W^+\), \(G=0\) together with \(s=-4\) and \(|W^+|^2=1/24\) forces \(\operatorname{Spec}(W^+)=(-1/6,1/12,1/12)\), after which the Step 6 projector contradiction applies [Step 42]. Step 42 did not yet prove the integral bound for \(G\); it flagged that if \(q_i=D_i-A_i/3\) is not assumed nonnegative, the terminal density must include \(912\pi^2(-q_i)_+\) [Step 42].

Step 43 used direct source reading of LeBrun’s proof of Theorem 2.3 to prove the needed terminal \(G\)-density bound [Step 43]. The user highlighted that LeBrun explicitly establishes
\[
\int\left(\left(\frac{2s}{3}+2w\right)_-\right)^2\ge 32\pi^2(a^+)^2
\]
for every \(H\)-adapted metric before passing to weaker modulus inequalities [Step 43]. In `workspace/notes/step43_terminal_density_G_lemma.md`, the agents derived
\[
\int G\le 6Q+48\pi^2(-q_{\rm top})_+
\]
and full terminal density
\[
\int\mathfrak D\le119Q+912\pi^2(-q_{\rm top})_+,
\quad
\mathfrak D=|E|^2+(s+4)^2+(s+8\sqrt6|W^+|)^2+G
\]
[Step 43]. This made the terminal proof shorter: strong curvature convergence plus \(G\to0\), \(s\to-4\), and \(|W^+|^2\to1/24\) gives the calibrated spectrum directly [Step 43].

Step 43 also attempted to resolve general-order unweighted \(T\) estimates, claiming that bounded \(|U|\) gives all-derivative finite-\(L^p\) bounds and smooth continuation [Step 43]. Step 44 corrected this: bounded \(aT\), metric equivalence, and finite total curvature do not imply uniform \(L^p\) bounds for unweighted \(T\) near the zero set of \(a\) [Step 44]. The missing seed is dynamical. In `workspace/notes/step44_zero_order_T_seed_repair.md`, Step 44 tested the zero-order shifted equation against \(|T|^{p-2}T\) and retained signed Hessian-\(a\) contractions [Step 44]. Since quadratic curvature reactions carry \(a\),
\[
a|T|^{p+1}=|U|\,|T|^p,
\]
and Hessian-\(a\) terms integrate by parts to \(|da|^2/a=4|d\chi|^2\), yielding a per-datum finite-slab estimate
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\int |T|^p
+c_p\int a|T|^{p-2}|\nabla T|^2
\le C_p(K+1+\|d\chi\|_\infty^2)\int |T|^p+C'_p\operatorname{Vol}
\]
[Step 44]. This supplies \(T_0\) in every finite \(L^p\) up to a finite endpoint, per datum and not collapse-uniform [Step 44].

Step 44 developed two start/restart routes [Step 44]. The normalized Yang route in `step44_normalized_yang_tame_start_restart.md` reads Yang Theorem 8.2 directly and formulates the transported system with \(\hat a=(\chi\circ\phi_t^{-1})^2\) [Step 44]. The normalization \(-2\hat a\hat g\) is order zero and should not affect Yang’s gauge cancellation; the transport variation has one cutoff factor, \(\delta\hat a\sim\chi\,d\chi(\zeta)\), not \(\chi^2\) [Step 44]. A coefficient-regularization route using \(b_\varepsilon=\chi^2+\varepsilon^2\) was also explored, with useful identities
\[
\nabla^r b_\varepsilon=\nabla^r a,\qquad |db_\varepsilon|^2/b_\varepsilon\le4|d\chi|^2,\qquad a/b_\varepsilon\le1,
\]
but constants may depend on the full smooth datum and must be uniform in \(\varepsilon\) only for the passage [Step 44]. A candidate arbitrary-order tensor ledger `step44_arbitrary_order_tensor_ledger.md` was written, but only scalar/exponent checks and TTCS partial support existed [Step 44].

Step 45 repaired structural inconsistencies in the tensor ledger [Step 45]. A user identified that the ledger declared a metric-compatible time derivative \(D_t\) but used coordinate-time identities. If \(D_tg=0\), then \(D_tG=0\), whereas the ledger used nonzero \(\partial_tG\); also \([D_t,\nabla]\) acts on derivative slots, so \(D_t(d\chi)\) need not vanish even for fixed scalar \(\chi\) [Step 45]. Step 45 switched to coordinate \(\partial_t\) throughout, retained the exact \(\partial_t\Gamma\) formula, and accounted for norm/measure variation only at tested-energy level [Step 45]. TTCS corrected the lower-order normalization formula to
\[
\partial_tG=-(S\wedge g+g\wedge S)/(n-1),\qquad S=\operatorname{Ric}(U)
\]
[Step 45].

The ledger also mishandled derivatives of \((db*db)T\) by expanding into derivatives of \(\chi\) too early and dropping factors [Step 45]. The correct starting family is
\[
\sum_{r+s+t=m}\nabla^{r+1}b*\nabla^{s+1}b*T_t
\]
before expanding \(B_k=\nabla^kb\) into cutoff jets [Step 45]. At order zero, \(db*db*T=4\chi^2d\chi*d\chi*T\), not \(d\chi*d\chi*T\); preserving \(\chi^2\) permits conversion through \(U=bT\) and controls regularized weights [Step 45]. The repaired artifact `Sessions/S0910A03/workspace/notes/step45_coordinate_tensor_ledger_and_regularized_closure.md` became the main reference for the staggered finite-exponent ordering
\[
T_0\to(U_1,C_2)\to T_1\to(U_2,C_3)\to T_2\to\cdots
\]
on a smooth bootstrap interval for \(b=\chi^2+\varepsilon^2\), but Step 45 emphasized that this was still a long tensor-energy construction supported by TTCS and ledger checks, not a polished source theorem or final gap proof [Step 45].

## Consolidation attempt, repaired support/terminal interfaces, and theorem-status caution [Steps 46-48]

Step 46 performed a connected verification of the restricted negative Ishida–LeBrun argument after the Step 45 repairs [Step 46]. It clarified a key separation of uniformities: weighted energies \(K_2,Y,J_6\), all-\(p\) defect ladder, metric drift, and global \(Q\) must be sequence-uniform across a collapsing Ishida–LeBrun sequence; short-time construction and higher-derivative continuation need only be finite for each individual smooth datum [Step 46]. The shifted tensor \(U=a(\operatorname{Rm}+G)\) was the interface: sequence-uniform Moser estimates bound \(U\) at positive time, while per-datum staggered \(T/U/C\) continuation consumes that bound without requiring unweighted pointwise curvature near \(a=0\) [Step 46].

Step 46 refined support geometry [Step 46]. Starting from geography-uniform \(\operatorname{Vol}(M)/A\approx32\pi^2/9\) and \(\int(1+|\operatorname{Rm}|^2)=O(A)\), choose an absorption number \(\kappa\) first and then a fixed physical radius \(r\) so that the maximal-function bad set has small volume proportion [Step 46]. A maximal \(r\)-separated good net is colored by weights \(\operatorname{Vol}B_r(x)\), not center count; choosing one weighted color and separating centers sufficiently makes \(B_{8r}\) Sobolev domains disjoint while retaining total inner-center volume \(\ge\alpha A\) [Step 46]. Smooth distance approximations produce \(\chi,\eta\) with uniform first derivative bounds but only datum-dependent higher jets [Step 46]. The small absorption quantity is \(\mathcal S_\alpha K_{2,\alpha}(0)^{1/2}\le C\kappa\); shrinking \(r\) alone does not improve a four-dimensional unnormalized curvature integral because model ball volume is proportional to \(r^4\) [Step 46].

Step 46 also firmed the terminal chain [Step 46]. LeBrun source lines 195–225 in `Knowledge/objects/papers/Ricci-curvature-minimal-volumes-and-Seiberg-Witten-theory--16b01946d13f--cab40be18df4/object.md` explicitly prove the spectral lower bound for every \(H\)-adapted metric, not just a Yamabe minimizer [Step 46]. Inner centers retain positive terminal volume by small metric drift; on \(a=1\) plateaux the normalized flow becomes ordinary Ricci flow after scaling/time change; local Shi estimates on a spacetime buffer give strong curvature convergence; exponential-pullback Liouville–Rauch averaging supplies a noncollapsed chart [Step 46]. The bounded-\(A\) versus unbounded-\(A\) split was noted: mixed monopole inequalities force \(q/A\to0\), and if \(A\) is bounded with \(q\in(1/3)\mathbb Z\), \(q=0\) eventually, but the same smoothing/terminal mechanism is still needed [Step 46]. The remaining load-bearing task was still the fully indexed Step 45 tensor family and common-time coefficient-regularization compactness [Step 46].

Step 47 consolidated the restricted theorem into `Sessions/S0910A03/workspace/notes/step47_consolidated_negative_IL_gap_theorem.md` and separated a topology-independent smoothing module \(S\) from an Ishida–LeBrun obstruction module \(O\) [Step 47]. It also repaired a terminal spectral error: knowing the calibrated spectrum at one point does not extend it to a neighborhood by continuity. The repair used core-ball geometry, Shi-derived Lipschitz control of \(\mathfrak D\), and Bishop–Gromov relative volume comparison: if the mean of \(\mathfrak D\) on a core ball is small and \(\mathfrak D\) has Lipschitz constant \(L\), then \(\sup_{\rm core}\mathfrak D=O(\delta^{2/5})\), so the limiting pullback ball has \(\mathfrak D\equiv0\) and hence constant calibrated spectrum [Step 47]. A01’s parallel approach via a quantitative local \(\Phi\) lower bound from elliptic-upgrade compactness closed the same gap differently [Step 47]. The \(K_2\) first-exit threshold was also corrected to use explicit Grönwall \(K_2(t)\le e^{C_K\theta(r^2+1)}K_2(0)\) with \(\theta\) chosen for a strict improvement, not a generic \(CK_2(0)\) bound [Step 47].

Step 48, prompted by a user correction, refused to certify Step 47’s theorem wording [Step 48]. It identified two load-bearing regressions. First, Step 47 transferred localized \(K_q,J_m,Q\) estimates to \(b_\varepsilon=\chi^2+\varepsilon^2\) and used them to obtain a common regularized time, but for \(\varepsilon>0\) the exterior evolves by \(-2\varepsilon^2(\operatorname{Ric}+g)\), so frozen complements, stationary collars, disjoint-support summation, and exterior-free global \(Q\) estimates are unavailable [Step 48]. The correct order is: obtain an exact per-datum \(a=\chi^2\) flow independently; apply sequence-uniform support estimates only after the exact flow exists [Step 48]. Second, Step 47 treated the curvature Moser endpoint as uniformly bounded on \([0,T]\), but the endpoint behaves like \(\gamma/t\); continuation can only use it on a positive-time slab \([T^*/2,T^*)\) near a hypothetical finite endpoint [Step 48].

Step 48 also repaired theorem hypotheses [Step 48]. The Step 47 assumptions “simply connected general type” and \(b_+(N)=0\) do not by themselves provide the monopole classes used in the scalar–Weyl inequalities [Step 48]. The theorem must assume an explicit monopole sign family, with source-supported sufficient cases from Ishida–LeBrun: two or three simply connected symplectic/general-type summands with \(b_+\equiv3\pmod4\), Bauer–Furuta/nonzero mod-2 Seiberg–Witten hypotheses as appropriate, and a negative-definite \(N\), yielding classes \(\sum\pm c_1(X_j)+\sum\pm E_\ell\) [Step 48]. Module \(S\) must also assume small initial \(\|\operatorname{Ric}+g\|_\infty\le\delta\); Ricci lower control plus curvature budget alone does not supply \(J_6\), \(Q(0)\), or metric drift [Step 48].

## Normalized cutoff-flow start: invalid attempts, source-based reductions, and current synchronized-output construction [Steps 49-54]

Step 49 attempted to construct a normalized cutoff-flow existence theorem and corrected restricted statement [Step 49]. It computed the normalization variation under \(h=-2bg\): the fully covariant curvature variation includes a positive Kulkarni–Nomizu source \(+g\wedge\nabla^2b\), and the \(L^p\) reaction coefficient is \((2p-n)\int b|\operatorname{Rm}|^p\), positive for \(p>n/2\) and neutral at the critical exponent [Step 49]. It also restructured metric drift away from integrating the divergent \(\gamma/t\) endpoint from \(t=0\) [Step 49]. But Step 50 found a deeper regression: metric equivalence does not control the evolving connection or covariant derivatives of the fixed cutoff, since
\[
\nabla_g^2a=\partial^2a-\Gamma(g)\partial a.
\]
Thus all higher \(\nabla_g^ka\) are coupled unknowns under the flow, not prescribed bounded source tensors [Step 50]. Critical \(L^{n/2}\) or any finite \(L^p\) curvature control without derivative estimates also does not yield pointwise curvature [Step 50]. Step 49’s nonlinear coefficient-regularized start and extension theorem were superseded [Step 50].

Step 50 isolated a sharper source-based start route through Yang’s transported DeTurck variables [Step 50]. In hatted variables with \(\widehat\chi=\chi\circ\varphi^{-1}\), \(\widehat a=\widehat\chi^2\), metric variation \(h=\delta\widehat g\), and Eulerian diffeomorphism variation \(\zeta=\delta\varphi\circ\varphi^{-1}\),
\[
\delta[-2\widehat a\,\widehat g]
=-2\widehat a h+4\widehat\chi\,d\widehat\chi(\zeta)\widehat g.
\]
This has no derivatives of \(h\) or \(\zeta\) and changes only Yang’s lower-order \(Dh+E\psi\) slots; it introduces no new composition type beyond the transported cutoff already present in Yang’s system [Step 50]. Step 50 stated this as a strict reduction to Yang’s imported neighborhood-uniform smooth-tame inverse, including transport symmetrization, time norms, reference-pair estimates, and higher parameter derivatives, not as a self-contained proof [Step 50]. Continuation remained separate and had to retain coupled cutoff jets via shifted variables \(T=\operatorname{Rm}+G\), \(U=aT\), using the staggered \(T/U/C\) hierarchy [Step 50].

Step 51 tried to convert the Yang perturbation idea into a precise \(L^p\) normalized perturbation estimate [Step 51]. It emphasized the conformal scaling identity: the normalization contributes \((2p-n)\int a|\operatorname{Rm}|^p\), vanishing at \(p=n/2\), and the Hessian source from \(+g\wedge\nabla^2a\) was claimed to reduce by integration by parts to gradient absorption plus \(\|d\chi\|_\infty^2\) coefficients [Step 51]. Step 51 reported a completed normalized Yang–Wang per-datum theorem [Step 51]. Step 52 superseded this conclusion using an inexpensive decisive test [Step 52]. On a flat torus with nonconstant smooth cutoff, the normalized flow immediately creates curvature through \(g\wedge\operatorname{Hess}(a)\), so any homogeneous Grönwall for \(\int|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\) would falsely force zero curvature energy [Step 52]. The script `workspace/scripts/step52_flat_cutoff_forcing_test.py` verified this for period-\(2\pi\) \(T^4\) with \(\chi=(1+\cos x_1)/2\): \(|g\wedge\operatorname{Hess}(a)|^2=12(a'')^2\), \(\int_0^{2\pi}(a'')^2=\pi/2\), and \(\int|{\rm Rm}(g(t))|^2=48\pi^4t^2+O(t^3)\) [Step 52]. The failure in Step 51 was precise: after one integration by parts, absorption by \(aF^{p-2}|\nabla{\rm Rm}|^2\) leaves \((|da|^2/a)F^{p-2}\), not \(F^p\); integrating again reintroduces \(\Delta_ga\), whose control is the evolving cutoff-jet problem [Step 52].

Step 52 then studied Xu’s detailed proof of local Ricci-flow start (`staging/downloads/0907.5604.pdf`, converted to `staging/processing/xu_local_ricci_flow.txt`) [Step 52]. In Xu’s fixed-coordinate frozen strictly parabolic map, adding the algebraic reaction \(-2\chi^2V\) is harmless: it does not change the principal symbol, preserves eigenvalue/positivity estimates after shortening time, and adds bounded terms to Sobolev energies and contraction [Step 52]. But TTCS found that a fixed Eulerian cutoff in the gauge-fixed equation pulls back to a transported cutoff, because \(\phi^*(a\widehat g)=(a\circ\phi)\phi^*\widehat g\), not \(a\,\phi^*\widehat g\) [Step 52]. Thus the metric-only Xu repair gives the wrong geometric flow [Step 52]. The correct system must transport the coefficient: \(\widehat a=a\circ\phi^{-1}\) or \(\widehat\chi=\chi\circ\phi^{-1}\), with a scalar transport equation coupled to the DeTurck metric equation, so that \(\widehat a\circ\phi=a\) and the pullback solves the fixed-coefficient geometric flow [Step 52].

Step 53 adopted the user’s suggestion to transport \(\widehat\chi\) rather than an arbitrary scalar \(\widehat a\), preserving the square structure \(\widehat a=\widehat\chi^2\) and identities such as \(|d\widehat a|^2/\widehat a=4|d\widehat\chi|^2\) by continuous extension [Step 53]. It proposed a coupled system
\[
\partial_t\widehat\chi=\widehat\chi^2 W(\widehat\chi)
\]
and claimed a staggered parabolic-ODE grading closes via weighted dissipation \(\int\psi^2|\nabla^{s+1}V|^2\) [Step 53]. TTCS corrected several features: the parabolic gain is weighted, the Lie cross-term \(2\operatorname{sym}(d(\psi^2)\otimes W^\flat)\) is not pointwise lower triangular but can be treated after energy-level integration by parts, and the contraction cannot use \(\|\delta U\|_{H^{\tilde p+1}}\le C\|\delta U\|_{H^{\tilde p}}\) [Step 53]. Step 53 nevertheless reported a structurally complete per-datum existence theorem, but Step 54 corrected this [Steps 53-54].

Step 54 identified the defect in Step 53’s Banach contraction [Step 54]. The frozen transport velocity depends on the input metric \(U\), so the transport difference contains one derivative of \(U_1-U_2\), while the weighted parabolic dissipation belongs to the output difference \(V_1-V_2\) [Step 54]. A bounded high-order ball gives only Hölder-\(1/2\) dependence by interpolation, not the Lipschitz dependence needed for contraction; the invariant ball in Step 53 did not supply the additional input derivative it invoked [Step 54]. Step 53’s theorem and scaling section were marked superseded [Step 54].

Step 54 then developed a synchronized-output construction as the current active start mechanism [Step 54]. Given a frozen metric path \(U\), solve jointly for an output metric \(V\) and transported cutoff \(\beta\), using \(\beta^2+\varepsilon\) as the metric diffusion coefficient and \(\beta^2W(V)\) as the transport velocity [Step 54]. At a fixed point \(U=V\), the \(\varepsilon\to0\) system is exactly the transported-cutoff DeTurck formulation whose pullback solves
\[
\partial_tg=-2\chi^2(\operatorname{Ric}+g)
\]
[Step 54]. The single-solution high-order energy has weighted dissipation
\[
\sum_{k\le s}\int(\beta^2+\varepsilon)|D^{k+1}V|^2.
\]
Top derivatives of \(\beta\) in the Lie term are integrated onto \(V\) and acquire a \(\beta\) factor; top derivatives of \(V\) in the transport equation already carry \(\beta^2\) [Step 54]. TTCS supported the finite-order single-solution estimate [Step 54].

For differences, Step 54 corrected the contraction strategy by working two Sobolev orders below the invariant ball, \(r=s-2\), and orienting both equations relative to branch 2 [Step 54]. The metric principal difference is decomposed with branch-2 operator \((\beta_2^2+\varepsilon)U_2^{-1}D^2Z\), and coefficient-difference sources are controlled directly by individual \(H^s\) bounds, avoiding interpolation of an input difference [Step 54]. The transport top term \(\beta_2^2D^{r+1}Z\) is absorbed by branch-2 metric dissipation [Step 54]. The Lie split
\[
d(\beta_1^2)W(U_1)-d(\beta_2^2)W(U_2)
=[d(\beta_1^2)-d(\beta_2^2)]W(U_1)+d(\beta_2^2)[W(U_1)-W(U_2)]
\]
uses
\[
d(\beta_1^2)-d(\beta_2^2)=2\beta_2d\omega+2\omega d\beta_1
\]
to provide a matching \(\beta_2\) factor for the top \(d\omega\) term [Step 54]. After TTCS corrected the top coefficient to \(W(U_1)\) under this split, no unsupported unweighted \(D^{r+1}(U_1-U_2)\), \(D^{r+1}\omega\), or \(D^{r+1}Z\) term and no inverse power of \(\varepsilon\) remained at finite order [Step 54]. These results are recorded in `workspace/notes/step54_exact_synchronized_output_ledger.md` and `workspace/notes/step54_route_reassessment_and_joint_weighted_iteration.md` [Step 54].

The start theorem is still unfinished after Step 54 [Step 54]. The remaining analytic work is to construct the fixed-\(\varepsilon\) coupled parabolic–transport inner solution, run the outer Xu-style contraction rigorously in \(H^r\), and derive an all-order \(\varepsilon\)-uniform tame hierarchy on one common interval:
\[
E_m'+cD_m\le C(E_s)E_m+C_m(E_{m-1}),
\]
together with uniform time-derivative bounds for \(V\) and \(\beta\), diagonal smooth compactness as \(\varepsilon\to0\), smoothness across the transported zero set without dividing by \(\beta\), recovery of the exact fixed-cutoff geometric flow by pullback, and restart from a smooth endpoint [Step 54]. Finite \(H^s\) compactness alone does not yield smooth zero-interface limits; this is now the precise unresolved interface [Step 54].

## Family-uniform normalization correction and status of the restricted Ishida–LeBrun route [Steps 46-54]

A strategic misreading arose in Step 53: A02’s scaling analysis was accepted as showing that the terminal density bound \(\int\mathfrak D\le119Q\sim\delta^2A\) forces local mean defect \(\delta^2A\), so any gap would shrink like \(A^{-1/2}\) and be only per-topology [Step 53]. Step 54 corrected this as false because it drops the volume-weighted normalization built into the support construction [Step 54]. The terminal construction retains eligible centers \(P\) with \(\operatorname{Vol}(P)\ge\alpha\operatorname{Vol}(M)\sim\alpha A\), and exponential-pullback averaging gives
\[
\operatorname{avg}_{p\in P}\operatorname{mean}_{\exp_p^*B}\mathfrak D
\le C\,\frac{\int\mathfrak D}{\operatorname{Vol}(P)}
\le C'\delta^2
\]
uniformly, with no residual \(A\) [Step 54]. The same correction applies to the support seed: the geography-uniform curvature-to-volume budget permits a small fixed physical radius, and on maximal-function good supports \(K_2(0)\le(1+\kappa^2)\operatorname{Vol}(B)\), while \(\mathcal S\le Cr^2\operatorname{Vol}(B)^{-1/2}\), so
\[
\gamma=\mathcal SK_2(0)^{1/2}\le Cr^2\sqrt{1+\kappa^2}
\]
with collapse volume cancellation [Step 54]. A02’s contrary audit had chosen \(r\propto A^{1/4}\) unnecessarily and turned an upper local energy bound into a lower bound for the Sobolev-energy product [Step 54]. Even if a proof produced only a sufficient \(c/\sqrt A\) threshold, it would not prove an upper bound on the true optimal gap or \(\inf_A\delta_0(A)=0\) [Step 54]. Peer correction #386 transmitted this repair, and A01 independently confirmed the proportional-volume cancellation [Step 54].

Thus the current restricted negative Ishida–LeBrun route is not blocked by an intrinsic \(A^{-1/2}\) normalization loss [Step 54]. Its conditional family-uniform obstruction remains plausible under the verified support normalization, terminal density, and exponential-pullback averaging, but it cannot be promoted until the exact transported-cutoff start theorem and common-flow sequence-uniform first-exit chain are real [Steps 48,54]. The main unresolved analytic statement is now the synchronized-output short-time theorem and all-order \(\varepsilon\)-uniform hierarchy, not the terminal density or volume normalization [Step 54].

The reusable architecture is clear: a topology-independent smoothing/chart-extraction mechanism takes small initial \(E=\operatorname{Ric}+g\), a curvature-to-volume budget, carefully weighted support selection, exact cutoff-flow smoothing, and exponential-pullback averaging to produce a smooth Einstein-scale chart with small defect; a topology-specific obstruction module supplies a nonnegative curvature density whose global integral is controlled by \(Q=\int|E|^2\), forcing an impossible calibrated Einstein germ [Steps 46-54]. The distinction remains important: extracting local Einstein patches does not recover an Einstein metric on the original smooth manifold, because topology may remain in discarded regions [Step 47 user message, Step 54]. The current mechanism is a negative-branch obstruction tool for specified four-dimensional geography, not an existence theorem [Steps 47,54].

## Positive branch, higher dimensions, and peer-session context [Steps 4-54]

The positive branch remained secondary but repeatedly influenced strategic judgment [Steps 4-54]. Cross-session communication with S0910A02 established that in dimension four, positive normalized tight pinching plus volume noncollapse gives strong finiteness consequences through Myers, Bishop–Gromov, and Cheeger–Naber; infinitely many \(\#_k(S^2\times S^2)\)-type examples would have to collapse [Steps 4-8]. The agents repeatedly corrected the idea that collapse itself obstructs Einstein existence, since round lens-space quotients are exact Einstein and can collapse [Steps 5-9]. A02 explored positive-branch candidates such as \(\#_5\mathbb{CP}^2\), toric/rod structures, and integral identities on \(\#_k(S^2\times S^2)\), but no reduction from arbitrary metrics to invariant/toric metrics was obtained [Steps 17-25]. Later A02 work found adversarial toric/ALF scenarios involving NUT transitions rather than simple edge-cone struts, reinforcing that positive collapse is unresolved and separate from the negative Ishida–LeBrun cutoff-flow route [Steps 34-36]. Around Steps 41-44, A02’s diagonal toric constant-\(K\) obstruction was corrected to about \(1.84\%\), not \(68.7\%\), and a positive noncollapsed first-order Ozuch route was reported to have a bi-Kähler loophole on an \((S^2\times S^2)/\mathbb Z_2\) stress configuration [Steps 41-44].

Steps 49-54 recorded new peer-session positive/existence context without redirecting the active negative-flow work [Steps 49-54]. A02 reported that positive branch mode-projection hits a rank-1 cascade at \(\#_3(S^2\times S^2)\), making Einstein existence/nonexistence the real wall for positive candidates [Step 49]. Step 50 preserved A02’s correction that for \(C^0\) operator pinching only the first Ozuch obstruction is load-bearing, rank-null \(A_1\) insertions may allow \(\|\operatorname{Ric}-\Lambda g\|_{\rm op}=O(t^{1/2})\), and mixed quotient rows become concrete topology/Einstein-existence targets [Step 50]. Step 52 noted A02’s message that mixed product-quotient rows remain a positive-branch hardness wall and that \(\mathbb Q\)-Gorenstein smoothing plus Aubin–Yau for negative/general-type product quotients does not directly cover positive \(S^2\times S^2\) mixed rows [Step 52]. Step 54 incorporated A01’s exact result for the BCGP \(\mathbb Z_4^2\), \(K^2=2\), six-\(A_1\) product-quotient resolution: A01 derived \(T_X^0\cong(\pi_*T_Y)^G\), computed \(H^2(X,T_X^0)=0\) by equivariant Serre duality, Künneth, and characters, globalized node smoothings, applied Aubin–Yau on the ample-canonical smooth fiber, and used ADE simultaneous resolution plus Ehresmann to transfer a negative Einstein metric to the minimal resolution [Step 54]. This is strong evidence that some serious near-Einstein/local-gluing candidates support unrelated exact Einstein metrics, reinforcing the output-metric quantifier warning [Step 54]. It does not address mixed positive fillings, arbitrary four-dimensional topology, dimensions \(n\ge5\), or dimension-only constants [Step 54].

Higher dimensions \(n\ge5\) remain largely untouched [Steps 2-54]. The four-dimensional machinery—Chern–Weil, Hitchin–Thorpe, Seiberg–Witten monopole classes, LeBrun/Ishida–LeBrun inequalities, and calibrated \(W^+\) spectra—does not transfer directly [Steps 2-18]. A02 observed that codimension-one positive Einstein collapse exists in higher dimensions via Kaluza–Klein-type constructions such as \(L(q,1)\times N^d\), unlike some four-dimensional Bochner-type restrictions [Step 22]. No broad high-dimensional no-Einstein family has yet been connected to two-sided Ricci pinching in a way that would deliver a Yau 26 counterexample [Steps 2-54].

Peer sessions materially shaped the work. S0910A01 and S0910A02 helped correct Min-Oo and scalar–Weyl overclaims, supported the projector obstruction, repaired nil\(^3\) signs, refined Taub–NUT–AdS interpretation, aligned the weighted Moser route, exposed and repaired the false half-power objection, supplied tensor-energy and continuation checks, and repeatedly prevented premature theorem claims [Steps 1-54]. Step 33’s Sobolev convention error and fixed-manifold conclusion were corrected with peer help [Step 34]. A01’s assembled theorem pushed A03 to inspect hidden interfaces; A03 Steps 42-45 repaired local uniformity, terminal density, unweighted \(T\), and coefficient-regularized flow issues [Steps 42-45]. Steps 48, 50, 52, and 54 show the same pattern continuing: user and TTCS stress tests prevented false promotion of Step 47, Step 49, Step 51, and Step 53 flow theorems [Steps 48,50,52,54]. Scripts and TTCS checks remain valuable for algebra, exponents, term ledgers, and stress tests, but they do not by themselves certify PDE existence, source theorem applicability, geometric convergence, or final theorem status [Steps 1-54].

The session has not proved or disproved Yau Problem 26 [Steps 1-54]. It has not established dimension-only constants, a full four-dimensional result, a positive-branch result, a high-dimensional result, or Lean 4 formalization [Steps 36-54]. The active restricted program is to make the exact transported-cutoff start real [Step 54]. The next load-bearing analytic theorem should start from `workspace/notes/step54_exact_synchronized_output_ledger.md`, `workspace/notes/step54_route_reassessment_and_joint_weighted_iteration.md`, Xu’s converted proof `staging/processing/xu_local_ricci_flow.txt`, and Yang’s Theorem 8.2 source [Steps 52-54]. obtain uniform time-derivative bounds and diagonal smooth compactness across the moving zero set of \(\beta\), pass \(\varepsilon\to0\), recover the fixed-cutoff geometric flow by pullback, and supply restart from smooth endpoints [Step 54]. That chain must verify, with the corrected support system and small initial \(\|\operatorname{Ric}+g\|_\infty\le\delta\), the moving Sobolev comparison, homogeneous \(K_2\) and \(Y\) propagation, fixed \(J_6\), all-\(p\) defect recurrence, curvature and defect Moser endpoints \(\|aF(t)\|_\infty\lesssim\gamma/t\) and \(\|aE(t)\|_\infty\lesssim\delta(r^2/t)^{1/3}\), integrable metric drift, global unweighted \(Q\) propagation, and continuation/restart [Steps 38-54]. \mathfrak D=|E|^2+(s+4)^2+(s+8\sqrt6|W^+|)^2+G,
\quad \int\mathfrak D\le119Q+912\pi^2(-q_{\rm top})_+,

core-ball \(\sup\mathfrak D\to0\), algebraic calibrated spectrum, and the Step 6 projector contradiction [Steps 42-47,54].
