  \]
  This clarified the remaining analytic problem: calibrated Weyl data controls a chiral traceless Riccati tensor, but trace directions, \(u\)–\(z\) cancellation, and quotient degeneration remain uncontrolled [Step 12].

### Metric-by-metric calibration, chart selection, and terminal density evidence

- A robust metric-by-metric critical Ishida–LeBrun inequality was established:
  \[
  \int\left(|W^+|-\frac1{2\sqrt6}\right)^2d\mu
  \le \frac7{24}\int |E|^2d\mu,
  \qquad E=\operatorname{Ric}+g.
  \]
  It uses Chern–Gauss–Bonnet, the genuine monopole inequality, and completion-square algebra. The constant \(7/24\) was obtained by sharper trace–traceless decomposition and checked computationally [Step 15].

- The same chain can be phrased as
  \[
  \int(s+8\sqrt6|W^+|)^2 \le 864\pi^2R
  \]
  together with
  \[
  \int|s+4|^2\le4\int|E|^2.
  \]
  Hence global \(L^2\)-smallness of \(E\), not pointwise \(O(\delta)\) control throughout a cutoff collar, suffices to recover global calibrated Weyl profile on an evolved closed topology [Step 15].

- The Step 15 assertion that a fixed-topology gap had been proved was withdrawn. The localized Li bootstrap had a domain mismatch: the proof checked covering balls for centers in an inner plateau, but the bootstrap supremum was over all centers in the working region; centers near the boundary require adjacent balls outside it. Ricci flow has no finite propagation speed, so buffer ratios do not make transition data irrelevant [Steps 15–16].

- Conditional on bounded sectional curvature on a positive-volume buffered plateau, exponential-pullback averaging avoids local-cover sheet-number and CFG-rank issues. If \(P\) is a positive-volume set of centers in a region with \(|\sec|\le K\) and \(r<\pi/(2\sqrt K)\), then for a nonnegative density \(F\),
  \[
  \int_P \operatorname{avg}_{B_r(0),\,\exp_p^*g}(F\circ\exp_p)d\mu(p)
  \le C(n,K,r)\int_MF\,d\mu.
  \]
  Rauch comparison bounds exponential Jacobians and pullback-ball volumes; Liouville invariance of geodesic flow controls the integral over centers and directions. Injectivity radius and sheet number do not enter [Step 16].

- If \(\operatorname{Vol}(P_i)\ge\theta\operatorname{Vol}(M_i)\), the exponential-pullback lemma selects a center with
  \[
  \operatorname{avg}_{\text{chart}}(D_i)
  \le (C/\theta)\frac{\int D_i}{\operatorname{Vol}(M_i)}.
  \]
  Thus global deficits small per unit volume can yield an absolutely small normalized defect on a fixed-radius chart, provided a smoothing theorem supplies positive-volume plateaux with uniform curvature bounds and volume proportion [Step 17].

- Unique continuation alone cannot supply a nonzero limiting harmonic form on selected charts. A sequence of globally normalized harmonic forms can be nonzero almost everywhere yet have local mass tend to zero on every chosen chart. The monopole/eigenline passage must include quantitative local amplitude and saturation errors in the chart-selection density [Step 16].

- The monopole completion-square argument was repaired for possibly sign-changing
  \[
  q=\sqrt6|W^+|-s
  \]
  by using \(q^+\). Smooth positive approximations \(f^2\approx q^++\varepsilon\) give the variational inequality without derivatives of \(f\), and the nonnegative decomposition gains a favorable \(\int q^-u^2\) term. A joint density including \(|E|^2\), calibrated modulus error, harmonic-amplitude error, and lowest-eigenline error can be used in exponential-chart averaging. On a smoothly convergent selected chart, this would produce a nonzero limiting harmonic self-dual form in the extremal lowest eigenline and hence the Step 6 calibrated spectrum [Step 16].

- Step 29 consolidated the terminal density bridge: terminal recalibration gives \(\int\mathfrak D\le C Q(T)\); positive-part rescaled monopole data with \(q^+\)-weights controls amplitude and lowest-eigenline density; exponential-pullback averaging selects a collapse-resistant chart; tangent-space compactness via Rauch yields a smooth local Einstein germ with spectrum \((-1/6,1/12,1/12)\); the projector/Einstein–Weyl identity gives the contradiction [Step 29].

- Step 30 corrected the terminal bridge for varying topology and support localization. Terminal errors must be normalized by \(A_i\) along varying near-critical families; \(\varepsilon_i=Q_i/\operatorname{Vol}_i\) is the appropriate positive-weight regularization scale because \(\varepsilon_i^2\operatorname{Vol}_i=o(Q_i)\), whereas \(\varepsilon_i=Q_i\) can create extensive errors when \(A_i\) grows. The lowest-eigenline density is controlled only on bounded-curvature buffered regions \(L_i\); it must be multiplied by \(1_{L_i}\) and extended by zero outside. Since chart geodesics from the strict center region remain in \(L_i\), exponential averaging still recovers local eigenline saturation on selected charts [Step 30].

- Step 30 also corrected support geometry. The useful construction is a maximal \(r\)-separated net in the maximal-function good set, coloring the graph connecting centers at distance \(\le12r\), then retaining a maximal-volume color. This gives disjoint \(B_{6r}\) auxiliary domains while preserving a fixed fraction of \(B_r\)-volume. One common cutoff \(a=\sum\chi_j^2\) is used, with strict centers \(P_j=B_r(p_j)\), larger plateau \(L_j=B_{4r}(p_j)\subset\{a=1\}\), support in \(B_{5r}\), and auxiliary Sobolev domain \(B_{6r}\). The earlier \(r/5\)-separation did not make the claimed supports disjoint, and choosing one component could lose all useful volume under collapse [Step 30].

### Cutoff-flow program: validated algebra, corrected status, and open estimates

- Ye Li’s four-dimensional smoothing theorem became relevant because maximal-function good points satisfy
  \[
  r^4\fint_{B_r}|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\le K_0r^4.
  \]
  Choosing small fixed physical \(r=r(K_0,\varepsilon)\) makes the dimensionless energy small uniformly. Bishop–Gromov comparison under a Ricci lower bound transfers centered curvature-mean control from a good point to nearby centers in a buffered region at comparable radii [Step 13].

- The initial Step 13 smoothing closure was invalid. The inequality \(Y'_{\rm inner}\le Cr^{-2}Y_{\rm outer}\) does not imply a Gronwall estimate for \(Y_{\rm inner}\), persistence of small curvature energy through the flow was assumed, and numerical absorption factors only illustrated algebra. Li’s proof uses a dynamic bootstrap over centers, Sobolev control, metric equivalence, and evolving curvature energy; a single good ball does not automatically provide these [Steps 13–14].

- For the normalized Einstein defect \(E=\operatorname{Ric}+g\), the normalized Ricci-flow identities are
  \[
  \partial_tE=\Delta_LE-2E,
  \]
  and
  \[
  (\partial_t-\Delta)|E|^2
  =
  -2|\nabla E|^2+4R_{ikjl}E_{ij}E_{kl}.
  \]
  The apparent damping from \(-2E\) cancels in the scalar equation. A pointwise Gronwall argument with \(|\operatorname{Rm}|\le C/t\) has divergent \(\int_0^Tdt/t\) and cannot propagate \(E\) uniformly from the initial slice [Steps 13–14, 18].

- Under Li’s full dynamic hypotheses, Corollary 3.5 gives a better curvature-potential estimate:
  \[
  |E(x,t)|\le C\delta\left(\frac{r^2}{t}\right)^{2/3},
  \]
  and
  \[
  \left|\log\frac{g(t)(v,v)}{g_0(v,v)}\right|
  \le C\delta r^{4/3}t^{1/3}.
  \]
  The singularity \(t^{-2/3}\) is integrable, giving metric drift \(O(\delta r^2)\) over \(t=\theta r^2\). This estimate remains conditional on Li’s dynamic curvature-energy/Sobolev/covering assumptions and was not directly available for the desired cutoff flow [Step 14].

- The normalized cutoff flow
  \[
  \partial_tg=-2\chi^2(\operatorname{Ric}+g)
  \]
  was introduced as a localization interface. For \(a=\chi^2\),
  \[
  \partial_tE=a(\Delta_LE-2E)+\mathcal C_a(E),
  \]
  where every term in \(\mathcal C_a(E)\) contains \(E\), \(\operatorname{tr}E\), or their first derivatives. Exact negative Einstein metrics are stationary even in transition annuli. In integrated defect energy, contracted Bianchi and integration by parts remove Hessian-cutoff terms; \(|d(\chi^2)|^2/\chi^2=4|d\chi|^2\) prevents a \(1/\chi\) loss. This homogeneity was symbolically checked [Step 14].

- Wang–Yang local Ricci-flow and Fei He sources support related local-flow architectures, but their hypotheses do not directly match the current data. Wang’s estimates assume global Sobolev and full-support critical energy conditions; Fei He assumes pointwise full-curvature scales and initial Ricci-defect derivatives unavailable here. The needed theorem is a collapse-uniform, transition-inclusive cutoff curvature-energy bootstrap derived from local normalized energy and defect bounds, not a direct citation [Step 14].

- The defect evolution for \(a=\chi^2\) has no explicit cubic defect reaction:
  \[
  (\partial_t-a\Delta)|E|^2
  =
  -2a|\nabla E|^2+4a\,\operatorname{Rm}(E,E)+2\langle E,\mathcal C_a(E)\rangle .
  \]
  Inverse-metric variation contributes \(+4a\operatorname{tr}(E^3)\), canceling the \(-4a\operatorname{tr}(E^3)\) from the Lichnerowicz/damping interaction [Step 17].

- A weighted pointwise curvature estimate \(|a\operatorname{Rm}|\le C/t\) alone cannot preserve defect via maximum principle because \(\int_0^Tdt/t\) diverges. Starting at \(t_0>0\) gives uncontrolled \((T/t_0)^C\) as \(t_0\to0\), and the initial metrics have no uniform pointwise curvature bound. The evolving Hessian of \(a\) also remains in coefficients; fixing \(\chi\) as a scalar does not fix its Hessian [Step 18].

- A useful integrable target for the weighted defect is
  \[
  |aE(t)|\le C_p\delta\left(\frac{r^2}{t}\right)^{2/p}
  \quad (p>2),
  \]
  whose time integral over \([0,\theta r^2]\) is finite:
  \[
  \int_0^{\theta r^2}\left(\frac{r^2}{t}\right)^{2/p}dt
  \sim \frac{p}{p-2}\theta^{1-2/p}r^2.
  \]
  The endpoint \(p=2\) reproduces logarithmic divergence [Step 18].

- With \(U=aE\), commuting \(a\) through the Laplacian cancels the leading \(a(\Delta a)E\) and \(2a\nabla a\cdot\nabla E\) terms. Apparent quotients by \(a\) are regular because \(da\otimes da/a=4d\chi\otimes d\chi\). Testing by \(\eta^2|U|^{p-2}U\) gives a localized fixed-\(p\) inequality
  \[
  \frac d{dt}\int\eta^2|U|^p
  +c_p\int\eta^2a|\nabla |U|^{p/2}|^2
  \le \text{cutoff terms}
  +C_p\int\eta^2a|\operatorname{Rm}||U|^p
  +C_p\int\eta^2|U|^{p+1}.
  \]
  Relative Sobolev absorption cancels collapsed volume in dimension four. This cannot be iterated naively to \(p=\infty\), because the reaction-to-dissipation coefficient grows with \(p\sqrt{\varepsilon_*}\) [Step 18].

- Wang’s curvature-control parameter
  \[
  \beta=A_0^2\|\operatorname{Rm}\|_{L^2}
  \]
  is volume-independent in dimension four at the Li scale: if \(A_0^2\sim C_S r^2\operatorname{Vol}^{-1/2}\) and \(\|\operatorname{Rm}\|_2\sim\sqrt{K_0\operatorname{Vol}}\), then
  \[
  \beta=C_Sr^2\sqrt{K_0}.
  \]
  This volume cancellation is critical-exponent cancellation; the use of \(L^2\) curvature energy and Chern–Weil control is specifically four-dimensional [Step 19].

- A \(p>4\) threshold was identified for weighted first-derivative control of cutoff-flow velocity:
  \[
  |U(t)|=|aE(t)|\le C_p\delta(r^2/t)^{2/p},
  \]
  \[
  |\chi\nabla U(t)|\le C_p\delta t^{-1/2}(r^2/t)^{2/p}.
  \]
  Metric drift is integrable iff \(p>2\), while connection/Hessian drift is integrable iff \(p>4\). For \(p=6\), metric drift is \(\sim(3/2)\delta\theta^{2/3}r^2\), and connection drift is \(\sim6\delta\theta^{1/6}\). Later work showed quantitative derivative control is not needed for the zero-order first-exit if continuation is handled by a triangular high-order induction and plateau interior estimates [Steps 19–21].

- The cutoff-flow problem was reorganized around Wang-compatible moments
  \[
  H_q=\int\eta^2a^{q-2}F^q,\qquad F=(1+|\operatorname{Rm}|^2)^{1/2},
  \]
  with Sobolev variable
  \[
  \eta\,a^{(q-1)/2}F^{q/2}.
  \]
  The fourth power of this Sobolev variable has the weight of the next moment; \(q=2\) is unweighted critical curvature energy and \(q=3\) is the weighted cubic potential \(\int\eta^2aF^3\). This avoids division by \(a\) near the transition [Step 20].

- For the defect, compatible moments are
  \[
  J_m=\int\eta^2a^{m-2}|E|^m,
  \]
  not the weaker \(\int|aE|^m=\int a^m|E|^m\). Initial pointwise pinching supplies \(J_6\). Interpolation and Sobolev support a positive-time iteration toward \(|aE|\) while preserving the initial \(\delta^6\) factor [Step 20].

- A proposed conformal-measure/Nash semigroup shortcut was rejected. On \(d\nu=a^{-2}d\mu\), weighted moments can be viewed as standard \(L^q\) norms for \(K=aF\), but small critical form bounds do not imply unweighted ultracontractivity. The scalar stress test on \(\mathbb R^4\) with inverse-square potential \(V=\kappa/|x|^2\), \(0<\kappa<1\), satisfies
  \[
  \int V\phi^2\le\kappa\int|\nabla\phi|^2
  \]
  but the heat semigroup has singular spatial weights \(r^{-\sigma}\), \(\sigma=1-\sqrt{1-\kappa}>0\). The critical \(H_2\to H_3\) upgrade is essential; a small quadratic form bound cannot replace it [Step 22].

- The correct quadratic form in the conformal-measure interpretation uses \(\nabla(a^{-1/2}\phi)\), not \(\nabla(a^{-1}\phi)\). The leading gradient weight is \(a^{-1}\), not \(a^{-2}\), near \(\{a=0\}\) [Step 22].

- The corrected architecture after the Nash rejection is two-stage: Stage 1 is the hard critical \(H_2\to H_3\) upgrade by Wang-type energy and Sobolev absorption with volume-independent critical parameter; Stage 2 is subcritical Moser from \(L^3\) potential to \(L^\infty\) bounds with convergent constants. The Nash route can at most compress Stage 2 [Step 22].

- The previous outer-dissipation argument was unmatched: bounded overlap alone cannot absorb an outer dissipation into an inner dissipation. The corrected single-good-support construction uses disjoint good macro-supports from maximal-function/Vitali thinning. On one support, with \(a=\chi_j^2\),
  \[
  H_{3,j}\le \|F\|_{L^2(U_j)}\|\eta_j\chi_j F\|_{L^4}^2.
  \]
  The Sobolev variable retains active dissipation \(\int\eta_j^2a|\nabla F|^2\), and derivatives of \(\eta_j\) produce zero-order neighboring/support terms instead of unmatched neighboring dissipation [Step 23].

- The \(q=2\) estimate gives only a spacetime integral of \(H_3\), hence a good earlier time slice. Preventing terminal spikes requires a separate \(q=3\) differential inequality:
  \[
  H_{3,j}'\le Cr^{-2}H_{3,j}
  \]
  on nested buffered domains. Propagating a good slice in \([t/4,t/2]\) gives
  \[
  S_j^2H_{3,j}(t)\le C\gamma_j^3/t
  \]
  in the correct normalization. A mean-value assertion alone is insufficient [Step 23].

- The homogeneous defect estimates are separate obligations. Global unweighted
  \[
  Q(t)=\int |E(t)|^2
  \]
  should obey \(Q'\le Cr^{-2}Q\) only after componentwise critical curvature absorption; curvature-only additive sources are unacceptable because they could be order \(\varepsilon A\). Fixed \(J_6\) testing is needed from time zero to preserve \(J_6(t)\lesssim J_6(0)\sim\delta^6\operatorname{Vol}\) before positive-time defect iteration [Steps 20, 23].

### Normalization, weighted Moser, and Sobolev coefficient corrections

- For the fully covariant curvature tensor under pure conformal velocity \(\partial_tg=-2ag\), there is a linear term \(-2a\operatorname{Rm}\). The constant scaling check is \(g(t)=e^{-2t}g_0\): Christoffel symbols and \(R^l{}_{ijk}\) are unchanged, while \(R_{ijkl}(t)=e^{-2t}R_{ijkl}(0)\), so \(\partial_tR_{ijkl}=-2R_{ijkl}\) [Step 24].

- Step 24 initially interpreted this \(-2a\operatorname{Rm}\) as beneficial curvature-energy damping, but Step 25 corrected it. For \(|\operatorname{Rm}|_g^2\), the tensor contribution \(-4a|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\) combines with \(+8a|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\) from four inverse metrics and \(-4a|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\) from the volume form in dimension four. Thus \(\int|\operatorname{Rm}|^2d\mu\) is exactly scale-invariant for spatially constant \(a\). The route cannot rely on artificial normalization coercivity [Steps 24–25].

- For
  \[
  F=(1+|\operatorname{Rm}|^2)^{1/2},
  \]
  the pure-normalization density contribution to \(F^p\,d\mu\) is
  \[
  2a\big[(p-2)F^p-pF^{p-2}\big]\,d\mu .
  \]
  Exact negative Einstein metrics remain stationary because of the full Lichnerowicz identity, not because curvature potential vanishes; \(H_3=\int\eta^2aF^3\) is generally positive even when \(E=0\) [Steps 24–25].

- Yang’s fixed-cutoff Moser exponents satisfy
  \[
  p_{j+1}=\frac32p_j,\qquad
  p'_{j+1}=\frac32p'_j+1.
  \]
  If \(p'_0=p_0-2\), then \(p'_j=p_j-2\), so Yang’s moments
  \[
  \chi^{2p'_j}\Phi^{p_j}
  \]
  exactly match \(a^{p_j-2}\Phi^{p_j}\). The endpoint is \(a\Phi\), the required weighted pointwise control [Step 25].

- Choosing potential exponent six makes Yang’s weighted potential \(H_3=\int aF^3\). The interpolation identity
  \[
  a^{p-1}F\Phi^p
  =
  (aF^3)^{1/3}
  \left(a^{3p/2-2}\Phi^{3p/2}\right)^{2/3}
  \]
  followed by Sobolev and Young gives a polynomial-in-\(p\) coefficient. The first script run exposed a Hölder-weight typo; the corrected version verified homothetic cancellation, \(F^p d\mu\) normalization, Yang-weight correspondence, high-exponent product convergence, and endpoint scales [Step 25].

- Step 26 reported a general-\(p\) weighted tensor inequality for \(p\ge3\). Boundary terms \(d(\eta^2a^{p-1})\) split into a \(d\eta\) part that vanishes in the chosen support geometry because \(a^{p-1}=0\) on \(\operatorname{supp}d\eta\), and an \(a\,da\) part bounded by
  \[
  Cp^2r^{-2}K_p
  \]
  using
  \[
  a^{p-3}|da|^2=4a^{p-2}|d\chi|^2.
  \]
  Hessian-\(a\) integration by parts gives the same type of remainder; algebraic reactions are bounded by
  \[
  Cp\int\eta^2a^{p-1}F\Phi^p.
  \]
  Later review found that the coarsened \(D_p\) term alone does not give a uniform coefficient for \(\|\nabla Z_p\|^2\) unless the \(p(p-2)\) scalar-gradient dissipation is retained or a polynomial loss is carried. A polynomial loss is acceptable because the Moser product still converges [Steps 26, 28–29].

- For the defect, Step 26 used the regularization
  \[
  \Phi_\varepsilon=(|E|^2+\varepsilon^2)^{1/2}
  \]
  and the chain rule
  \[
  (\partial_t-a\Delta)\Phi_\varepsilon^p
  =
  \frac p2\Phi_\varepsilon^{p-2}(\partial_t-a\Delta)|E|^2
  -p(p-2)a\Phi_\varepsilon^{p-2}|\nabla\Phi_\varepsilon|^2.
  \]
  Estimates are \(\varepsilon\)-uniform if all zero-order and gradient terms are retained correctly; later Step 35 showed the fixed \(J_6\) seed can avoid norm regularization entirely [Steps 26, 35].

- Noninteger powers in the Moser sequence \(p_j=3(3/2)^j\) require attention at the support edge. The naive assertion that \(\chi^\alpha\) is smooth for arbitrary noninteger \(\alpha\) is invalid unless the cutoff is chosen infinitely flat at the boundary or approximated in \(W^{1,\infty}\) [Step 26].

- Maheux–Saloff-Coste’s local Sobolev theorem was used as the collapse-adapted Sobolev source: under \(\operatorname{Ric}\ge kg\), any geodesic ball has a local Sobolev inequality with coefficient of the form
  \[
  \mathcal S=C(n,Kr^2)\,r^2\,\operatorname{Vol}(B_r)^{-1/2}
  \]
  in the squared embedding convention
  \[
  \|u\|_4^2\le \mathcal S\big(\|\nabla u\|_2^2+r^{-2}\|u\|_2^2\big).
  \]
  Compact support or mean-subtraction adds only lower-order \(r^{-2}\|u\|_2^2\) terms. Exact primary-source formulation and enlarged-ball conventions still require checking [Steps 26, 28, 34].

- A Step 33 claim that the true absorption coefficient was \(S^2H_2^{1/2}\) and therefore diverged under collapse was corrected in Step 34 as a Sobolev-constant convention error. Written in the squared embedding convention above, the \(p=2\) absorption is
  \[
  K_3\le K_2^{1/2}\|\chi F\|_4^2
  \le C\mathcal S K_2^{1/2}(D_2+r^{-2}K_2).
  \]
  On a matched good support \(K_2\le K_0V\), so
  \[
  \gamma=\mathcal S K_2^{1/2}\le Cr^2\sqrt{K_0},
  \]
  and collapse volume cancels. If the embedding is instead written with an unsquared constant \(S\), then \(S^2=\mathcal S\); Step 33 squared the old coefficient’s scaling and manufactured a false collapse obstruction. The family-uniform route is not disproved by this Sobolev factor, but the full first-exit theorem is still unproved [Steps 33–34].

- Step 33’s fixed-manifold rescue was independently invalid: Ricci lower bounds and total-volume bounds do not imply bounded diameter or fixed-radius ball-volume lower bounds, even on one smooth topology. Products of closed hyperbolic surfaces with one factor degenerating by pinching a geodesic have fixed topology, fixed volume, exact \(\operatorname{Ric}=-g\), diameter tending to infinity, and vanishing local ball volumes in thin regions. This refutes the compactness inference, not the Ishida–LeBrun obstruction [Step 34].

- The alleged half-power mismatch in weighted Moser was rejected. With
  \[
  K_p=\int\eta^2a^{p-2}\Phi^p,\qquad
  Z_p=\eta a^{(p-1)/2}\Phi^{p/2},
  \]
  on the active region one has
  \[
  K_{2p}=\|Z_p\|_4^4,\qquad
  K_{3p/2}\le K_p^{1/2}K_{2p}^{1/2}.
  \]
  The problematic \(\|Z_p\|_3^3\), which has an extra \(a^{1/2}\) mismatch, is not the interpolation used by the parabolic iteration. This correction was communicated to parallel sessions and later confirmed by independent reconstruction [Steps 30–31].

- Conversely, ordinary unweighted Moser iteration on \(U=aT\) is not a replacement: diffusion still controls only \(a|\nabla U|^2\). A triangular bump near a regular zero \(\chi=0\), modeled by \(a=x^2\), gives a degenerate Sobolev ratio diverging like \(\varepsilon^{-1/2}\). This demonstrates that no ordinary unweighted Sobolev step is available in general [Step 31].

- The Step 31 claim that the weighted route and first-exit theorem were already closed was withdrawn. The correct recurrence is spacetime:
  \[
  \int_IK_{3p/2}
  \le
  \big(\sup_IK_p\big)^{1/2}
  \mathcal S\int_I\big(\|\nabla Z_p\|_2^2+r^{-2}K_p\big),
  \]
  not a bound using unsupported \(\sup_IK_{2p}\) or a false four-dimensional Ladyzhenskaya product inequality. TTCS also corrected that the recurrence coefficient cannot use a mere \(L^1_t\)-average of \(\mathcal S^2Y\); one needs an essential supremum on each slab or another correlation argument. The fixed \(q=2,3\) machinery is expected to supply
  \[
  \operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{[t/2,t]}\mathcal S^2Y(s)\le C\gamma^3/t.
  \]
  With this dyadic input, the curvature endpoint has the positive-time form
  \[
  \|aF(t)\|_\infty\lesssim \gamma/t,
  \]
  not a time-uniform near-zero bound [Steps 32, 34].

### Fixed \(J_6\), global \(Q\), and defect drift evidence

- Step 35 produced a genuine simplification for the \(J_6\) seed. Set
  \[
  s=|E|^2.
  \]
  Then
  \[
  J_6=\int\eta^2a^4s^3
  \]
  is smooth even where \(E=0\), and
  \[
  (\partial_t-a\Delta)s^3
  =
  3s^2(\partial_t-a\Delta)s-6as|\nabla s|^2.
  \]
  The nonlinear test in the integrated Hessian-\(a\) identity is simply \(q=3\eta^2a^4s^2\), also smooth. Thus fixed \(J_6\) persistence does not require Kato/norm regularization [Step 35].

- The Sobolev variable for the fixed \(J_6\) proof is
  \[
  w_6=\eta\chi^5|E|^3=\eta a^{5/2}|E|^3,
  \]
  which has a weak first derivative and does not introduce a singularity at \(E=0\). A notation correction from Step 36: the cutoff cross term has power \(a^4|da|s^{5/2}|\nabla E|\), not \(s^{3/2}\) [Steps 35–36].

- The defect reaction is linear in curvature, not cubic in curvature: the relevant potential is
  \[
  P_6=\int Fw_6^2,
  \]
  controlled by two-factor Hölder and Sobolev:
  \[
  P_6\le \|F\|_2\|w_6\|_4^2
  \le \gamma\big(X_6+r^{-2}J_6\big),
  \qquad
  \gamma=\mathcal S\|F\|_2
  \]
  in the squared Sobolev convention. This uses only \(K_2\), not the separate \(q=3\) curvature seed \(Y=\int aF^3\). Under smooth first-exit geometry and small \(\gamma\), this gives
  \[
  J_6(t)\le e^{C(1+r^{-2})t}J_6(0).
  \]
  The result is a strong conditional component of the program, but it presupposes a smooth cutoff flow on the first-exit interval, moving Sobolev/support comparability, and localized \(K_2\) control [Steps 35–36].

- Step 36 emphasized that terminal calibration requires the separate global unweighted defect energy
  \[
  Q(t)=\int_M|E(t)|^2d\mu,
  \]
  not just weighted \(J_6\) or \(\|aE\|_\infty\). Weighted quantities can miss defect near \(\{a=0\}\). The needed homogeneous estimate has the schematic form
  \[
  Q'+c\int a|\nabla E|^2
  \le
  C\int\left(\frac{|da|^2}{a}+a\right)|E|^2
  +C\int a|\operatorname{Rm}|\,|E|^2,
  \]
  with the last term absorbed support-by-support by the same \(\gamma\)-type product. This should yield \(Q(t)\le e^{C\theta}Q(0)\) under the simultaneous first-exit hypotheses. It remains an independent lemma to write fully; it is not implied by \(J_6\) [Steps 20, 23, 36].

- If \(J_6\) persistence is available from time zero, the defect Moser iteration is expected to give
  \[
  \|aE(t)\|_\infty\lesssim \delta\left(\frac{r^2}{t}\right)^{1/3}
  \]
  for \(p_0=6\). Its integral is finite:
  \[
  \int_0^{\theta r^2}\|aE(t)\|_\infty dt
  \lesssim C\delta\,\theta^{2/3}r^2.
  \]
  This integrable drift is the uniform zero-order quantity required by first-exit metric/Sobolev comparison. This endpoint remains dependent on completing the corrected spacetime recurrence and simultaneous bootstrap [Steps 25–26, 34–35].

### Shifted curvature, transported DeTurck, and continuation status

- Step 27 introduced the shifted-curvature package after a user correction showed that the normalized velocity \(-2ag\) creates high cutoff-derivative terms in curvature variation:
  \[
  G=\frac{g\wedge g}{2(n-1)},\qquad
  T=\operatorname{Rm}+G,\qquad
  U=aT.
  \]
  With \(\operatorname{Ric}(G)=g\),
  \[
  \operatorname{Ric}(T)=E=\operatorname{Ric}+g,\qquad
  \operatorname{Ric}(U)=aE,
  \qquad
  \nabla G=0.
  \]
  Thus
  \[
  \partial_tg=-2\operatorname{Ric}(U),
  \]
  packaging the normalization in the same curvature-contraction structure as the cutoff flow [Step 27].

- In shifted variables, schematically
  \[
  (\partial_t-a\Delta)T
  =
  da*\nabla T+\operatorname{Hess}(a)*T+a(T*T+G*T),
  \]
  and the equation for \(U=aT\) has no singular division by \(a\) and no independent \(\operatorname{Hess}(a)*G\) source. The reaction vanishes at \(T=0\), so there is no true constant forcing term after the shift [Step 27].

- The genuine highest cutoff term remains
  \[
  \chi\,\nabla^{m+2}\chi * U.
  \]
  One integration by parts absorbs the derivative falling on \(\nabla^mU\) into the \(a=\chi^2\) weighted diffusion and lowers the remaining cutoff order to \(m+1\), not \(m\). TTCS resolved a Wang-indexing discrepancy: the high-order proof requires the current Volterra pair
  \[
  \nabla^mU \leftrightarrow \nabla^{m+1}\chi,
  \]
  while a prior unweighted \(\nabla^{m-1}T\) quantity needs only \(\nabla^m\chi\). No algebraic cancellation removes the \(m+1\) cutoff jet [Step 27].

- Step 28’s completed Codex review supported the shifted-curvature mechanism, including \(G\)-terms, \(\operatorname{Ric}(U)=aE\), the true \(\chi\nabla^{m+2}\chi\) term, the current \(\nabla^mU\leftrightarrow\nabla^{m+1}\chi\) dependence, finite unweighted \(L^p\) bounds for \(T\), smooth terminal reconstruction, and transported-coefficient DeTurck restart. However, the proof still imported grouped integrations and finite staggered-exponent estimates from Wang rather than reproducing every term [Step 28].

- Step 30 sharpened the high-order issue: in the \(m=2\) continuation expansion, terms analogous to Wang’s \(\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2,\Gamma_3\) retain \(\nabla^3\chi\)-level dependence after one integration by parts. A viable induction must couple
  \[
  X=\|\nabla^mU\|_p^p,\qquad Z=\|\nabla^{m+1}\chi\|_p^p
  \]
  at the same order, schematically
  \[
  \frac d{dt}(X+Z)+cD\le C(1+X+Z),
  \]
  then estimate \(\nabla^mT\). A finite \(p,2p,4p\) inventory suffices for lower-order products. \(G\)-linear terms are either bounded current-order terms or lower-order terms [Step 30].

- Step 32 isolated a lowest-order continuation test: the Codex expansion leaves
  \[
  I=\int\chi|\nabla^2\chi|\,|\nabla^2U|^p .
  \]
  Direct Young absorption into
  \[
  D_p=\int\chi^2|\nabla^3U|^2|\nabla^2U|^{p-2}
  \]
  would introduce negative powers of \(\chi\). A promising four-dimensional estimate sets
  \[
  u=\chi|\nabla^2U|^{p/2},\qquad B=\nabla^2\chi,
  \]
  and gives
  \[
  I\le \varepsilon D_p
  +C_{\varepsilon}p^2\mathcal S\|B\|_4^2(1+r^{-2})\|\nabla^2U\|_p^p,
  \]
  provided \(\|\nabla^2\chi\|_4\) is controlled in the evolving geometry. This is not supplied by bilipschitz comparison or initial smoothness alone; it requires the coupled connection-evolution estimates [Step 32].

- Step 36 corrected the continuation interface further. A terminal extension theorem must be stated on \([0,T_{\max})\), not an already smooth closed interval. Step 35’s use of unweighted \(\|T\|_\infty\) and \(\|a\nabla\operatorname{Rm}\|_\infty\) as finite Gronwall coefficients is not justified, because the zero-order bootstrap controls \(|aF|\), not unweighted \(|T|\) near \(a=0\), and gives no pointwise first-derivative control. The viable route remains preserving
  \[
  \partial_t\Gamma=g^{-1}*\nabla\operatorname{Ric}(U)
  \]
  and proving the base pair \((\nabla U,\nabla^2\chi)\) by signed weighted energy estimates involving terms such as
  \[
  \chi\nabla^3\chi*U,\quad
  \nabla\chi*\nabla^2\chi*U,\quad
  \chi\nabla^2\chi*\nabla U,\quad
  \chi\nabla\chi*\nabla^2U.
  \]
  The continuation theorem remains unproved [Step 36].

- Step 36 also corrected the DeTurck existence interface. A fixed-coefficient gauged equation with gauge term \(a\mathcal L_Wg\) is not geometrically equivalent to the fixed-cutoff flow. Cancellation by a diffeomorphism generated by \(aW\) uses
  \[
  \mathcal L_{aW}g=a\mathcal L_Wg+da\otimes W^\flat+W^\flat\otimes da,
  \]
  and the scalar cutoff is transported. The correct formulation is a transported-coefficient normalized DeTurck system with \(\hat a=a\circ\phi_t^{-1}\), Lie derivative \(\mathcal L_{\hat a W}\hat g\), and zeroth-order term \(-2\hat a\hat g\), pulling back to
  \[
  \partial_tg=-2a(\operatorname{Ric}+g).
  \]
  Step 35’s \(\varepsilon\)-regularized Schauder argument did not give \(\varepsilon\)-independent smooth existence, since ordinary parabolic constants depend on lower ellipticity and the small-\(a\) top-derivative estimate was not closed. A Yang/DeTurck-style degenerate energy/tame construction with the transported coefficient is still needed [Steps 35–36].

- Replacing \(a\) by \(a+\varepsilon\) remains unsafe unless one proves exterior-curvature-independent estimates: it activates the uncontrolled exterior where the selected-support strategy intentionally leaves \(a=0\), creating \(U_\varepsilon=\varepsilon(\operatorname{Rm}+G)\) there. Kato regularization of tensor norms is acceptable; coefficient regularization is not automatically acceptable [Steps 32, 36].

### Current status of the four-dimensional negative Ishida–LeBrun route

- The most developed conditional route now consists of: maximal-function macro-support selection; collapse-adapted local Sobolev with critical volume cancellation; \(q=2\to q=3\) curvature seed; fixed unregularized \(J_6\) defect persistence; separate global \(Q\) preservation; corrected spacetime Moser recurrence yielding \(|aF|\lesssim\gamma/t\) and, if \(J_6\) persists, \(|aE|\lesssim\delta(r^2/t)^{1/3}\); transported-coefficient degenerate local flow and shifted-curvature continuation; positive-time plateau regularity; terminal calibrated density and exponential-pullback chart averaging; and the Step 6 local projector/Einstein–Weyl contradiction [Steps 16–36].

- This route is not yet a proved pinching gap, even for a fixed Ishida–LeBrun manifold. The weighted interpolation, Sobolev coefficient cancellation, and fixed \(J_6\) lemma are significant validated components, but the following load-bearing estimates remain unproved: transported-coefficient degenerate DeTurck existence; simultaneous first-exit closure carrying \(K_2\), \(Y\), \(J_6\), \(Q\), moving Sobolev, support geometry, and integrable metric drift; shifted-curvature continuation from the base pair \((\nabla U,\nabla^2\chi)\); and the fully written terminal density passage on the same evolved closed metric [Steps 32–36].

- Evidence explicitly not to reuse as established: Step 15 fixed-topology gap theorem; Step 17 unconditional coupled-energy theorem; Step 21 Nash ultracontractivity shortcut; Step 24 net-damping interpretation of \(-2a\operatorname{Rm}\); Step 29 family-uniform gap theorem as a completed result; Step 31 closed first-exit/continuation theorem; Step 33 extra Sobolev-factor collapse obstruction; Step 33 fixed-manifold ball-volume rescue; Step 35 generic fixed-coefficient DeTurck/\(\varepsilon\)-Schauder existence proof; and any claim that \(J_6\) plus \(|aE|\) replaces global \(Q\) [Steps 15–36].

### Positive branch and higher-dimensional evidence

- Positive normalized pinching has structural advantages but no complete proof. Myers gives diameter control when \(\operatorname{Ric}\approx+g\), and positive scalar curvature kills Seiberg–Witten monopole obstructions, but there is no dimension-only volume lower bound. Round lens-space quotients have exact \(\operatorname{Ric}=g\) and volumes tending to zero in fixed odd dimensions while already satisfying the conclusion because they are Einstein. Thus input collapse is compatible with the desired output and cannot simply be ruled out [Steps 4–5].

- In dimension \(4\), peer work from S0910A02, accepted only in its stated scope, used Cheeger–Naber Theorem 1.12 to support: for \(|\operatorname{Ric}-g|_{\rm op}\le\delta_0<1/2\) plus a volume lower bound, there are finitely many diffeomorphism types. Therefore any positive-pinching sequence on pairwise distinct manifolds, if it exists, must be volume-collapsed. This is a finiteness/dichotomy result, not an Einstein-existence theorem [Step 8].

- A02 positive-branch work found codimension-one positive Einstein collapse in every \(n\ge5\) via Kaluza–Klein-type constructions \(L(q,1)\times N^d\), while dimension \(4\) is blocked by a Bochner-type mechanism in that peer analysis. High-dimensional positive-branch strategies therefore cannot rely on collapse obstruction alone [Step 22].

- A02’s later toric analysis on \(\#_k(S^2\times S^2)\) reported a “BREAK” verdict: integral identities alone did not obstruct the relevant \(\alpha\)-family, suggesting that the positive branch may require a global PDE solvability obstruction rather than only topological/integral constraints. This does not affect the negative critical-family route but indicates structural difference [Steps 24–25].

- A02’s Step 36 positive collapsed-front correction warned that alternating toric collapsed adversaries survive current coarse edge-cone/strut accounting because problematic transitions are NUTs rather than codimension-two struts. This reinforces that the positive branch remains open and cannot be settled by the negative Ishida–LeBrun analysis [Step 36].

- For \(n\ge5\), no analogue of the four-dimensional Seiberg–Witten/Chern–Weil machinery has been developed in this session. Producing a high-dimensional counterexample would require identifying closed manifolds known to carry no Einstein metric of any sign, which remains nontrivial. Current evidence mainly concerns the four-dimensional negative critical family and does not settle higher dimensions [Steps 2, 9, 18, 27, 36].

### Research Line

The research began by locking the exact quantifier structure of Yau Problem 26 and refusing to replace it by a nearby stability statement. The first structural move was the positive/negative branch normalization. This clarified the logic of both proof and disproof: proving \(Q_n\) requires only one suitable interval per dimension, while disproving it requires failure of both same-sign normalized branches in the same dimension. Later, the user clarified that the two branch failures need not occur on the same manifold, which removed an unnecessary strengthening from counterexample thinking [Steps 1, 10].

The first explored mechanisms were broad geometric and analytic counterexample/existence routes. Orbifold desingularization was attractive because obstructed Einstein desingularization could appear to produce manifolds with near-Einstein metrics but no Einstein metric. The unweighted ALE residual computation changed this: first obstruction terms survive in the Ricci norm relevant to the problem, so the route only remains meaningful under special obstruction-vanishing conditions, and even then only local non-desingularizability is shown. This left a reusable lesson: failure of a specific Einstein construction is not absence of every Einstein metric on the smooth manifold [Step 1].

The agents simultaneously checked known convergence/flexibility claims. Min-Oo/Ye/Anderson sources did not yield the needed pure Ricci-pinching convergence theorem; Lohkamp’s flexibility did not meet the two-sided near-\(-g\) requirement. The flat-symbol computation then eliminated a simple high-frequency perturbative homogenization mechanism by showing the linear Ricci kernel is pure gauge. These checks narrowed the field without resolving whether a nonlinear or degenerating Ricci-flexibility mechanism exists [Steps 1-2].

The research then moved to four-dimensional topology because that is where strong no-Einstein obstructions are available. Step 2 initially overread Seiberg–Witten/Chern–Weil estimates and tried to prove quantitative gaps for known families. The user’s Step 3 correction forced a significant route change: the pure \(W^+\) estimate was invalid, and the sharp mixed scalar–Weyl inequality left the critical Ishida–LeBrun boundary \(D=A/3\) unresolved. The target became near-equality geometry at this boundary rather than a quick obstruction conclusion [Steps 2-3].

At the critical boundary, the agents built a diagnostic profile for any hypothetical tight negative-pinching sequence. Scalar, Weyl, volume, curvature-energy, and monopole period data would have to approach a calibrated configuration. This did not imply compactness or noncollapse. Its main value was to exclude ordinary geometric pictures: negative Kähler–Einstein bulk pieces have the wrong \(W^+\) magnitude and scalar-flat connectors carry too much Ricci defect after normalization. The line moved from “reuse known \(L^2\)-minimizing gluing pictures” to “identify whether any geometry can satisfy both pointwise near-\(-g\) Ricci pinching and the calibrated \(W^+\) profile” [Steps 3-4].

The local analysis then produced the first strong obstruction. Any noncollapsed regular fixed-scale patch of a near-saturated sequence would converge to an Einstein local limit with calibrated \(W^+\)-spectrum \((-1/6,1/12,1/12)\). The Step 6 projector argument showed such a local Einstein germ cannot exist. This replaced an attempted Derdziński/conformal-Kähler interpretation by a direct contradiction. For fixed critical topology, the consequence was that any tight sequence must be everywhere collapsed at unit scale while maintaining nontrivial total calibrated volume/energy [Steps 5-6].

Collapse became the central unresolved regime. Early model work used Lott’s orbit-volume equation for regular abelian collapse and nil\(^3\) equations to test whether exact negative-Einstein collapse is possible. Corrections in Steps 7-8 prevented overclaiming: finite volume does not imply the required bounded orbit-volume hypotheses, exact symmetry is not available for the actual metrics, and the nil\(^3\) sign allows cusp-ray models. The normal-cover transfer was repaired by switching from absolute integrals to local averages with buffer. The research line thus retained model equations as filters and intuition, not classification theorems [Steps 7-8].

Step 9 initially treated Taub–NUT–AdS as evidence that curvature averages cannot force noncollapsed local universal covers, because the short circle is contractible through a NUT. The user’s Step 10 correction refined this sharply. The failure depends on choosing a large cover containing the NUT; choosing a smaller buffered annular domain before covering unwraps the circle. Moreover, the annular limit is real hyperbolic with zero \(W^+\) and large calibrated deficit, while the NUT core has bad curvature averages. This changed the scientific understanding: Taub–NUT–AdS is a warning about domain choice and contractible fibers, not a counterexample to every adjustable-buffer regularity route [Steps 9-10].

The Pontryagin direction underwent a similar refinement. Initially it was tempting to count NUT or singular-core charges. Step 10 showed the Levi–Civita \(\Lambda^2_+\) characteristic density is asymptotically a constant multiple of volume in the calibrated sequence, so vanishing-volume cores cannot carry all the characteristic mass. Step 11 then showed that mixed curvature lower bounds are automatic for any negative Einstein metric and not themselves coercive. The surviving content is more subtle: calibrated anisotropy of \(W^+\), not total Pontryagin density or mixed curvature magnitude, must be tied to collapse/accessibility failure [Steps 10-11].

The circle-reduction line was useful but repeatedly corrected. Step 11 fixed the static formula and twist sign, and Step 12 withdrew the proposed high-twist/fiber-death dichotomy as an established framework. Toric orthogonal transitivity does not imply a chosen Hopf circle is static; small scaled twist amplitude does not suppress derivative twisting; quotient geometry control cannot be assumed; and \(H^2\times H^2\) prevents general static classification. The complete \(u,z,a_\pm\) chiral reduction remains a valuable representation of possible failure, especially after smoothing, but it no longer drives the main proof attempt [Steps 11-12].

The next major route recovery was smoothing. Step 12 had treated nonzero background curvature as an obstacle to Ye Li’s small-energy theorem. The user in Step 13 corrected this by emphasizing the \(r^4\) factor: bounded mean \(|{\rm Rm}|^2\) at all radii gives small dimensionless energy at a sufficiently small fixed radius. This made Li-type smoothing a concrete way to get bounded geometry from collapsed good points without first constructing a circle action. The first attempted closure used \(L^2\) Sobolev absorption for the Einstein defect, but Steps 14 and 16 corrected the analytic gaps: inner/outer estimates did not close, Li’s global all-centers proof could not simply be localized to an inner plateau, and parabolic flow has no finite propagation speed [Steps 13-16].

The normalized cutoff flow emerged as the best localization interface because it keeps the flow on the original closed topology and is stationary on exact negative Einstein metrics. This matters because global Chern–Weil and monopole inequalities are available only on the closed manifold. Step 14 showed the defect evolution is homogeneous in \(E\), and Step 15 separated what different estimates must accomplish: metric equivalence from weighted \(aE\), global \(L^2\) defect for calibration, and bounded geometry on plateaux. This reoriented the route away from demanding pointwise \(O(\delta)\) control everywhere [Steps 14-15].

Step 15 also supplied a durable algebraic bridge: the \(7/24\) completion-square inequality turns global \(L^2\)-small Einstein defect into the calibrated Weyl-modulus profile on the fixed critical topology. This made global \(Q(t)=\int|E|^2\) preservation a central analytic objective. However, Step 15 overclaimed by presenting the full fixed-topology gap chain as established. Step 16’s review withdrew that theorem because the localized Li bootstrap had a domain mismatch and unsupported finite-propagation reasoning. The valid pieces—completion-square calibration, homogeneous cutoff algebra, and the general proof architecture—were retained, while the theorem conclusion was removed [Steps 15-16].

Step 16 reduced downstream geometric burdens through the exponential-pullback averaging lemma. Instead of first proving CFG accessibility or noncollapsed normal covers almost everywhere, a bounded-curvature positive-volume plateau would allow fixed-radius tangent-space pullback charts that are noncollapsed independent of injectivity radius. Averaging nonnegative joint deficits over centers and tangent balls can select a chart with small normalized local deficit. This also changes the potential scope: if plateau centers occupy a positive volume proportion, global deficits small per unit volume, not absolutely small, can suffice for local chart calibration. This reopened possible use in varying-topology critical families, conditional on uniform analytic constants [Steps 16-17].

The monopole/eigenline part was repaired in tandem. Unique continuation alone cannot ensure local mass of harmonic forms on selected charts. The positive-part \(q^+\) monopole decomposition supplies quantitative nonnegative densities for amplitude and eigenline saturation, which can be included in exponential-chart selection. Thus the downstream contradiction would proceed by selecting a bounded-curvature pullback chart where the metric is near Einstein, Weyl modulus is calibrated, and a nontrivial harmonic self-dual form saturates the lowest-eigenline condition; a smooth local limit would then have the forbidden calibrated spectrum and contradict Step 6 [Step 16].

Step 17 tried to complete the transition-inclusive energy layer for the cutoff flow using coupled local curvature–defect energies and four-dimensional Sobolev-volume cancellation. It identified the right flavor of estimates and recorded agreement with peer work, but Step 18 corrected the logical order. The coupled \(L^2\) inequalities assume the very geometric comparability and Sobolev/control quantities they are meant to produce, so they must be embedded in a simultaneous first-exit bootstrap. A weighted \(C/t\) curvature bound alone cannot propagate the defect because its time integral diverges. The active analytic mechanism therefore shifted to fixed-\(p>2\) estimates for \(U=aE\), whose eventual pointwise bound has an integrable \(t^{-2/p}\) singularity [Steps 17-18].

Step 19 sharpened this by separating metric drift from connection drift. The user highlighted that \(\partial_t\Gamma\) is linear in \(\nabla U\), and for the scalar cutoff \(a=\chi^2\), \(\partial_t(\operatorname{Hess}_g a)=-(\partial_t\Gamma)\cdot da\), so the dangerous derivative is \(\chi\nabla U\), matched to the degenerate diffusion coefficient. The recorded threshold was \(p>4\) for integrating a derivative estimate of the form \(|\chi\nabla U|\le C\delta t^{-1/2}(r^2/t)^{2/p}\), whereas \(p>2\) suffices for metric drift. This clarified that if quantitative connection drift is used, a fixed exponent such as \(p=6\) or \(8\) should be chosen from the start; however, the derivative estimate was still a target and not a consequence [Step 19].

Step 19 also made the curvature-potential route more plausible by showing that Wang’s critical parameter \(\beta=A_0^2\|{\rm Rm}\|_{L^2}\) is volume-independent at the four-dimensional Li radius. This gave analytic meaning to the earlier “collapse-volume cancellation”: collapsed volume worsens the Sobolev constant but also lowers the \(L^2\) norm at fixed average curvature, so their product remains controlled. TTCS emphasized that this algebra is not itself the localized degenerate theorem: Wang’s proof is global-degenerate, Li’s is local-nondegenerate, and the needed proof must combine both features with separate flow and localization cutoffs [Step 19].

Step 20 corrected the attempted transition to Li’s unweighted potential. The user noted that small \(\beta\) controls reaction coefficients but does not restore ellipticity where \(\chi\to0\); \(\int a|{\rm Rm}|^3\) is not Li’s unweighted \(\int|{\rm Rm}|^3\) in the transition. The route therefore adopted Wang’s weighted moments \(H_q\) and the corresponding defect moments \(J_m\). This was a significant representation change: the powers of \(\chi\) are no longer boundary nuisances but the mechanism that makes the degenerate Sobolev hierarchy close without dividing by \(a\) [Step 20].

The same step demoted global derivative estimates. TTCS argued that weak \(H_q\), \(J_m\), and \(Q\) estimates can integrate Hessian-\(a\) terms away, while bilipschitz metric control transfers fixed cutoff-gradient norms, relative Sobolev inequalities, volumes, and buffered containment. Smooth continuation may generate qualitative derivative bounds internally; uniform derivative compactness is recovered later on the plateau. Thus the research line shifted from proving a global weighted Bernstein theorem to proving a derivative-free zero-order first-exit plus qualitative continuation [Steps 20-21].

Step 21 articulated the two-layer architecture. Layer A is the uniform weak/zero-order bootstrap on the whole active support: metric comparability, Sobolev, \(H_2\), \(Q\), and weighted pointwise curvature/defect. Layer B is positive-time interior regularity on strict plateaux, where \(a=1\) and standard normalized Ricci-flow estimates give uniform derivatives for smooth local compactness. This distinction resolved a conceptual tension: qualitative continuation may depend on each individual initial smooth metric and cutoff, while the final local limit requires only uniform plateau estimates after a common positive time [Step 21].

A proposed abstract Nash reformulation was then stress-tested and rejected. The inverse-square Hardy example showed that a small critical form bound can coexist with singular heat-kernel weights and no ordinary ultracontractivity. This changed the line from “maybe an abstract semigroup theorem replaces Moser” to “the \(H_2\to H_3\) upgrade is indispensable.” The Nash/conformal-measure idea survived only as a possible language for subcritical Stage 2, not as a replacement for the critical Wang step [Step 22].

Step 22 also clarified the hard/soft split in the smoothing theorem. The hard step is to prove \(A_0^4H_3(t)\le C\gamma^3/t\) from \(H_2\) using critical Sobolev absorption and volume-independent \(\beta\). Once an \(L^3\) potential exists at positive time, it is subcritical and all-exponent Moser constants can converge. This refined the target from a broad “localized degenerate Moser theorem” to a concrete critical energy lemma plus later standard subcritical iteration [Step 22].

Step 23 repaired the localization structure. The user pointed out that using an outer dissipation \(D_2^{out}\) in the Sobolev step and then absorbing it into an inner \(D_2\) was unjustified. The line shifted to a single-good-support construction: choose buffered supports from maximal-function/Vitali good centers so that the auxiliary cutoff equals one around the flow cutoff. Then \(v_2=\chi F\) and \(v_3=\chi^2F^{3/2}\) have gradients controlled by the same component dissipation plus zero-order cutoff terms. This removed the artificial global component graph through uncontrolled bad regions and aligned the proof with Yang’s one-support theorem and Wang’s fixed \(q=2,3\) calculations [Step 23].

Step 23 also separated spacetime and terminal control. A spacetime integral of \(H_3\) only yields a good time slice; narrow terminal spikes require a fixed-\(q=3\) differential inequality to propagate that slice to the endpoint. The same logic kept \(J_6\) and \(Q\) separate: \(J_6\) must retain its initial \(\delta^6\) factor from time zero, and global unweighted \(Q\) must be preserved by a homogeneous integrated identity, not by a curvature-only source estimate. This made the conditional chain more complex but less circular [Step 23].

Step 24 found a real tensor convention error: the fully lowered curvature tensor under the conformal part of the normalized flow has a \(-2a{\rm Rm}\) term. The sparse record from Step 24 overstated this as beneficial damping. Step 25 corrected the scientific understanding: once the norm and volume are varied in dimension four, pure homothety leaves \(\int|{\rm Rm}|^2\) invariant, so there is no free curvature-energy coercivity. The remaining valid use of the calculation is to keep tensor, inverse-metric, and measure terms consistently in the energy inequality; success still depends on matched Sobolev absorption [Steps 24-25].

Step 25 also corrected an over-simplification about plateau regularity. Step 21’s distinction remains valuable, but it does not remove transition-region zero-order needs: the first-exit argument still uses whole-support metric distortion, Sobolev, cutoff gradients, and support containment. Thus the proof must restore whole-support weighted estimates for \(a{\rm Rm}\) and \(aE\), then use plateau regularity only afterward for derivatives and compactness. This preserved the derivative-free advantage without pretending transition control is unnecessary [Step 25].

The subsequent repair connected the weighted hierarchy directly to Yang’s iteration. Yang’s exponent relation \(p'_j=p_j-2\) exactly matches \(a^{p_j-2}\Phi^{p_j}\), and the \(H_3=\int aF^3\) potential is precisely the needed subcritical input. This supplied a clearer endpoint route: positive-time \(H_3\) plus Moser gives \(|a{\rm Rm}|\lesssim\bar\beta/t\), and propagated \(J_6\) plus the same potential gives \(|aE|\lesssim\delta(r^2/t)^{1/3}\). The latter integrability supplies the collar metric comparison missing from plateau-only reasoning [Step 25].

Step 26 then resolved two foundational inputs for this route. First, it extended the tensor inequality from fixed \(q=2,3\) to general \(p\ge3\), with polynomial \(p^3\) loss and correct regularization of the defect. Second, it verified the collapse-adapted local Sobolev inequality via Maheux–Saloff-Coste under a Ricci lower bound. These removed two major analytic initialization obstacles. The remaining obstacle at that point was smooth continuation of the normalized degenerate cutoff flow once \(|a{\rm Rm}|\) is bounded [Step 26].

Step 27 corrected the continuation specification at the highest-derivative level. The added velocity \(-2ag\) cannot be treated as a harmless lower-order source in Wang’s derivative induction, because its curvature variation includes \(-(\operatorname{Hess}a)\wedge g\), leading to \(\nabla^{m+2}a\) after commuting derivatives. The solution was to package the flow with the shifted curvature \(T={\rm Rm}+G\), where \(G\) has Ricci contraction \(g\). This converts the normalization into the same structural family as the Ricci source: Hessian-\(a\) terms contract with \(T\), first-derivative terms with \(\nabla T\), and cutoff jets are driven by \(\operatorname{Ric}(U)=aE\). The continuation problem was reorganized as a triangular induction on \(\nabla^mU\) and \(\nabla^{m+1}\chi\), followed by \(\nabla^mT\), preserving Wang’s derivative mechanism in normalized form [Step 27].

By Step 27, the four-dimensional negative critical program had become a concentrated conditional chain. Starting from a hypothetical near-\(-g\) Ricci sequence on critical Ishida–LeBrun manifolds, choose positive-volume good supports with collapse-adapted Sobolev control; run the normalized cutoff flow; use general-\(p\) weighted inequalities to preserve \(H_2\), obtain terminal \(H_3\), propagate \(J_6\) and global \(Q\), and derive weighted pointwise \(a{\rm Rm}\) and \(aE\); integrate \(aE\) to improve metric/Sobolev/support first-exit quantities; use shifted-curvature continuation to reach a common positive time; obtain uniform derivatives on strict plateaux by interior normalized Ricci-flow estimates; use completion-square, \(q^+\) monopole/eigenline densities, and exponential-pullback averaging to select a smooth local Einstein limit with calibrated \(W^+\)-spectrum; then apply the Step 6 projector contradiction [Steps 16, 20-27].

The latest handoff did not ask for final writing. It asked Agent4 to rigorously read the now-developed four-dimensional negative chain, inspect the still-running Codex worker when complete, compare A01’s unified weak Moser/continuation notes with A03’s Steps 23–27, and verify the downstream geometric bridge: reapplying \(7/24\) and Seiberg–Witten deficits to the terminal closed metric, quantifying retained volume/buffer of plateaux, checking exponential-pullback averaging with joint monopole density, ensuring positive-time curvature/derivative bounds on geodesics used by charts, and confirming passage to the calibrated Einstein germ. Any unresolved interface should remain further Execute/Explore work [Step 27].

The topology-uniform aspect remains precise but limited. Fixed-topology absolute smallness is no longer the only conceivable target because exponential averaging can use volume-normalized deficits over positive-volume plateau centers. Step 18 retained a Noether-based \(\chi(M)/A\le65/6\) bound for a standard minimal general-type Ishida–LeBrun subclass with \(b_+(N)=0\), so analytic constants depending on \(\chi/A\) might be uniform there. No corresponding result is available for arbitrary symplectic summands or the full negative branch [Steps 17-18, 26-27].

## Simultaneous cutoff-flow bootstrap, weighted defect, and topology-uniform considerations [Steps 17-19]

Step 17 began developing the transition-inclusive normalized cutoff-flow theorem [Step 17]. A cleaner defect evolution identity under \(a=\chi^2\) was derived: inverse-metric variation \(+4a\operatorname{tr}(E^3)\) cancels the \(-4a\operatorname{tr}(E^3)\) from the Lichnerowicz/damping interaction, leaving
\[

=
-2a|\nabla E|^2+4a\,\operatorname{Rm}(E,E)+2\langle E,\mathcal C_a(E)\rangle
\]
with no explicit cubic defect reaction [Step 17]. TTCS corrected an overclaim: a maximum-principle bound for \(|E|^2\) requires \(\|a\,\operatorname{Rm}(g(t))\|_\infty\), not just initial curvature mean, because \(C^0\) metric closeness does not control curvature [Step 17]. Thus curvature regularity and defect preservation remained coupled [Step 17].

The same step proposed a finite-neighbor \(L^2\) curvature–defect energy system with local energies \(H_\alpha=R_\alpha+\kappa P_\alpha\) [Step 17]. The idea was the four-dimensional Sobolev-energy cancellation: products such as \(C_S\|\operatorname{Rm}\|_{L^2}\) become \(O(\sqrt{\varepsilon_*})\) under small normalized critical energy, allowing absorption of curvature cubic terms, \(\int a|\operatorname{Rm}||E|^2\), and transition cross terms [Step 17]. Step 17 initially stated this as closed critical curvature-energy persistence [Step 17].

Step 18 repaired the logical order [Step 18]. The coupled \(L^2\) estimates are conditional bootstrap inequalities: they assume smooth existence, metric comparability, relative Sobolev geometry, fixed ball/overlap control, cutoff control, and small neighboring energies. They can improve these inside a first-exit argument but do not independently produce them [Step 18]. Two shortcuts were ruled out: a weighted curvature bound \(|a\operatorname{Rm}|\le C/t\) gives a nonintegrable \(\int_0^Tdt/t\) factor for defect by maximum principle, and small velocity \(O(\delta)\) does not imply small transition-curvature change because curvature evolution contains second derivatives of \(aE\) [Step 18].

The main Step 18 construction was to weight the defect before higher-power estimates [Step 18]. With \(U=aE\), commuting \(a\) through the Laplacian cancels the leading \(a(\Delta a)E\) and \(2a\nabla a\cdot\nabla E\) terms; quotients by \(a\) remain regular because \(da\otimes da/a=4\,d\chi\otimes d\chi\) [Step 18]. Testing by \(\eta^2|U|^{p-2}U\) gives a localized fixed-\(p\) inequality
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\int\eta^2|U|^p
+c_p\int\eta^2a|\nabla |U|^{p/2}|^2
\le
\text{cutoff terms}
+C_p\int\eta^2a|\operatorname{Rm}||U|^p
+C_p\int\eta^2|U|^{p+1}
\]
[Step 18]. In dimension four, relative Sobolev absorption cancels collapsed volume, so for a fixed \(p>2\), under provisional first-exit geometry and small neighboring curvature/defect energies, spatial \(L^p\) norms of \(aE\) can be propagated [Step 18]. It was explicitly noted that this cannot be iterated to \(p=\infty\) with one critical threshold because coefficients grow with \(p\) [Step 18]. The desired second stage would be Li/Yang-like: from a curvature-potential estimate such as \(S_\alpha^4\int a|\operatorname{Rm}|^3\le C/t\), a time-cylinder Moser iteration could yield
\[
|aE(t)|\le C_p\delta(r^2/t)^{2/p},
\]
integrable in time for \(p>2\) [Step 18]. The active file became `workspace/notes/step18_simultaneous_bootstrap_and_fixed_p_defect.md` [Step 18].

A user message in Step 19 sharpened the role of \(p\) by focusing on connection and cutoff-Hessian drift [Step 19]. Since \(\partial_tg=-2U\), connection variation is linear in \(\nabla U\), and for the fixed scalar cutoff \(a=\chi^2\),

\partial_t(\operatorname{Hess}_g a)=-(\partial_t\Gamma)\cdot da
\]
so the dangerous derivative is naturally \(\chi\nabla U\), not unweighted \(\nabla U\) [Step 19]. The target derivative estimate

has time integral finite iff \(p>4\), whereas metric drift only requires \(p>2\) [Step 19]. Step 19 verified the threshold and recorded that \(p=6\) or \(p=8\) would give an integrability margin for both metric and connection drift if such derivative estimates were proved [Step 19]. has the volume factor in \(A_0^2\) cancel the volume factor in \(\|\operatorname{Rm}\|_2\), giving \(\beta=C\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\rm Li}}\) after choosing \(r_*\) by Li’s small-energy condition [Step 19]. ## Weighted Wang hierarchy, Nash rejection, and single-support repair [Steps 20-23]

## Normalization correction, whole-support Yang iteration, and Sobolev initialization [Steps 24-26]

Step 24 found an important curvature-evolution correction but initially overinterpreted its energy effect [Step 24]. The correction was that the conformal component \(h=-2ag\) contributes a linear term \(-2a\operatorname{Rm}\) to the fully covariant \((0,4)\) curvature tensor by index lowering, even though the mixed tensor formula cancels lower-order \(R\cdot h\) terms for conformal \(h\) [Step 24]. The constant-conformal test \(g(t)=e^{-2t}g_0\) verifies this: Christoffel symbols and \(R^l{}_{ijk}\) are unchanged, but \(R_{ijkl}(t)=e^{-2t}R_{ijkl}(0)\), so \(\partial_tR_{ijkl}=-2R_{ijkl}\) [Step 24]. The corrected evolution was recorded schematically as
\[
\partial_t\operatorname{Rm}
=
a\Delta\operatorname{Rm}
+aQ(\operatorname{Rm})
-2a\operatorname{Rm}
+C(\nabla a,\nabla E)
-(\nabla^2a\wedge E)
\]
[Step 24]. Step 24 temporarily called this a beneficial damping term in the \(H_2\) inequality and rebuilt a conditional chain around it [Step 24].

Step 25 corrected that interpretation [Step 25]. Although \(-2a\operatorname{Rm}\) is correct for the fully covariant tensor, it is not a net damping term for the evolving curvature norm-energy [Step 25]. Under pure homothety \(\partial_tg=-2ag\) with spatially constant \(a\), the tensor contribution gives \(-4a|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\), the four inverse metrics give \(+8a|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\), and in dimension four the measure variation gives \(-4a|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\), so \(|\operatorname{Rm}|^2d\mu\) is scale invariant [Step 25]. For \(F=(1+|\operatorname{Rm}|^2)^{1/2}\), the pure-normalization density term is
\[
2a\big[(p-2)F^p-pF^{p-2}\big]\,d\mu
\]
[Step 25]. The route must rely on matched Sobolev absorption and homogeneous defect control, not artificial normalization coercivity [Step 25]. Step 24’s note was prefaced with a supersession notice [Step 25].

Step 25 also restored whole-support transition control as necessary [Step 25]. Plateau regularity suffices later for positive-time higher derivatives and smooth local limits, but it cannot preserve metric distortion, relative Sobolev constants, cutoff-gradient norms, or support geometry in the collar \(0<a<1\) during the first-exit [Step 25]. The correct bridge is a whole-support weighted iteration using the fixed \(q=2,3\) estimates, terminal \(H_3(t)\), and preserved \(J_6\) [Step 25]. On one buffered good support, the safe critical parameter is \(\bar\beta=\mathsf S H_2^{1/2}\), or one must explicitly subtract stationary auxiliary collar energy; the active-region norm cannot be silently identified with a larger auxiliary norm [Step 25].

A central Step 25 observation was the exact match between the weighted hierarchy and Yang’s fixed-cutoff Moser iteration in four dimensions [Step 25]. Yang’s exponents satisfy \(p_{j+1}=3p_j/2\), \(p'_{j+1}=3p'_j/2+1\), and if \(p'_0=p_0-2\), then \(p'_j=p_j-2\), so Yang moments \(\chi^{2p'_j}\Phi^{p_j}\) are exactly \(a^{p_j-2}\Phi^{p_j}\) [Step 25]. Choosing potential exponent six makes Yang’s weighted potential \(H_3=\int aF^3\) [Step 25]. The interpolation identity

a^{p-1}F\Phi^p
=(aF^3)^{1/3}\big(a^{3p/2-2}\Phi^{3p/2}\big)^{2/3}

followed by Sobolev and Young gives polynomial-in-\(p\) coefficients, e.g. \(Cp^3(r^{-2}+\mathsf S^2H_3)\), so after \(H_3\) is known the later iteration no longer needs shrinking critical-smallness thresholds [Step 25]. Starting at \(p_0=3\) yields whole-support \(\|a\operatorname{Rm}(t)\|_\infty\lesssim\bar\beta/t\); starting at \(p_0=6\) with propagated \(J_6\) yields \(\|aE(t)\|_\infty\lesssim\delta(r^2/t)^{1/3}\), integrable at zero and able to control collar metric comparison [Step 25]. `workspace/scripts/verify_step25_normalization_and_moser_exponents.py` initially exposed and then corrected a Hölder-weight typo; the final run verified homothetic cancellation, \(F^pd\mu\), Yang weights, product convergence, and endpoint scales [Step 25].

## Shifted-curvature continuation package and current review target [Step 27]

Step 27 repaired the continuation specification at the highest-derivative level [Step 27]. A user pointed out that the Step 26 continuation note omitted the term most likely to determine whether Wang’s induction transfers: under the added velocity \(-2ag\), the covariant curvature variation contains both \(-2a\operatorname{Rm}\) and \(-(\operatorname{Hess}a)\wedge g\) in the tensor convention already used [Step 27]. Commuting \(m\) derivatives reaches \(\nabla^{m+2}a\), and the weighted curvature evolution contains derivatives of \(a\,\operatorname{Hess}a\); these do not disappear because \(\nabla g=0\) [Step 27]. Neither metric comparability nor bounded \(a\operatorname{Rm}\) controls higher cutoff jets by itself; they must be produced by the triangular induction [Step 27].

The response was to repackage the normalized problem by adding a parallel constant-curvature background tensor [Step 27]. Let
\[
G=\frac{g\wedge g}{2(n-1)}
\]
in the chosen convention, so \(\operatorname{Ric}(G)=g\), and define
\[
T=\operatorname{Rm}+G,\qquad U=aT.
\]
Then \(\operatorname{Ric}(T)=E=\operatorname{Ric}+g\), \(\operatorname{Ric}(U)=aE\), and \(\nabla G=0\), while \(\partial_tG\) is algebraic in \(aE\) and \(g\) [Step 27]. This restores the structural relationship between curvature, its Ricci contraction, and cutoff derivatives that was obscured when the normalization source was separated [Step 27]. The shifted evolution has Wang-like form:
\[
(\partial_t-a\Delta)T
=
da*\nabla T+\operatorname{Hess}(a)*T+a(T*T+G*T)
\]
schematically, and the weighted \(U=aT\) equation contains no singular division by \(a\) and no independent \(\operatorname{Hess}(a)*G\) forcing [Step 27]. The reaction vanishes at \(T=0\); there is no true constant curvature forcing [Step 27].

The genuine highest cutoff term \(\chi\nabla^{m+2}\chi*U\) remains and was not suppressed [Step 27]. One integration by parts absorbs the derivative on \(\nabla^mU\) into the \(a=\chi^2\) weighted diffusion and lowers the remaining cutoff order to \(m+1\) [Step 27]. The cutoff jets are then driven by derivatives of \(\operatorname{Ric}(U)=aE\) [Step 27]. TTCS resolved an apparent indexing discrepancy in Wang’s printed Proposition 4.14: the high-order proof requires the current Volterra pair \(\nabla^mU\leftrightarrow\nabla^{m+1}\chi\), while the prior unweighted quantity \(\nabla^{m-1}T\) needs only \(\nabla^m\chi\) after its own integration by parts [Step 27]. No algebraic cancellation removes the \(m+1\) cutoff jet [Step 27].

Under a terminal bound on \(a\operatorname{Rm}\), Step 27’s shifted formulation gives bounded \(U\) because \(0\le a\le1\) and \(G\) is dimension-controlled, metric equivalence persists, finite unweighted \(L^p\) norms of \(T\) follow across zeros of \(a\), and the staggered Wang induction can propagate all \(U\)-derivatives in the developed framework [Step 27]. These bounds reconstruct a smooth positive terminal metric and permit a transported-coefficient normalized DeTurck restart; the principal symbol is unchanged by adding the lower-order \(-2\hat\chi^2\hat g\) term [Step 27]. The \(C/t\) whole-support Moser estimate is enough near a positive maximal time because it is uniformly bounded on a terminal half-interval, while ordinary smooth short-time existence covers the initial interval [Step 27]. This removes the structural continuation obstruction in the session’s internal chain, though the agents explicitly left an independent detailed term ledger desirable and a session Codex worker launched from `workspace/codex_loop/Research_Project_Proposal.md` was still running when Step 27 closed [Step 27]. ## Positive branch, higher dimensions, and peer-session context [Steps 4-27]

The positive branch remained secondary throughout this period [Steps 4-27]. Communication with S0910A02 established that in dimension four, if \(|\operatorname{Ric}-g|_{\rm op}\le\delta_0<1/2\) and volume has a positive lower bound, Myers, Bishop–Gromov, and Cheeger–Naber finiteness give strong finiteness consequences; infinitely many \(\#_k(S^2\times S^2)\)-type manifolds with positive normalized tight pinching would have to collapse [Steps 4-8]. The agents repeatedly corrected the idea that collapse itself obstructs Yau 26, because round lens-space quotients are exact Einstein and can collapse in volume [Steps 5-9]. A02 later noted positive-branch constraints such as \(\#_5\mathbb{CP}^2\) admitting Ricci-positive input but no Einstein metric, and pursued toric/rod and integral-identity analyses on \(\#_k(S^2\times S^2)\), but no reduction from arbitrary metrics to invariant or toric ones was obtained [Steps 17-25]. A02’s later toric verdict was that integral identities alone do not obstruct the relevant \(\alpha\)-families, so the positive branch would need a global PDE solvability obstruction, not just local or toric integral constraints [Steps 24-25].

Higher dimensions \(n\ge5\) remain largely untouched by the main route [Steps 2-27]. The four-dimensional machinery—Chern–Weil Hitchin–Thorpe constraints, Seiberg–Witten monopole classes, LeBrun–Ishida–LeBrun inequalities, and calibrated \(W^+\) spectra—does not transfer directly [Steps 2-18]. A02 observed that codimension-one positive Einstein collapse exists in higher dimensions via Kaluza–Klein-type constructions \(L(q,1)\times N^d\), while dimension four has Bochner-type restrictions; this reinforces that collapse cannot be a universal positive-branch obstruction in higher dimensions [Step 22]. No broad stock of closed high-dimensional manifolds is yet known in this session to lack Einstein metrics of all signs in a way that would deliver a Yau 26 counterexample [Steps 2-27].

Collaboration with S0910A01 and S0910A02 materially shaped the research. A02’s positive-branch and collapse observations were useful dimensional context but were not conflated with the negative critical route [Steps 11-27].
