## Results, Observations, and Their Meaning

### Problem quantifiers, normalization, and low dimensions

- For fixed dimension \(n\), the interval version of Yau Problem 26 was reduced to normalized one-sign branches \(P_n^+\) and \(P_n^-\). Since every nondegenerate real interval contains a one-sign subinterval and constant rescaling \(h=|\mu|g\) rescales the Ricci endomorphism in the needed way, the original statement \(Q_n\) is equivalent to \(P_n^+\lor P_n^-\). A strict disproof in one fixed dimension must defeat both normalized signs, but the two witnessing manifolds need not be the same; requiring one manifold to realize both signs is an unnecessary strengthening [Step 1; corrected Step 10].

- Dimensions \(2\) and \(3\) are already covered in the sense required by the original problem: dimension \(2\) by uniformization, and dimension \(3\) by Hamilton’s positive Ricci theorem giving a positive branch. The unresolved range begins at dimension \(4\) [Step 1].

### Orbifold desingularization route and its limitation

- In the Morteza–Viaclovsky Einstein-orbifold desingularization setting, weighted gluing estimates were converted into the unweighted Ricci-endomorphism defect relevant to Yau 26. In the ALE core the refined metric was written
  \[
  g_t=t h_t=t(g_{\rm cal}+t h),
  \]
  with local expansion
  \[
  \operatorname{Ric}(h_t)=t\Lambda h_t+t\lambda o+R_t,\qquad
  |R_t|_{g_{\rm cal}}\le C t^2\rho^2 .
  \]
  Since constant scaling does not change the \((0,2)\)-Ricci tensor,
  \[
  g_t^{-1}(\operatorname{Ric}(g_t)-\Lambda g_t)
  =\lambda h_t^{-1}o+t^{-1}h_t^{-1}R_t .
  \]
  On fixed ALE core sets the first term converges to \(\lambda g_{\rm cal}^{-1}o\), while the remainder is \(O(t^{1/2})\) on the core range \(\rho\le Ct^{-1/4}\) [Step 1].

- The explicit tensor \(o\) has eigenvalues
  \[
  -\frac1{1+r^{2n}}
  \quad\text{in horizontal real directions, multiplicity }2n-2,
  \]
  and
  \[
  \frac{n-1}{1+r^{2n}}
  \quad\text{in radial and Hopf directions}.
  \]
  Thus the unweighted defect has core supremum tending to \((n-1)|\lambda|\) when the first obstruction \(\lambda\ne0\). Weighted norms and ALE rescaling do not remove this obstruction [Step 1].

- In transition annuli for the same gluing framework, residual terms are \(O(t^{1/2})\), and the obstruction contribution decays like \(O(t^{n/2})\) when \(o=O(r^{-2n})\) and \(r\approx t^{-1/4}\). Therefore this desingularization route can yield uniform Ricci pinching only if all first obstructions at all singular points vanish; even then, higher obstructions and global no-Einstein topology remain unresolved [Step 1].

- Local nonexistence near a chosen Einstein-orbifold degeneration is not evidence of global no-Einstein topology. The two-point football Eguchi–Hanson resolution gives \(S^2\times S^2\), which has a product Einstein metric, separating “no Einstein metric near this degeneration” from “no Einstein metric on the smooth manifold” [Step 1].

### Perturbative Ricci-symbol route

- The flat-background principal symbol of \(D\operatorname{Ric}\) has no nongauge kernel:
  \[
  \ker\sigma_\xi(D\operatorname{Ric})
  =
  \{\xi\otimes v+v\otimes\xi\}
  \]
  for every nonzero covector \(\xi\). In coordinates \(\xi=e_1\), the kernel equations force all transverse components \(h_{ab}\), \(a,b>1\), to vanish, leaving exactly infinitesimal diffeomorphism directions. This was checked algebraically and numerically for \(n=3,4,5\) [Steps 2–3].

- Consequently, the proposed high-frequency averaged-cone construction from nongauge linear Ricci-flat modes is unavailable. Second-order Ricci terms from truncated gauge perturbations cancel when completed to an exact pullback of the flat metric [Steps 2–3].

### Four-dimensional Chern–Weil pinching constraints

- A strengthened Hitchin–Thorpe estimate was derived for four-dimensional metrics satisfying
  \[
  \|g^{-1}(\operatorname{Ric}-\Lambda g)\|_\infty\le \delta|\Lambda|.
  \]
  If
  \[
  \delta<\frac{\sqrt3-1}{2}\approx0.366,
  \]
  then
  \[
  2\chi>3|\tau|.
  \]
  Hence Hitchin–Thorpe-violating manifolds and equality-boundary manifolds cannot support sufficiently tight normalized Ricci pinching of either sign [Step 2].

- For LeBrun/Ishida–LeBrun no-Einstein families, the valid gauge-theoretic input is Ishida–LeBrun Proposition 4:
  \[
  \frac1{4\pi^2}\int\left(\frac{s^2}{24}+2|W^+|^2\right)d\mu
  \ge \frac23(a^+)^2
  \]
  under the applicable monopole hypotheses. Combined with pointwise Ricci pinching and Chern–Weil identities, this gives quantitative restrictions on negative pinching in these families [Steps 2–3].

- A claimed independent pure \(W^+\) lower bound
  \[
  \int |W^+|^2\ge \frac{4\pi^2}{3}(a^+)^2
  \]
  was withdrawn. The derivation incorrectly dropped a negative gradient term in LeBrun’s Weitzenböck estimate and treated \(F_A^+\) as generally harmonic. The usable evidence is the published mixed scalar–Weyl inequality, not the stronger Weyl-only claim. This correction invalidated the earlier overstatement that all known no-Einstein families had been eliminated by a uniform gap [Step 3].

### Ishida–LeBrun critical family and near-saturation profile

- The main four-dimensional negative-branch test interface is the Ishida–LeBrun Theorem 7 family
  \[
  M=\left(\#_{j=1}^mX_j\right)\# N,
  \qquad
  A=\sum_j c_1^2(X_j),
  \qquad
  D=4m-(2\chi+3\tau)(N),
  \]
  for \(m=2\) or \(3\). The theorem excludes Einstein metrics when \(D\ge A/3\). At the boundary \(D=A/3\), strictness in the exact Einstein equality argument does not by itself produce a positive infimum of the Ricci-pinching defect over all metrics, so this boundary remains the main known no-Einstein/topological obstruction interface for possible \(\delta\to0\) negative pinching [Step 3].

- For a hypothetical fixed critical Ishida–LeBrun manifold with metrics satisfying
  \[
  \delta_i=\|g_i^{-1}(\operatorname{Ric}_{g_i}+g_i)\|_\infty\to0,
  \]
  normalized Chern–Weil quantities \(S_i,W_i,R_i,I_i\) were defined and gave
  \[
  I_i-R_i=\frac{2A}{3},\qquad R_i=O(A\delta_i^2).
  \]
  Thus \(R_i/A\to0\) and \(I_i/A\to2/3\). The calibrated energy profile recorded was
  \[
  \operatorname{Vol}(g_i)\to \frac{32\pi^2A}{9},
  \]
  \[
  \int |W_i^+|^2/(\pi^2A)\to \frac4{27},
  \]
  \[
  \int |\operatorname{Ric}_i^\circ|^2/(\pi^2A)\to0,
  \qquad
  \int |\operatorname{Ric}_i|^2/(\pi^2A)\to\frac{128}{9}.
  \]
  These are necessary consequences of a hypothetical pinching sequence, not evidence such a sequence exists [Step 3].

- Averaging over Bauer–Furuta sign classes gave period-plane constraints: positive spaces must asymptotically contain the canonical positive directions of symplectic summands and asymptotically reject the negative directions from \(N\). The recorded estimate was
  \[
  \sum \|c_{j,i}^-\|^2+\sum \|E_{\ell,i}^+\|^2
  \le \frac32 R_i=O(A\delta_i^2).
  \]
  This supports possible spatial separation of monopole classes in a collapsing sequence but does not prove a global symplectic structure [Step 3].

### Weyl profile, bubbles, and quantitative equality defects

- From the genuine scalar–Weyl inequality and uniform scalar convergence \(s_i\to -4\), the completed-square identity gave
  \[
  \int\left(|W_i^+|-\frac1{2\sqrt6}\right)^2\,d\mu_i
  =O(A\delta_i^2).
  \]
  The calibrated value \(1/(2\sqrt6)\) is one quarter of the value \(|W^+|=2/\sqrt6\) for a normalized negative Kähler–Einstein metric in its complex orientation. Therefore positive-volume regions of a hypothetical critical sequence cannot converge to ordinary negative Kähler–Einstein bulk geometry [Step 4].

- Scalar-flat ASD connector regions cannot represent the pointwise pinched sequence because scalar-flat regions have \(|s+4|=4\), forcing \(\delta\ge1\) regardless of their small volume [Step 4].

- For fixed topology \(A\) fixed, the Weyl profile implies that on subsets whose volume tends to zero, \(W^+\)-energy tends to zero in absolute terms. Because four-dimensional Weyl energy is scale invariant, any smooth noncollapsed shrinking-scale blow-up of a hypothetical fixed-topology sequence must be Ricci-flat and \(W^+=0\), hence locally hyperkähler in the relevant orientation. This allows anti-self-dual hyperkähler bubbles such as Eguchi–Hanson but rules out arbitrary Ricci-flat bubbles in that orientation. For varying topology \(A_i\to\infty\), only normalized smallness is available unless \(A_i\delta_i^2\to0\), so finite absolute \(W^+\)-energy bubbles are not excluded by this argument alone [Step 4].

- The Codex worker decomposed the Ishida–LeBrun near-equality proof chain into nonnegative defects. In the recorded normalization,
  \[
  \Delta_a\le108\pi^2 R,
  \]
  and Hodge projection error, spinor amplitude variation, Weitzenböck slack, Kato/quadratic-map discrepancy, harmonic projection error, and lowest-eigenline deviation are controlled by the same small trace-free Ricci budget. This verified Step 3 constants and made the equality mechanism quantitative under fixed-topology hypotheses [Step 4].

- Walsh polarization of sign classes gives \(L^1\)-type orthogonality and phase-separation evidence for canonical harmonic/self-dual forms. It does not yield pointwise Gram nondegeneracy or a global definite triple; upgrading would require additional eigenline or unique-continuation control. The defect decomposition controls amplitude, approximate harmonicity, and eigenline alignment, but not near-parallelness of the forms [Steps 4, 9].

- A convention ambiguity in the Weitzenböck formula for two-forms was resolved by testing candidate curvature endomorphisms against constant-holomorphic-sectional-curvature Kähler–Einstein metrics with \(\operatorname{Ric}=-g\), \(S^4\), and K3 checks. The convention retained is
  \[
  q(R)(\omega)_{ij}
  =
  \operatorname{Ric}_{ik}\omega_{kj}
  +\operatorname{Ric}_{jk}\omega_{ik}
  -2R_{ikjl}\omega_{kl}.
  \]
  Under the calibrated spectrum \((-1/6,1/12,1/12)\), harmonic self-dual forms are not nearly parallel: for the simple eigenform,
  \[
  \int|\nabla H|^2=\int |H|^2,
  \]
  and for the double eigenspace coefficient,
  \[
  \int|\nabla H|^2=\frac32\int |H|^2
  \]
  in the aligned case. This corrected arguments trying to force collapse rank from “almost parallel” monopole forms; the saturated profile requires controlled nonzero eigenline rotation [Step 9].

### Regular-patch obstruction and collapse reduction

- If a fixed critical sequence had a unit ball with a uniform positive volume lower bound, Cheeger–Naber four-dimensional regularity gives a fixed-scale regular harmonic-coordinate patch. With \(L^\infty\) Ricci defect and harmonic-coordinate Ricci equations, the local limit satisfies \(\operatorname{Ric}=-g\) distributionally and hence smoothly by elliptic regularity. Finite \(W^{2,p}_{\rm loc}\) convergence is enough to pass algebraic curvature defects [Steps 5–6].

- Regularized monopole data can be chosen diagonally so the limiting patch carries a nonzero self-dual eigenform and the sharp spectral relation
  \[
  \operatorname{Spec}(W^+)=\left(-\frac16,\frac1{12},\frac1{12}\right),
  \qquad |W^+|^2=\frac1{24}.
  \]
  This conclusion is local and fixed-topology; it does not restore global topology or control distant bubbles [Steps 5–6].

- The sign dispute about Derdziński’s theorem was resolved by a direct first-order projector argument. For an Einstein four-metric with \(W^+\) having two distinct constant eigenvalues \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\), let \(\omega\) be a local unit self-dual eigenform for the simple eigenvalue. Writing
  \[
  W^+=\mu\Pi_+ +(\lambda-\mu)\omega\otimes\omega
  \]
  and using \(\delta W^+=0\), the product rule gives
  \[
  (\nabla^a\omega_{ab})\omega_{cd}
  +\omega_{ab}\nabla^a\omega_{cd}=0.
  \]
  Contracting with \(\omega^{cd}\) and using \(|\omega|\) constant yields \(\nabla^a\omega_{ab}=0\), then \(\omega_{ab}\nabla^a\omega_{cd}=0\). A nonzero self-dual two-form in dimension four is nondegenerate, so \(\nabla\omega=0\) and hence \(\nabla W^+=0\). This is independent of whether the simple eigenvalue is positive or negative [Step 6].

- The calibrated spectrum contradicts the Einstein–Weyl identity
  \[
  \Delta|W^+|^2
  =
  2|\nabla W^+|^2+s|W^+|^2-36\det W^+.
  \]
  For \(s=-4\), \(\operatorname{Spec}(W^+)=(-1/6,1/12,1/12)\), \(|W^+|^2=1/24\), and \(\det W^+=-1/864\), the identity forces
  \[
  |\nabla W^+|^2=\frac1{16},
  \]
  contradicting \(\nabla W^+=0\). Derdziński 1983 Proposition 5 independently supports this: for \(\delta W^+=0\) and at most two eigenvalues, \((24|W^+|^2)^{1/3}g\) is locally Kähler, and constant \(|W^+|^2\) is equivalent to \(\nabla W^+=0\). The earlier local-conformal-scalar equation idea based on \(\Delta f=-f/2\) was withdrawn as insufficient; it omitted the Kähler closure/harmonic-Weyl conditions [Steps 5–6].

- Combining regular-patch extraction with the local spectral obstruction gives a fixed-topology collapse conclusion: any hypothetical \(\delta_i\to0\) sequence on a fixed critical Ishida–LeBrun manifold must satisfy
  \[
  \sup_{p\in M}\operatorname{Vol}_{g_i}B_1(p)\to0.
  \]
  Since total volume tends to \(32\pi^2A/9>0\), Bishop–Gromov comparison then forces diameter to diverge. This is not a proof of a negative-branch gap; it only reduces any such sequence to everywhere unit-scale collapse [Step 6].

### Exact collapse models, cover-transfer, and maximal-function evidence

- Lott’s adapted free-abelian Einstein equation was recorded as
  \[
  \Delta_B v=\left(\frac{|F|^2}{4}-\lambda N\right)v,\qquad v=\sqrt{\det G},
  \]
  where \(N\) is orbit dimension. For \(\lambda=-1\), the zero-order coefficient is positive:
  \[
  \Delta_B v=\left(\frac{|F|^2}{4}+N\right)v.
  \]
  In exact adapted symmetric settings this strongly restricts regular pure abelian negative-Einstein collapse on closed or suitable parabolic bases. A near-Einstein version with \(|E|=|\operatorname{Ric}+g|\le\delta\) formally gives a lower coefficient \(N(1-\delta)\), but applying it to arbitrary pinched metrics requires control of approximate local symmetries and transition laws; averaging a metric to make it invariant may destroy the Ricci defect [Steps 6–7].

- Capacity-based estimates previously used with the orbit-volume equation were found false. The inequality \(c\int\eta^2\le\int|\nabla\eta|^2\) was based on an invalid integration-by-parts/AM–GM sign; examples like \(v=e^{\sqrt c x}\) show the issue. Finite total volume gives \(v\in L^1\), not a uniform upper bound for \(v\). Model exclusions depending on these arguments were narrowed [Steps 7–8].

- For cohomogeneity-one nil\(^3\) collapse, the corrected equation is
  \[
  v''=(3-\mu)v,
  \qquad
  \mu=\frac{a_3^2}{2a_1^2a_2^2},
  \]
  equivalently \(v''=(3-\rho/2)v\) if \(\rho=a_3^2/(a_1^2a_2^2)\). The sign was checked against the complex hyperbolic cusp model; the alternative \(3+\mu\) formula was rejected. In the circle-base case, the ODE for \(\rho\) and its maximum principle imply \(\rho\le2/3\), hence \(v''\ge(8/3)v\), contradicting periodicity. Thus exact nil\(^3\) circle collapse is excluded. For finite intervals, convexity exclusion only holds under extra endpoint control such as \(\limsup\rho<6\); \(\rho\) can blow up at endpoints, so \(v\to0\) alone is insufficient [Steps 7–8].

- The complex hyperbolic cusp remains a real collapse model: \(v(s)=Ce^{4s/\sqrt6}\) on a half-line/ray has finite volume but infinite base length. This disproves any claim that finite volume alone bounds cusp length and shows that cusp segments and singular attachments remain genuine collapse mechanisms to analyze [Steps 7–8].

- A previous attempt to transfer global absolute smallness of calibrated deficit to local universal covers was invalid because it dropped covering multiplicity. In a collapsed product \(U\times S^1(\ell_i)\), a fixed defect density has downstairs integral \(O(\ell_i)\), while a fixed-size unwrapped patch has \(O(1)\) integral. Thus absolute smallness downstairs does not imply small lifted integral on arbitrary cover patches [Step 8].

- A corrected normal-cover local mean transfer lemma was established. If \(\operatorname{Ric}\ge -(n-1)K\), \(\pi:\widehat U\to U\) is a normal local Riemannian cover with sufficient buffer, and \(\phi\ge0\), then for corresponding radius-\(r\) balls,
  \[
  \fint_{B_r(\hat p)}\pi^*\phi
  \le
  \frac{V_{-K}^{(n)}(3r)}{V_{-K}^{(n)}(r)}
  \fint_{B_r(p)}\phi .
  \]
  The proof uses a Borel section, disjointness of deck translates, and Bishop–Gromov comparison; it avoids any sheet-number bound. It requires a genuine normal cover and buffered balls, not arbitrary truncated unwrapped patches [Step 8].

- With Ricci lower bound and Hardy–Littlewood maximal-function estimates, one can select large-volume sets on the fixed critical manifold where local averages of calibrated nonnegative defect \(F_i\) tend to zero at all small scales. This selection was extended to \(|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\): since total curvature energy is uniformly bounded and total volume has a positive limit, there are positive-volume good sets where \(M_1|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\le K_0\) and \(M_1F_i\to0\). The normal-cover mean lemma transports local mean bounds to buffered covers, but this still does not imply cover noncollapse or regular charts [Step 9].

### Taub–NUT–AdS model: corrected scope

- Taub–NUT–AdS metrics with NUT parameter \(\nu\to0\) were initially interpreted as exact \(\operatorname{Ric}=-g\) countermodels to “curvature energy control plus small calibrated defect implies local-cover noncollapse.” Later calculations and user correction narrowed this. The model refutes noncollapse in a prescribed oversized cover containing the NUT, but it does not satisfy the simultaneous good-point inputs required by the argument and does not preclude choosing a smaller buffered domain before taking the cover [Steps 9–10].

- Exact symbolic computation for the used Taub–NUT–AdS normalization verified \(\operatorname{Ric}+g=0\), the NUT smoothness condition, corrected volume density, and
  \[
  |W|^2=\frac{32\nu^2(4\nu^2-3)^2}{3(r+\nu)^6}.
  \]
  In the script orientation \(W^+=0\), while \(W^-\) has eigenvalues two copies of
  \[
  \frac{2\nu(4\nu^2-3)}{3(r+\nu)^3}
  \]
  and one copy of
  \[
  -\frac{4\nu(4\nu^2-3)}{3(r+\nu)^3}.
  \]
  The corrected cumulative full-Weyl energy tends to \(32\pi^2\); the NUT core has curvature means diverging at relevant fixed scales [Step 10].

- Around a point at fixed positive distance from the NUT, a sufficiently small fixed domain lies over a contractible annular base patch; its circle bundle is trivial, and the local cover unwraps the circle. With \(z=2\nu\psi\), the unwrapped annular limit is real hyperbolic four-space with sectional curvature \(-1/3\). In that limit \(W^+=0\), and the scalar–Weyl completed-square deficit is \(16\), not small. Thus standard Taub–NUT–AdS explains a failure of cover choice but is not itself a good-point calibrated escape model [Step 10].

- Under homothety, Ricci and Weyl curvature endomorphism spectra scale by the square of the physical radius when a radius-\(r\) ball is blown up. The forbidden local spectrum becomes \((-r^2/6,r^2/12,r^2/12)\) rather than staying numerically unchanged. The Step 9 claim that the Weyl spectrum is unchanged under such rescaling was corrected; the projector/Derdziński contradiction is homogeneous for every fixed positive Einstein scale \(\kappa\), but degenerates only if the useful scale tends to zero [Step 10].

### Pontryagin density and diffuse non-basic curvature

- The Levi–Civita Chern–Weil representative for \(\Lambda^2_+\) is
  \[
  \rho_+=\frac1{4\pi^2}\left(\frac{s^2}{24}+2|W^+|^2-\frac12|\operatorname{Ric}_0|^2\right).
  \]
  For a fixed critical near-saturating sequence,
  \[
  \int\left|\rho_+-\frac3{16\pi^2}\right|\,d\mu\to0.
  \]
  Hence characteristic density follows volume asymptotically; vanishing-volume cores cannot carry all of it [Step 10].

- Counting hypothetical NUT charges is therefore not the right starting point. Non-basic connection curvature may persist diffusely throughout the collapsed bulk. If a basic/split comparison connection \(B\) is introduced on a base of dimension \(\le3\), then \(P(F_B)=0\) but
  \[
  P(F_A)-P(F_B)=dT_P(A,B),
  \]
  so the Chern–Simons transgression must be controlled. Local charge is not automatically integral without boundary data [Step 10].

- A proposed lower bound for the mixed component \(\Xi=i_VF_{A_+}\) was reinterpreted after user correction. For the Levi–Civita connection on \(\Lambda^2_+\), any exact Einstein metric has self-dual curvature in the two-form argument, so for every unit vector \(V\),
  \[
  |\iota_VF|^2=|F|^2/2.
  \]
  Near Einstein, the anti-self-dual component is controlled by \(\operatorname{Ric}_0\), so substantial \(\Xi\) is a consistency identity present even in benign locally unwrappable real-hyperbolic cusp collapse. The discriminating feature of the critical sequence is the anisotropy of the self-dual curvature block, not the mere size of \(\Xi\) or \(\rho_+\) [Step 11].

### Rank-one circle reduction and chiral variables

- For a static circle reduction \(g=g_B+\ell^2d\psi^2\) with \(\operatorname{Ric}=-g\), the corrected formula is
  \[
  \operatorname{Spec}(W^+)=\{1/3-\eta_i\},
  \]
  where \(\eta_i\) are eigenvalues of \(h=\operatorname{Hess}(\ell)/\ell\), with \(\operatorname{tr}h=1\). The initial formula \(W^+=2J(h-I/3)\) was wrong; TTCS and model checks corrected it. The calibrated Hessian eigenvalues are \((1/2,1/4,1/4)\), not \((3/8,3/8,1/4)\). In a spherical cohomogeneity-one calculation the incompatibility strengthens to \(a''=a/4\) versus \(a''=a/2\), but this excludes only that symmetric static ansatz [Step 11].

- With twist, the trace relation becomes
  \[
  \operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{Hess}\ell/\ell)
  =1+\frac{\ell^2|F|^2}{4}
  \]
  for \(\operatorname{Ric}=-g\), not \(<1\). Near a smooth NUT, \(h\) and twist correction terms diverge individually and can cancel in the smooth total curvature; static terms do not dominate near the NUT and do not force \(W^+\to0\) [Step 11].

- A proposed “fiber survival/high-twist dichotomy” was formulated: if a circle fiber survives at fixed buffer scale, a cover might unwrap it and trigger the forbidden germ; if it dies at every fixed scale, persistent twist would be needed to maintain calibrated anisotropy. Later corrections showed this dichotomy was not established: low \(\ell^2|F|^2\) does not imply a static limit without derivative estimates, and failure of accessibility has not been shown to force a positive-volume lower bound for \(\ell^2|F|^2\) [Steps 11–12].

- Toric orthogonal transitivity from a \(T^2\)-symmetric setting does not make an individual Hopf circle action static. Vanishing connection curvature for the full \(T^2\) action means the two-dimensional planes perpendicular to torus orbits are integrable; it does not imply integrability of the three-dimensional planes perpendicular to a chosen circle. Taub–NUT–AdS itself has a polar \((\psi,\phi)\)-torus over \((r,\theta)\) while the Hopf-circle connection \(A=\cos\theta\,d\phi\) has nonzero curvature [Step 12].

- \(H^2\times H^2\), written as
  \[
  dr^2+\sinh^2 r\,d\psi^2+g_{H^2},
  \]
  is a static \(\operatorname{Ric}=-g\) example with \(\operatorname{Hess}\ell/\ell\) spectrum \((1,0,0)\) and constant
  \[
  \operatorname{Spec}(W^+)=(-2/3,1/3,1/3).
  \]
  Thus the spherical cohomogeneity-one exclusion is not a general static classification. The general calibrated constant-spectrum exclusion remains the Step 6 projector/Derdziński forbidden-germ argument [Step 12].

- For a regular circle reduction
  \[
  g=q+\ell^2\theta^2,\qquad u=d\log\ell,\qquad Z=\ell F,\qquad z=*_{q}Z,\qquad H=\operatorname{Hess}_q\ell/\ell,
  \]
  the negative-Einstein reduced Weyl blocks were recorded as
  \[
  E=\frac{\kappa}{3}I-H+\frac{|z|^2I-z\otimes z}{4},
  \]
  \[
  B=\frac12\left(\operatorname{sym}\nabla z+u\otimes z+z\otimes u-\langle u,z\rangle I\right),
  \]
  with reduced equations
  \[
  \operatorname{tr}H=\kappa+\frac{|z|^2}{2},\qquad
  dz=-2u\wedge z,\qquad
  \operatorname{div}z=\langle u,z\rangle,
  \]
  and, depending on orientation, \(W^\pm=E\pm B\). Here \(Z\) appears algebraically in \(E\), while \(\nabla z\) and \(u\otimes z\) enter \(B\), so small \(Z\) does not give a static limit [Step 12].

- In chiral variables
  \[
  a_+=u-z/2,\qquad a_-=u+z/2,
  \]
  the reduction has Riccati/Maurer–Cartan structure
  \[
  W^+=-\big[\operatorname{sym}\nabla a_+ +a_+\otimes a_+\big]_0,\qquad
  W^-=-\big[\operatorname{sym}\nabla a_- +a_-\otimes a_-\big]_0
  \]
  up to orientation convention, and
  \[
  da_+=a_+\wedge a_-,\qquad da_-=-a_+\wedge a_-.
  \]
  This representation clarifies the remaining analytic problem: calibrated Weyl data controls a chiral traceless Riccati tensor, but trace directions, \(u\)–\(z\) cancellation, and quotient degeneration remain uncontrolled [Step 12].

### Ye Li smoothing and cutoff-flow program before the weighted-Wang repair

- Ye Li’s four-dimensional smoothing theorem became relevant because at maximal-function good points
  \[
  r^4\fint_{B_r}|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\le K_0r^4.
  \]
  Choosing a sufficiently small but fixed physical radius \(r=r(K_0,\varepsilon)>0\) makes the dimensionless energy small uniformly along the sequence. This does not require the calibrated background curvature to vanish; its dimensionless energy scales like \(r^4\). Bishop–Gromov comparison under the Ricci lower bound transfers centered curvature-mean control from a good point to nearby centers in a buffered region at comparable radii [Step 13].

- The initial Step 13 smoothing closure was not valid. The inequality \(Y'_{\rm inner}\le Cr^{-2}Y_{\rm outer}\) does not imply a Gronwall estimate for \(Y_{\rm inner}\), persistence of small curvature energy through the flow was assumed, and numerical absorption/amplification factors only illustrated algebra. Li’s proof uses a dynamic bootstrap over all relevant centers, Sobolev control, metric equivalence, and evolving curvature energy; a single good ball does not supply these automatically [Steps 13–14].

- For the normalized Einstein defect \(E=\operatorname{Ric}+g\), the exact normalized Ricci-flow identities are
  \[
  \partial_tE=\Delta_LE-2E,
  \]
  and
  \[
  (\partial_t-\Delta)|E|^2=-2|\nabla E|^2+4R_{ikjl}E_{ij}E_{kl}.
  \]
  Kato regularization of \(|E|\) gives a subsolution with potential \(|\operatorname{Rm}|\). The apparent damping from \(-2E\) cancels in the scalar equation, so pointwise Gronwall with \(|\operatorname{Rm}|\le C/t\) has a divergent \(\int_0^Tdt/t\) coefficient and cannot propagate \(E\) uniformly from the initial slice [Steps 13–14; reinforced Step 18].

- Under Li’s full dynamic hypotheses, Corollary 3.5 gives a better curvature-potential estimate. After exact normalized-to-unnormalized conversion, the scaling yields
  \[
  |E(x,t)|\le C\delta\left(\frac{r^2}{t}\right)^{2/3},
  \qquad
  \left|\log\frac{g(t)(v,v)}{g_0(v,v)}\right|
  \le C\delta r^{4/3}t^{1/3}.
  \]
  The singularity \(t^{-2/3}\) is integrable, so metric drift over time \(t=\theta r^2\) is \(O(\delta r^2)\). This estimate is conditional on dynamic curvature-energy/Sobolev/covering assumptions; it is not yet available for the desired localized cutoff flow [Step 14].

- The normalized cutoff flow
  \[
  \partial_t g=-2\chi^2(\operatorname{Ric}+g)
  \]
  was introduced as a plausible localization interface on the original closed manifold. For \(a=\chi^2\),
  \[
  \partial_tE=a(\Delta_LE-2E)+\mathcal C_a(E),
  \]
  where every term in \(\mathcal C_a(E)\) contains \(E\), \(\operatorname{tr}E\), or their first derivatives. Exact negative Einstein metrics are stationary even in the transition annulus. In integrated defect energy, contracted Bianchi and integration by parts remove Hessian-cutoff terms; \(|d(\chi^2)|^2/\chi^2=4|d\chi|^2\) prevents a \(1/\chi\) loss. This homogeneity was symbolically checked [Step 14].

- Wang–Yang local Ricci-flow and Fei He sources support related compactly supported/local-flow architectures, but their hypotheses do not match the current data. Wang’s estimates assume global Sobolev and full-support critical energy conditions; Fei He’s framework assumes pointwise full-curvature scales and initial Ricci-defect derivatives unavailable here. The needed theorem is a collapse-uniform, transition-inclusive cutoff curvature-energy bootstrap derived from local normalized energy and defect bounds, not a direct citation [Step 14].

### Metric-by-metric \(L^2\) calibration inequality and exponential-chart selection

- A robust algebraic/topological weakening was established: for any smooth metric on a fixed critical Ishida–LeBrun manifold, the Einstein defect
  \[
  E=\operatorname{Ric}+g
  \]
  controls the calibrated Weyl modulus by
  \[
  \int\left(|W^+|-\frac1{2\sqrt6}\right)^2\,d\mu
  \le \frac7{24}\int |E|^2\,d\mu .
  \]
  This uses the Chern–Gauss–Bonnet identity \(I-R=2A/3\), the genuine monopole inequality, and completion-square algebra. The constant \(7/24\) was obtained by a sharper trace–traceless decomposition and checked computationally [Step 15].

- The same chain can be phrased through the identity
  \[
  \int(s+8\sqrt6|W^+|)^2 \le 864\pi^2 R
  \]
  with \(R=(8\pi^2)^{-1}\int|\operatorname{Ric}_0|^2\), together with
  \[
  \int|s+4|^2\le4\int|E|^2.
  \]
  Hence global \(L^2\)-smallness of \(E\), rather than pointwise \(O(\delta)\) control throughout a cutoff collar, suffices to recover the global calibrated Weyl profile on the evolved closed topology [Step 15].

- The Step 15 assertion that the fixed-topology gap had been proved was withdrawn. The proposed localized Li bootstrap had a definite domain mismatch: the proof checked covering balls for centers in an inner plateau stay inside a working region, but the bootstrap supremum was over all centers in the working region; centers near the boundary require adjacent balls outside it. Restricting the supremum to the inner plateau restores the uncontrolled inner/outer estimate. Ricci flow has no finite propagation speed, so buffer ratios do not make transition data irrelevant. Thus no fixed-topology negative-branch gap was established [Steps 15–16].

- Conditional on obtaining bounded sectional curvature on a positive-volume buffered plateau, an exponential-pullback averaging lemma avoids relying on CFG rank strata or normal-cover noncollapse. If \(P\) is a positive-volume set of centers in a region with \(|\sec|\le K\) and \(r<\pi/(2\sqrt K)\), then for a nonnegative density \(F\),
  \[
  \int_P \operatorname{avg}_{B_r(0),\,\exp_p^*g}(F\circ\exp_p)\,d\mu(p)
  \le C(n,K,r)\int_M F\,d\mu .
  \]
  Rauch comparison bounds exponential Jacobians and pullback-ball volumes, and Liouville invariance of geodesic flow controls the integral over centers and directions. The number of sheets downstairs and the injectivity radius do not enter [Step 16].

- This exponential-pullback lemma has a stronger normalized consequence than earlier absolute-cover arguments. If \(\operatorname{Vol}(P_i)\ge\theta\operatorname{Vol}(M_i)\), it selects a center with
  \[
  \operatorname{avg}_{\text{chart}}(D_i)
  \le (C/\theta)\,\frac{\int D_i}{\operatorname{Vol}(M_i)}.
  \]
  Thus global deficits that are small per unit volume can yield an absolutely small normalized deficit on a fixed-radius chart. This removes the earlier unnecessary requirement \(A_i\delta_i^2\to0\) for the chart-selection step, provided the smoothing theorem gives positive-volume plateaux with uniform curvature bounds and volume proportion [Step 17].

- Unique continuation alone cannot supply the nonzero limiting harmonic form on selected charts. A sequence of globally normalized harmonic forms can be nonzero almost everywhere yet have local mass tend to zero on every chosen chart. The monopole/eigenline passage must therefore include quantitative local amplitude and saturation errors in the chart-selection density [Step 16].

- The monopole completion-square argument was repaired for possibly sign-changing
  \[
  q=\sqrt6|W^+|-s
  \]
  by using \(q^+\). Smooth positive approximations \(f^2\approx q^++\varepsilon\) give the needed variational inequality without derivatives of \(f\), and the exact nonnegative decomposition gains a favorable term \(\int q^-u^2\). A joint nonnegative density including \(|E|^2\), \((q^+-9/2)^2\), harmonic-amplitude error, and the lowest-eigenline error can be fed into the exponential-chart averaging lemma. On a smoothly convergent selected chart this would produce a nonzero limiting harmonic self-dual form in the extremal lowest eigenline and hence the calibrated spectrum needed for the Step 6 contradiction [Step 16].

### Cutoff-flow estimates through Step 18

- Step 17 found useful algebra for the cutoff flow but initially overstated it as a completed integral layer. The defect evolution for \(a=\chi^2\) has no explicit cubic defect reaction:
  \[
  (\partial_t-a\Delta)|E|^2
  =
  -2a|\nabla E|^2+4a\,\operatorname{Rm}(E,E)+2\langle E,\mathcal C_a(E)\rangle .
  \]
  The cancellation occurs because inverse-metric variation contributes \(+4a\operatorname{tr}(E^3)\), canceling the \(-4a\operatorname{tr}(E^3)\) from the Lichnerowicz/damping interaction. This is consistent with Step 14 [Step 17].

- The Step 17 “coupled \(L^2\) energy system closes” statement was demoted to a conditional bootstrap estimate, not an unconditional theorem. The TTCS generator assumed smooth existence, comparable evolving metric/Sobolev geometry, small neighboring energies, finite-overlap control, and cutoff derivative control before deriving its finite-neighbor inequality. These hypotheses are exactly part of what the first-exit argument must improve, not outputs already established [Steps 17–18].

- The useful conditional \(L^2\) mechanism is four-dimensional Sobolev-energy cancellation. For local normalized curvature energy \(R_\alpha\) and defect energy \(P_\alpha\), a combined energy \(H_\alpha=R_\alpha+\kappa P_\alpha\) can satisfy a finite-neighbor inequality of the form
  \[
  \frac{d}{dt}H_\alpha\le Cr^{-2}\sum_{\beta\sim\alpha}H_\beta
  \]
  under provisional metric/Sobolev/energy hypotheses. The key absorption is that \(C_S\|\operatorname{Rm}\|_{L^2}=O(\sqrt{\varepsilon_*})\) in dimension four after collapsed-volume cancellation. This absorbs terms like \(\int a|\operatorname{Rm}|^3\), \(\int a|\operatorname{Rm}||E|^2\), and \(\int|\nabla a||\nabla E||\operatorname{Rm}|\) when \(\varepsilon_*\) is small enough [Steps 17–18].

- A weighted pointwise curvature estimate \(|a\operatorname{Rm}|\le C/t\) would not by itself preserve the defect via maximum principle, because
  \[
  \int_0^T \frac{dt}{t}
  \]
  diverges. Starting at \(t_0>0\) gives an uncontrolled \((T/t_0)^C\) factor as \(t_0\to0\), and the initial metrics have no uniform pointwise curvature bound. The evolving covariant Hessian of \(a\) also remains in maximum-principle coefficients; fixing \(\chi\) as a scalar does not fix its Hessian [Step 18].

- The correct metric-equivalence route was identified as an integrable weighted-defect estimate, ideally
  \[
  |aE(t)|\le C_p\delta\left(\frac{r^2}{t}\right)^{2/p}
  \quad\text{for some }p>2.
  \]
  Its time integral is finite:
  \[
  \int_0^{\theta r^2}\left(\frac{r^2}{t}\right)^{2/p}dt
  \sim \frac{p}{p-2}\theta^{1-2/p}r^2,
  \]
  while the endpoint \(p=2\) reproduces logarithmic divergence [Step 18].

- The Step 18 structural calculation used
  \[
  U=aE.
  \]
  Commuting \(a\) through the Laplacian cancels the leading \(a(\Delta a)E\) and \(2a\nabla a\cdot\nabla E\) terms. Apparent quotients by \(a\) are regular because \(da\otimes da/a=4d\chi\otimes d\chi\). Testing the tensor equation by \(\eta^2|U|^{p-2}U\) and integrating Hessian-\(a\) terms by parts yields a localized fixed-\(p\) inequality of the form
  \[
  \frac{d}{dt}\int \eta^2|U|^p
  +c_p\int \eta^2a\,|\nabla |U|^{p/2}|^2
  \le \text{cutoff terms}
  +C_p\int\eta^2a|\operatorname{Rm}||U|^p
  +C_p\int\eta^2|U|^{p+1}.
  \]
  Relative Sobolev absorption again cancels collapsed volume in dimension four. For any fixed \(p>2\), sufficiently small local curvature and defect energies conditionally propagate a spatial \(L^p\) bound for \(aE\). This cannot be iterated naively to \(p=\infty\), because the reaction-to-dissipation coefficient grows with \(p\sqrt{\varepsilon_*}\) [Step 18].

- A sufficient second-stage curvature-potential input was identified:
  \[
  S_\alpha^4\int a|\operatorname{Rm}|^3\le C/t,
  \]
  or the stronger weighted estimate \(|a\operatorname{Rm}|\le C/t\) together with persistent local \(L^2\) energy. Combined with the fixed supercritical \(L^p\) bound, a Li/Yang-type time-cylinder iteration could produce the integrable estimate for \(|aE|\). The unresolved analytic tasks at that point were deriving this weighted curvature potential for the degenerate transition operator, controlling evolving connection and cutoff Hessian, closing finite-neighbor geometry and Sobolev persistence, and preserving the unweighted global defect
  \[
  Q(t)=\int|E(t)|^2
  \]
  since weighted pointwise control near \(a=0\) does not imply unweighted \(Q(t)\) control [Step 18].

- The shortcut “small \(O(\delta)\) metric velocity gives \(O(\delta)\) transition-curvature change” was rejected. Curvature evolution contains second derivatives of \(aE\), and initial good-region hypotheses give curvature means, not pointwise curvature or derivative control. Using this shortcut would reintroduce the derivative-control assumption the smoothing program was designed to avoid [Step 18].

### Weighted derivative threshold and volume-independent critical parameter

- Wang’s curvature-control parameter
  \[
  \beta=A_0^2\|\operatorname{Rm}\|_{L^2}
  \]
  is volume-independent in dimension \(4\) at the Li scale: if \(A_0^2\sim C_S r^2\operatorname{Vol}^{-1/2}\) and \(\|\operatorname{Rm}\|_2\sim \sqrt{K_0\operatorname{Vol}}\), then
  \[
  \beta=C_S r^2\sqrt{K_0}.
  \]
  With \(r_*=(\varepsilon_{\rm Li}/K_0)^{1/4}\), this gives \(\beta=C\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\rm Li}}\). TTCS clarified that analogous volume cancellation is dimension-general at the critical \(L^{n/2}\) exponent, but the use of \(L^2\) curvature energy and Chern–Weil control is specifically four-dimensional [Step 19].

- A \(p>4\) threshold was identified for weighted first-derivative control of the cutoff-flow velocity. If
  \[
  |U(t)|=|aE(t)|\le C_p\delta(r^2/t)^{2/p}
  \]
  and the companion derivative estimate
  \[
  |\chi\nabla U(t)|\le C_p\delta t^{-1/2}(r^2/t)^{2/p}
  \]
  held, then the metric drift is integrable iff \(p>2\), while connection/Hessian drift is integrable iff \(p>4\). For \(p=6\), the metric drift is \(\sim(3/2)\delta\theta^{2/3}r^2\) and connection drift is \(\sim6\delta\theta^{1/6}\) over time \(\theta r^2\). This threshold remains valid, but later work showed such quantitative derivative control is not needed for the zero-order first-exit if continuation is handled by a triangular high-order induction and plateau interior estimates [Steps 19–21].

- TTCS corrected an attempted use of Wang’s theorem by simple restriction. Wang is degenerate but global; Li is local but nondegenerate. The needed theorem is local and degenerate, with two cutoff scales: the flow weight \(a=\chi^2\) and the Moser/test cutoff. The normalized-flow correction includes an additive \( \nabla^2(\chi^2)\odot g\)-type source in curvature evolution, which is not multiplicatively absorbable in a curvature equation, although the defect equation remains homogeneous in \(E\). Later shifted-curvature work refined how this source should be packaged [Steps 19, 27].

### Weighted Wang hierarchy and rejection of the Nash shortcut

- The cutoff-flow problem was reorganized around Wang-compatible weighted moments
  \[
  H_q=\int \eta^2 a^{q-2}F^q,
  \qquad F=(1+|\operatorname{Rm}|^2)^{1/2},
  \]
  with Sobolev variable
  \[
  \eta\,a^{(q-1)/2}F^{q/2}.
  \]
  Its fourth power has the weight of the next moment, while \(q=2\) is the unweighted critical curvature energy and \(q=3\) is the weighted cubic potential \(\int\eta^2aF^3\). This avoids dividing by \(a\) near the transition region [Step 20].

- For the defect, the compatible moments are
  \[
  J_m=\int\eta^2a^{m-2}|E|^m,
  \]
  not the weaker \(\int|aE|^m=\int a^m|E|^m\). Initial pointwise pinching supplies \(J_6\), and the interpolation
  \[
  F z_m^2=(aF^3)^{1/3}(a^{-1/3}z_m^2)
  \]
  together with \(J_{3m/2}\le\sqrt{J_mJ_{2m}}\) and Sobolev supports a positive-time iteration toward \(|aE|\) pointwise while preserving the initial \(\delta^6\) factor [Step 20].

- A proposed conformal-measure/Nash semigroup shortcut was rejected. On \(d\nu=a^{-2}d\mu\), the weighted moments can be viewed as standard \(L^q\) norms for \(K=aF\), but small critical form bounds alone do not imply unweighted ultracontractivity. The scalar stress test in \(\mathbb R^4\) with inverse-square potential
  \[
  V=\kappa/|x|^2,\qquad 0<\kappa<1,
  \]
  satisfies the Hardy form bound
  \[
  \int V\phi^2\le\kappa\int|\nabla\phi|^2
  \]
  but the heat semigroup has singular spatial weights \(r^{-\sigma}\), \(\sigma=1-\sqrt{1-\kappa}>0\). TTCS confirmed this via Milman–Semenov-type estimates. Therefore the critical \(H_2\to H_3\) upgrade is essential; a small quadratic form bound cannot replace it [Step 22].

- The correct quadratic form in the conformal-measure interpretation uses \(\nabla(a^{-1/2}\phi)\), not \(\nabla(a^{-1}\phi)\). The leading gradient weight is \(a^{-1}\), not \(a^{-2}\), which matters near \(\{a=0\}\) [Step 22].

- The architecture after this correction is two-stage: Stage 1 is the hard critical step \(H_2\to H_3\) via Wang-type energy and Sobolev absorption with volume-independent \(\beta\); Stage 2 is standard subcritical Moser from \(L^3\) potential to \(L^\infty\) bounds with convergent constants. The Nash route can at most compress Stage 2 and cannot eliminate Stage 1 [Step 22].

### Single-good-support construction and terminal-time control

- The previous outer-dissipation argument was unmatched: bounded overlap alone cannot absorb an outer dissipation \(D_2^{\rm out}\) into an inner dissipation \(D_2\). The corrected construction uses disjoint good macro-supports from maximal-function/Vitali thinning. Each selected center has a centered maximal-function curvature budget on a fixed multiple of the Li radius; after bounded-loss separation, one chooses an active support \(\Omega_j\), plateau where \(\chi_j=1\), and auxiliary domain \(U_j\) where \(\eta_j=1\) near \(\operatorname{supp}\chi_j\) [Step 23].

- On a single such support, with \(a=\chi_j^2\), the unweighted factor in the critical Hölder estimate is controlled by the same component:
  \[
  H_{3,j}\le \|F\|_{L^2(U_j)}\|\eta_j\chi_j F\|_{L^4}^2.
  \]
  The Sobolev variable retains the active dissipation \(\int\eta_j^2a|\nabla F|^2\), while derivatives of \(\eta_j\) produce zero-order neighboring/support terms rather than unmatched neighboring dissipation. This removes the need for a maximal net through uncontrolled bad regions [Step 23].

- The temporal distinction was made explicit. The \(q=2\) estimate gives only a spacetime integral of \(H_3\), hence a good earlier time slice. To prevent narrow terminal spikes, a separate \(q=3\) differential inequality is needed:
  \[
  H_{3,j}'\le Cr^{-2}H_{3,j}
  \]
  on nested buffered domains. Propagating a good slice in \([t/4,t/2]\) gives the terminal estimate in the correct normalization
  \[
  S_j^2H_{3,j}(t)\le C\gamma_j^3/t,
  \qquad \gamma_j=S_j\|F\|_{2,U_j}.
  \]
  A mean-value assertion alone is insufficient without this differential inequality [Step 23].

- The homogeneous defect estimates remain separate obligations. Global unweighted
  \[
  Q(t)=\int |E(t)|^2
  \]
  should obey \(Q'\le Cr^{-2}Q\) only after componentwise critical curvature absorption; there is no acceptable curvature-only additive source because it could be order \(\varepsilon A\) and need not preserve \(Q/A\to0\). Fixed \(J_6\) testing is required from time zero to preserve \(J_6(t)\lesssim J_6(0)\sim\delta^6\operatorname{Vol}\) before positive-time defect iteration [Steps 20, 23].

### Normalization correction for curvature energy

- The fully covariant curvature tensor under the conformal velocity \(\partial_tg=-2ag\) contains a linear term \(-2a\operatorname{Rm}\) because lowering an index contributes \(h_{lm}R^m{}_{ijk}\). The decisive constant scaling check is \(g(t)=e^{-2t}g_0\): Christoffel symbols and \(R^l{}_{ijk}\) are unchanged, while \(R_{ijkl}(t)=e^{-2t}R_{ijkl}(0)\), so \(\partial_tR_{ijkl}=-2R_{ijkl}\) [Step 24].

- Step 24 initially interpreted this \(-2a\operatorname{Rm}\) as beneficial curvature-energy damping, but Step 25 corrected that interpretation. For \(|\operatorname{Rm}|^2_g\), the tensor contribution \(-4a|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\) is combined with \(+8a|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\) from the four inverse metrics and \(-4a|\operatorname{Rm}|^2\) from the volume form in dimension four. Thus \(\int|\operatorname{Rm}|^2d\mu\) is exactly scale-invariant for spatially constant \(a\). The route cannot rely on artificial normalization coercivity; it must rely on matched Sobolev absorption and homogeneous defect control [Steps 24–25].

- For
  \[
  F=(1+|\operatorname{Rm}|^2)^{1/2},
  \]
  the pure-normalization density contribution to \(F^p\,d\mu\) is
  \[
  2a\big[(p-2)F^p-pF^{p-2}\big]\,d\mu .
  \]
  This formula replaces the earlier false beneficial \(-4aF^2\) energy term. Exact negative Einstein metrics remain stationary because of the full Lichnerowicz identity, not because the curvature potential vanishes; \(H_3=\int\eta^2aF^3\) is generally positive even when \(E=0\) [Steps 24–25].

- The corrected schematic curvature evolution, before the shifted-curvature repackaging, is
  \[
  \partial_t\operatorname{Rm}
  =
  a\Delta\operatorname{Rm}+aQ(\operatorname{Rm})-2a\operatorname{Rm}
  +C(\nabla a,\nabla E)-(\nabla^2a\wedge E),
  \]
  with all norm and measure variations treated consistently when deriving energy inequalities [Steps 24–25].

### Whole-support Moser iteration and general-\(p\) weighted inequalities

- The weighted hierarchy exactly matches Yang’s fixed-cutoff Moser iteration in dimension four. Yang’s exponents satisfy
  \[
  p_{j+1}=\frac32p_j,\qquad p'_{j+1}=\frac32p'_j+1.
  \]
  If \(p'_0=p_0-2\), then \(p'_j=p_j-2\), so Yang’s moments
  \[
  \chi^{2p'_j}\Phi^{p_j}
  \]
  are exactly
  \[
  a^{p_j-2}\Phi^{p_j}.
  \]
  The endpoint is \(a\Phi\), which is the required weighted pointwise control [Step 25].

- Choosing potential exponent six makes Yang’s weighted potential exactly
  \[
  H_3=\int aF^3.
  \]
  The interpolation identity
  \[
  a^{p-1}F\Phi^p
  =
  (aF^3)^{1/3}\left(a^{3p/2-2}\Phi^{3p/2}\right)^{2/3}
  \]
  followed by Sobolev and Young inequalities gives a polynomial-in-\(p\) coefficient of the form
  \[
  Cp^3\left(r^{-2}+S^2H_3\right).
  \]
  Since the high-exponent product satisfies \(\sum(j+\log p_j)/p_j<\infty\), later subcritical iteration does not require an ever-shrinking smallness threshold [Step 25].

- Starting at \(p_0=3\) gives the whole-support curvature scale
  \[
  \|a\operatorname{Rm}(t)\|_\infty\lesssim \bar\beta_*/t,
  \]
  where \(\bar\beta\) is safest taken as \(S H_2^{1/2}\) on the active region. Starting at \(p_0=6\), with propagated \(J_6\), gives
  \[
  \|aE(t)\|_\infty\lesssim \delta(r^2/t)^{1/3}.
  \]
  The latter is integrable at zero and supplies the collar metric comparison needed for the first-exit framework [Steps 25–26].

- Step 26 reported a complete general-\(p\) weighted tensor inequality for all \(p\ge3\), extending A01’s index-level \(q=2,3\) template. The boundary term \(d(\eta^2a^{p-1})\) has a \(d\eta\) part that vanishes in the chosen support geometry because \(a^{p-1}=0\) on \(\operatorname{supp}d\eta\), and an \(a\,da\) part bounded by
  \[
  Cp^2r^{-2}K_p
  \]
  using
  \[
  a^{p-3}|da|^2=4a^{p-2}|d\chi|^2.
  \]
  Hessian-\(a\) integration by parts produces the same type of remainder, and algebraic reactions are bounded by
  \[
  Cp\int\eta^2a^{p-1}F\Phi^p.
  \]
  TTCS-supported corrections included removing an erroneous extra \(S^{-1}\) factor, using active-region \(\widehat H_2(0)\) in the first-exit condition, and not adding a collar constant because all cutoff remainders are supported in \(\{a>0\}\) [Step 26].

- For the defect, Step 26 used the regularization
  \[
  \Phi_\varepsilon=(|E|^2+\varepsilon^2)^{1/2}
  \]
  with the chain-rule identity
  \[
  (\partial_t-a\Delta)\Phi_\varepsilon^p
  =
  \frac p2\Phi_\varepsilon^{p-2}(\partial_t-a\Delta)|E|^2
  -p(p-2)a\Phi_\varepsilon^{p-2}|\nabla\Phi_\varepsilon|^2.
  \]
  Estimates are \(\varepsilon\)-uniform; the limit \(\varepsilon\to0\) uses dominated convergence for zero-order terms and weak lower semicontinuity for gradient dissipation [Step 26].

- Noninteger powers in the Moser sequence \(p_j=3(3/2)^j\) require proper treatment at the support edge. The naive assertion that \(\chi^\alpha\) is smooth for arbitrary noninteger \(\alpha\) is not valid unless the cutoff is chosen infinitely flat at the boundary or approximated in \(W^{1,\infty}\). This correction is part of the current proof specification [Step 26].

- The initial relative Sobolev input on collapsed selected balls was reported resolved through the Maheux–Saloff-Coste theorem, Math. Ann. 303 (1995), Theorem 1.1: under \(\operatorname{Ric}\ge kg\), any geodesic ball has
  \[
  S=C(n,Kr^2)\,r^2\,\operatorname{Vol}(B_r)^{-1/2}
  \]
  for the local Sobolev inequality, with \(C\) independent of the volume. For compactly supported functions, the mean-subtraction passage adds only a lower-order \(r^{-2}\|u\|_2^2\) term. In dimension four with \(K=1+\delta\) and \(r=r_*\), \(Kr^2\) is uniformly bounded, so the explicit volume factor is exactly the one used in the collapse-canceling energy estimates [Step 26].

### Shifted-curvature continuation and normalized local-flow extension

- Step 26’s continuation specification treated the added velocity \(-2ag\) as essentially lower-order, but the Step 27 user correction identified the missing high-derivative issue: the covariant curvature variation of \(-2ag\) contains both \(-2a\operatorname{Rm}\) and \(-(\operatorname{Hess}a)\wedge g\). Commuting \(m\) derivatives reaches \(\nabla^{m+2}a\), and neither metric comparability nor a bound for \(a\operatorname{Rm}\) controls higher covariant derivatives of \(\chi\) by itself [Step 27].

- The useful repackaging introduces the parallel algebraic constant-curvature tensor
  \[
  G=\frac{g\wedge g}{2(n-1)}
  \]
  with convention \(\operatorname{Ric}(G)=g\), and defines
  \[
  T=\operatorname{Rm}+G,\qquad U=aT.
  \]
  Then
  \[
  \operatorname{Ric}(T)=E=\operatorname{Ric}+g,\qquad
  \operatorname{Ric}(U)=aE,\qquad
  \nabla G=0,
  \]
  and \(\partial_tG\) is algebraic in \(aE\) and \(g\). This preserves the relationship between curvature, its Ricci contraction, and cutoff derivatives, rather than treating the normalization Hessian source as independent forcing [Step 27].

- In shifted variables the schematic evolution has Wang’s structure:
  \[
  (\partial_t-a\Delta)T
  =
  da*\nabla T+\operatorname{Hess}(a)*T+a(T*T+G*T),
  \]
  while the weighted \(U=aT\) equation has no singular division by \(a\) and no independent \(\operatorname{Hess}(a)*G\) source. The reaction vanishes at \(T=0\), so there is no true constant forcing term after the shift [Step 27].

- The genuine highest cutoff term remains
  \[
  \chi\,\nabla^{m+2}\chi * U.
  \]
  One integration by parts absorbs the derivative-on-\(\nabla^mU\) component into the \(a=\chi^2\) weighted diffusion and lowers the remaining cutoff order to \(m+1\). The cutoff jets are driven by derivatives of
  \[
  \operatorname{Ric}(U)=aE.
  \]
  TTCS resolved an indexing discrepancy in Wang’s printed Proposition 4.14: the high-order proof requires the current Volterra pair
  \[
  \nabla^mU \leftrightarrow \nabla^{m+1}\chi,
  \]
  while the prior unweighted \(\nabla^{m-1}T\) quantity needs only \(\nabla^m\chi\) after its own integration by parts. No algebraic cancellation removes the \(m+1\) cutoff jet [Step 27].

- Step 27 developed a normalized local-flow extension theorem in these shifted variables. Under a terminal bound on \(a\operatorname{Rm}\), \(U\) is bounded because \(0\le a\le1\) and \(G\) is dimension-controlled. The metrics remain uniformly equivalent, finite unweighted \(L^p\) norms of \(T\) follow from the shifted energy equation even across zeros of \(a\), and the staggered-exponent Wang induction can propagate all \(U\) derivatives and cutoff jets. These bounds reconstruct a smooth positive terminal metric and permit a transported-coefficient normalized DeTurck restart [Step 27].

- The continuation evidence is strong but still marked for scientific review rather than final use. The session Codex worker started from `workspace/codex_loop/Research_Project_Proposal.md` to produce an independent detailed shifted-curvature term ledger was still running when Step 27 closed. Therefore the shifted continuation should be treated as a developed, TTCS-supported theorem candidate, not as independently audited final evidence [Step 27].

### Current conditional four-dimensional negative-branch chain and what remains unproved

- The most developed conditional route for a critical Ishida–LeBrun negative sequence is now:
  1. select good macro-supports with maximal-function curvature and calibrated-defect budgets [Steps 9, 16, 23];
  2. use Maheux–Saloff-Coste local Sobolev and volume-independent \(\beta\) to run the critical \(H_2\to H_3\) weighted Wang layer [Steps 19, 22–26];
  3. propagate \(J_6\) and global \(Q\) homogeneously, preserving the \(\delta^6\) and \(L^2\)-smallness needed for the calibration chain [Steps 20, 23, 26];
  4. use subcritical Yang/Moser iteration to obtain whole-support weighted bounds \(|a\operatorname{Rm}|\lesssim \bar\beta/t\) and \(|aE|\lesssim\delta(r^2/t)^{1/3}\), giving integrable metric drift and first-exit improvement [Steps 25–26];
  5. use shifted-curvature Wang continuation to keep the degenerate normalized cutoff flow alive to a common positive time [Step 27];
  6. recover uniform higher derivatives only on a smaller \(a=1\) plateau at positive time by ordinary normalized Ricci-flow interior estimates/Shi estimates [Steps 21, 24–27];
  7. apply exponential-pullback chart averaging with joint monopole/calibrated density to obtain a smooth local Einstein germ carrying the calibrated \(W^+\) spectrum and nonzero lowest-eigenline harmonic data [Steps 16, 21, 27];
  8. use the Step 6 projector plus Einstein–Weyl identity contradiction [Steps 6, 27].

- This route is not yet a proved gap theorem. Step 27 explicitly handed off a rigorous scientific reading of the entire chain: compare the pending Codex ledger, A01’s unified weak Moser and continuation notes, the \(H_3/J_6/Q\) estimates, first-exit closure, terminal support bounds, and the geometric bridge through exponential-pullback averaging and monopole density. Exact unresolved interfaces include retained plateau volume and buffer quantification, terminal reapplication of the \(7/24\) and Seiberg–Witten deficit identities to the evolved closed metric, compatibility of exponential charts with positive-time derivative bounds on all required geodesics, and passage of harmonic-form amplitude/eigenline saturation to the smooth Einstein germ [Step 27].

- The Step 6 terminal contradiction must remain the projector/Einstein–Weyl identity contradiction. A proposed shortcut through local symmetric classification was rejected: \(\nabla W^+=0\) does not imply the full curvature is locally symmetric. No \(H^4\)/\(\mathbb{CH}^2\) classification argument is needed or justified for the local obstruction [Steps 24–25].

### Topology-normalized scope for critical families

- The exponential-chart averaging lemma means the cutoff-flow theorem, if proved with constants depending only on normalized global curvature energy and buffer ratios, could have more than fixed-topology value. If a positive-volume plateau proportion is maintained and \(Q(t)/\operatorname{Vol}(t)\to0\), terminal calibrated defects per unit volume can select a calibrated fixed-radius chart even when \(A\to\infty\). This remains conditional on a simultaneous flow theorem and terminal geometry; no topology-uniform theorem is established [Steps 17, 27].

- The Step 17 claim that Bogomolov–Miyaoka–Yau automatically gives the needed upper bound on normalized curvature energy was corrected. BMY gives \(c_1^2\le3c_2\), a lower bound in the wrong direction for \(c_2/c_1^2\). For minimal general-type summands, Noether’s inequality gives a usable upper bound:
  \[
  c_2(X)\le5c_1^2(X)+36.
  \]
  For
  \[
  M=\left(\#_{j=1}^mX_j\right)\#N,\qquad m=2,3,
  \]
  with critical relation \(D=A/3\) and standard Ishida–LeBrun assumption \(b_+(N)=0\), the corrected negative-definite convention is
  \[
  D=4(m-1)+b_-(N),
  \]
  not \(D=b_-(N)\). The same assumptions yield \(\chi(N)\le A/3\) and \(A\ge12(m-1)\); connected-sum arithmetic then gives
  \[
  \chi(M)/A\le65/6
  \]
  for minimal general-type summands. This supports possible topology-uniform analytic constants for that subclass if the simultaneous flow theorem is proved, but it does not apply to arbitrary symplectic summands without a separate Euler-to-\(A\) upper bound [Step 18].

### Positive branch and higher-dimensional evidence

- Positive normalized pinching has structural advantages but no complete proof. Myers gives diameter control when \(\operatorname{Ric}\approx+g\), and positive scalar curvature kills Seiberg–Witten monopole obstructions, but there is no dimension-only volume lower bound. Round lens-space quotients have exact \(\operatorname{Ric}=g\) and volumes tending to zero in fixed odd dimensions while already satisfying the conclusion because they are Einstein. Thus collapse in the input metric is compatible with the desired output and cannot simply be ruled out as a prerequisite [Steps 4–5].

- In dimension \(4\), peer work from S0910A02, accepted only in its stated scope, used Cheeger–Naber Theorem 1.12 to support: for \(|\operatorname{Ric}-g|_{\rm op}\le\delta_0<1/2\) plus a volume lower bound, there are only finitely many diffeomorphism types. Therefore any positive-pinching sequence on pairwise distinct manifolds, if it exists, must be volume-collapsed. This is a finiteness/dichotomy result, not an Einstein-existence theorem [Step 8].

- A02 positive-branch work found that codimension-one positive Einstein collapse exists in every \(n\ge5\) via Kaluza–Klein-type constructions \(L(q,1)\times N^d\), while dimension \(4\) is blocked by a Bochner-type mechanism in that peer analysis. This means high-dimensional positive-branch strategies cannot rely on collapse obstruction alone [Step 22].

- A02’s later toric analysis on \(\#_k(S^2\times S^2)\) reported a “BREAK” verdict: integral identities alone did not obstruct the relevant \(\alpha\)-family, so the positive branch likely needs a global PDE solvability obstruction rather than only topological/integral constraints. This does not affect the negative critical-family route but is evidence that the positive branch is structurally different [Steps 24–25].

- For dimensions \(n\ge5\), no analogue of the four-dimensional Seiberg–Witten/Chern–Weil machinery has been developed in this session. Producing a high-dimensional counterexample would require identifying closed manifolds known to carry no Einstein metric of any sign, which remains nontrivial. Current evidence mainly concerns the four-dimensional negative critical family and does not settle higher dimensions [Steps 2, 9, 18, 27].

### Research Line

The research began by locking the exact quantifier structure of Yau Problem 26 and refusing to replace it by a nearby stability statement. The first structural move was the positive/negative branch normalization. This clarified the logic of both proof and disproof: proving \(Q_n\) requires only one suitable interval per dimension, while disproving it requires failure of both same-sign normalized branches in the same dimension. Later, the user clarified that the two branch failures need not occur on the same manifold, which removed an unnecessary strengthening from counterexample thinking [Steps 1, 10].

The first explored mechanisms were broad geometric and analytic counterexample/existence routes. Orbifold desingularization was attractive because obstructed Einstein desingularization could appear to produce manifolds with near-Einstein metrics but no Einstein metric. The unweighted ALE residual computation changed this: first obstruction terms survive in the Ricci norm relevant to the problem, so the route only remains meaningful under special obstruction-vanishing conditions, and even then only local non-desingularizability is shown. This left a reusable lesson: failure of a specific Einstein construction is not absence of every Einstein metric on the smooth manifold [Step 1].

The agents simultaneously checked known convergence/flexibility claims. Min-Oo/Ye/Anderson sources did not yield the needed pure Ricci-pinching convergence theorem; Lohkamp’s flexibility did not meet the two-sided near-\(-g\) requirement. The flat-symbol computation then eliminated a simple high-frequency perturbative homogenization mechanism by showing the linear Ricci kernel is pure gauge. These checks narrowed the field without resolving whether a nonlinear or degenerating Ricci-flexibility mechanism exists [Steps 1-2].

The research then moved to four-dimensional topology because that is where strong no-Einstein obstructions are available. Step 2 initially overread Seiberg–Witten/Chern–Weil estimates and tried to prove quantitative gaps for known families. The user’s Step 3 correction forced a significant route change: the pure \(W^+\) estimate was invalid, and the sharp mixed scalar–Weyl inequality left the critical Ishida–LeBrun boundary \(D=A/3\) unresolved. The target became near-equality geometry at this boundary rather than a quick obstruction conclusion [Steps 2-3].

At the critical boundary, the agents built a diagnostic profile for any hypothetical tight negative-pinching sequence. Scalar, Weyl, volume, curvature-energy, and monopole period data would have to approach a calibrated configuration. This did not imply compactness or noncollapse. Its main value was to exclude ordinary geometric pictures: negative Kähler–Einstein bulk pieces have the wrong \(W^+\) magnitude and scalar-flat connectors carry too much Ricci defect after normalization. The line moved from “reuse known \(L^2\)-minimizing gluing pictures” to “identify whether any geometry can satisfy both pointwise near-\(-g\) Ricci pinching and the calibrated \(W^+\) profile” [Steps 3-4].

## Review and repair: fixed-topology gap withdrawn; exponential charts replace CFG dependence downstream [Step 16]

\int_P \operatorname{avg}_{B_r(0),\,\exp_p^*g}(F\circ\exp_p)\,d\mu(p)
\le C(n,K,r)\int_M F\,d\mu,
\]
with no dependence on sheet number or injectivity radius [Step 16]. This makes it possible, after terminal global nonnegative deficits are small, to select a fixed-radius noncollapsed pullback chart with small normalized deficit [Step 16]. Positive-time curvature-derivative estimates remain needed to pass to a smooth local limit [Step 16].

The harmonic-form passage was also repaired [Step 16]. Unique continuation alone does not ensure a nonzero limiting harmonic form on selected charts; normalized harmonic forms can have local mass escape or tend to zero on the chosen region [Step 16]. Instead, the agents reconstructed the current-metric monopole data using the positive part \(q^+\) of \(q=\sqrt6|W^+|-s\) to handle sign changes under only \(L^2\) terminal control [Step 16]. The exact nonnegative deficit decomposition gains a favorable \(\int q^-u^2\) term and controls harmonic-amplitude and lowest-eigenline errors without derivatives of the approximating weight [Step 16]. A joint density containing \(|E|^2\), \((q^+-9/2)^2\), harmonic-amplitude error, and lowest-eigenline error can be fed into the exponential-chart averaging lemma [Step 16]. ## Cutoff-flow estimates: conditional coupled energy, weighted defect \(U=aE\), and simultaneous bootstrap [Steps 17-18]

Step 17 tried to develop the transition-inclusive normalized cutoff-flow theorem [Step 17]. =

with no explicit cubic defect reaction [Step 17]. TTCS corrected an overclaim: a maximum-principle bound for \(|E|^2\) requires \(\|a\,{\rm Rm}(g(t))\|_\infty\) as input, not merely an initial curvature-mean bound, because \(C^0\) metric closeness does not control curvature [Step 17]. Step 17 also proposed a finite-neighbor \(L^2\) curvature–defect energy system with local energies \(H_\alpha=R_\alpha+\kappa P_\alpha\) [Step 17]. The mechanism was the four-dimensional Sobolev-energy cancellation: products like \(C_S\|{\rm Rm}\|_{L^2}\) become \(O(\sqrt{\varepsilon_*})\) under small normalized critical energy, so curvature cubic terms, \(\int a|{\rm Rm}||E|^2\), and transition cross terms can be absorbed by gradient dissipations [Step 17]. Step 18 repaired the logical order of that claim [Step 18]. The coupled \(L^2\) estimates are valid as conditional bootstrap inequalities, but they assume smooth existence, evolving metric comparability, relative Sobolev geometry, fixed ball/overlap control, cutoff control, and small neighboring energies; they can improve these inside a first-exit argument, but do not independently produce them [Step 18]. The old proof hierarchy “\(L^2\) energy closed, then only transition \(\varepsilon\)-regularity remains” was replaced by a simultaneous first-exit framework in which every provisional quantity must be improved together [Step 18].

Step 18 also ruled out two shortcuts [Step 18]. First, even a weighted curvature bound \(|a\,{\rm Rm}|\le C/t\) does not by itself preserve \(E\) by maximum principle, because \(\int_0^T dt/t\) diverges; starting at \(t_0>0\) gives a nonuniform factor as \(t_0\to0\), and initial metrics have only curvature-mean control [Step 18]. Second, small flow velocity \(O(\delta)\) cannot imply \(O(\delta)\) transition-curvature change, because curvature evolution contains second derivatives of \(aE\), and initial curvature is not pointwise controlled [Step 18].

The main constructive advance in Step 18 was to weight the Einstein defect before higher-power estimates [Step 18]. With \(U=aE\), commuting \(a\) through the Laplacian cancels the leading \(a(\Delta a)E\) and \(2a\nabla a\cdot\nabla E\) terms; apparent quotients by \(a\) are regular because \(da\otimes da/a=4\,d\chi\otimes d\chi\) [Step 18]. Testing the tensor equation by \(\eta^2|U|^{p-2}U\) and integrating Hessian-\(a\) terms by parts yields a localized fixed-\(p\) inequality of the form
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\int\eta^2|U|^p
+c_p\int\eta^2a|\nabla |U|^{p/2}|^2
\le
\text{cutoff terms}
+C_p\int\eta^2a|{\rm Rm}||U|^p
+C_p\int\eta^2|U|^{p+1}.
\]
In dimension 4, relative Sobolev absorption again cancels collapsed volume, so for one fixed \(p>2\), under provisional first-exit geometry and small neighboring curvature/defect energies, the spatial \(L^p\) norm of \(aE\) can be propagated [Step 18]. The agents explicitly noted that this cannot be iterated to \(p=\infty\) with a fixed critical-energy threshold because coefficients grow with \(p\) [Step 18].

The desired second stage now follows the Li/Yang pattern rather than repeated \(L^2\) absorption [Step 18]. A sufficient transition estimate would be a curvature-potential bound such as

S_\alpha^4\int a|{\rm Rm}|^3\le C/t,
\]
or stronger weighted \(|a\,{\rm Rm}|\le C/t\) plus local \(L^2\) energy [Step 18]. Starting from a fixed supercritical \(L^p\) bound for \(U\), a time-cylinder Moser iteration could then yield

\]
whose time integral is finite exactly for \(p>2\) and gives metric comparability [Step 18]. The unresolved analytic problem is deriving this weighted curvature potential for the degenerate transition operator while controlling the connection, evolving Hessian of \(a\), finite-neighbor geometry, and unweighted global defect \(Q(t)=\int|E|^2\) [Step 18]. Weighted pointwise control near \(a=0\) cannot replace unweighted \(Q(t)\) [Step 18].

## Topology-uniformity considerations for critical Ishida–LeBrun families [Steps 17-18]

Step 17, prompted by the exponential-chart averaging lemma, noted that volume-normalized deficits could extend the potential reach beyond fixed topology [Step 17]. If a positive-volume plateau-center set satisfies \(\mathrm{Vol}(P_i)\ge\theta\mathrm{Vol}(M_i)\), the exponential averaging lemma selects a chart with average deficit bounded by \((C/\theta)\int D_i/\mathrm{Vol}(M_i)\) [Step 17]. Thus the downstream reconstruction can use global deficits per unit volume, not only absolute \(\int D_i\to0\), and harmonic representatives need not be in one fixed cohomology class across a sequence [Step 17]. This makes the analytic cutoff theorem potentially valuable for varying critical families if its constants depend only on averaged curvature energy and fixed ratios [Step 17].

Step 17 initially suggested that Bogomolov–Miyaoka–Yau might bound \(\chi(M)/A\) uniformly, but Step 18 corrected the direction [Steps 17-18]. BMY gives \(c_1^2\le3c_2\), equivalently a lower bound on \(c_2/c_1^2\), not an upper bound on curvature energy per unit volume [Step 18]. For minimal complex surfaces of general type, Noether’s formula and inequality instead give
\[
c_2(X)\le5c_1^2(X)+36
\]
under the assumptions checked in Step 18 [Step 18]. For \(M=(\#X_j)\#N\) with \(m=2,3\), the critical relation \(D=A/3\) gives
\[
\chi(N)=A/3+6-4m+6(b_+(N)-b_1(N)),
\]
so \(D\) alone does not bound \(\chi(N)\) [Step 18]. Under the standard Ishida–LeBrun hypothesis \(b_+(N)=0\), Step 18 derived \(\chi(M)/A\le65/6\) for the subclass with minimal general-type summands, after correcting the negative-definite convention to \(D=4(m-1)+b_-(N)\) rather than \(D=b_-(N)\) [Step 18]. This supports possible topology-uniform analytic constants for that subclass if the simultaneous flow theorem is eventually established, but it is not available for arbitrary symplectic summands without a separate Euler-to-\(A\) upper bound [Step 18]. The derivation was checked by `workspace/scripts/verify_step18_noether_topology_bound.py` [Step 18].

## Results, Observations, and Their Meaning

### Problem quantifiers, normalization, and low dimensions

- For fixed dimension \(n\), the interval version of Yau Problem 26 was reduced to normalized one-sign branches \(P_n^+\) and \(P_n^-\). Since every nondegenerate real interval contains a one-sign subinterval and constant rescaling \(h=|\mu|g\) rescales the Ricci endomorphism in the required way, the original statement \(Q_n\) is equivalent to \(P_n^+\lor P_n^-\). A strict disproof in one fixed dimension must defeat both normalized signs, but the two witnessing manifolds need not be the same; requiring one manifold to realize both signs is an unnecessary strengthening [Step 1; corrected Step 10].

- Dimensions \(2\) and \(3\) are already covered in the sense needed for the problem: dimension \(2\) by uniformization, and dimension \(3\) by Hamilton’s positive Ricci theorem giving a positive branch. The unresolved range begins at dimension \(4\) [Step 1].

### Orbifold desingularization route and its limitation

- In the Morteza–Viaclovsky Einstein-orbifold desingularization setting, weighted gluing estimates were converted into the unweighted Ricci-endomorphism defect relevant to the original problem. In the ALE core the refined metric was written
  \[
  g_t=t h_t=t(g_{\rm cal}+t h),
  \]
  with local expansion
  \[
  \operatorname{Ric}(h_t)=t\Lambda h_t+t\lambda o+R_t,\qquad
  |R_t|_{g_{\rm cal}}\le C t^2\rho^2 .
  \]
  Since constant scaling does not change the \((0,2)\)-Ricci tensor,
  \[
  g_t^{-1}(\operatorname{Ric}(g_t)-\Lambda g_t)
  =\lambda h_t^{-1}o+t^{-1}h_t^{-1}R_t .
  \]
  On fixed ALE core sets the first term converges to \(\lambda g_{\rm cal}^{-1}o\), while the remainder is \(O(t^{1/2})\) on the core range \(\rho\le Ct^{-1/4}\) [Step 1].

- The explicit tensor \(o\) has eigenvalues
  \[
  -\frac1{1+r^{2n}}\quad(\text{horizontal real directions, multiplicity }2n-2),
  \qquad
  \frac{n-1}{1+r^{2n}}\quad(\text{radial and Hopf directions}).
  \]
  Thus the unweighted defect has core supremum tending to \((n-1)|\lambda|\) when the first obstruction \(\lambda\ne0\). Weighted norms and ALE rescaling do not remove this obstruction [Step 1].

- In transition annuli for the same gluing framework, residual terms are \(O(t^{1/2})\), and the obstruction contribution decays like \(O(t^{n/2})\) when \(o=O(r^{-2n})\) and \(r\approx t^{-1/4}\). Therefore this desingularization route can yield uniform Ricci pinching only if all first obstructions at all singular points vanish; even then, higher obstructions and global no-Einstein topology remain unresolved [Step 1].

- Local nonexistence near a chosen Einstein-orbifold degeneration is not evidence of global no-Einstein topology. The two-point football Eguchi–Hanson resolution gives \(S^2\times S^2\), which has a product Einstein metric, separating “no Einstein metric near this degeneration” from “no Einstein metric on the smooth manifold” [Step 1].

### Perturbative Ricci-symbol route

- The flat-background principal symbol of \(D\operatorname{Ric}\) has no nongauge kernel:
  \[
  \ker \sigma_\xi(D\operatorname{Ric})=\{\xi\otimes v+v\otimes\xi\}
  \]
  for every nonzero covector \(\xi\). In coordinates \(\xi=e_1\), the kernel equations force all transverse components \(h_{ab}\), \(a,b>1\), to vanish, leaving exactly infinitesimal diffeomorphism directions. This was checked algebraically and numerically for \(n=3,4,5\) [Steps 2–3].

- Consequently, the proposed high-frequency averaged-cone construction from nongauge linear Ricci-flat modes is unavailable. Second-order Ricci terms from truncated gauge perturbations cancel when completed to an exact pullback of the flat metric [Steps 2–3].

### Four-dimensional Chern–Weil pinching constraints

- A strengthened Hitchin–Thorpe estimate was derived for four-dimensional metrics satisfying
  \[
  \|g^{-1}(\operatorname{Ric}-\Lambda g)\|_\infty\le \delta|\Lambda|.
  \]
  If
  \[
  \delta<\frac{\sqrt3-1}{2}\approx0.366,
  \]
  then
  \[
  2\chi>3|\tau|.
  \]
  Hence Hitchin–Thorpe-violating manifolds and equality-boundary manifolds cannot support sufficiently tight normalized Ricci pinching of either sign [Step 2].

- For LeBrun/Ishida–LeBrun no-Einstein families, the valid gauge-theoretic input is Ishida–LeBrun Proposition 4:
  \[
  \frac1{4\pi^2}\int\left(\frac{s^2}{24}+2|W^+|^2\right)d\mu
  \ge \frac23(a^+)^2
  \]
  under the applicable monopole hypotheses. Combined with pointwise Ricci pinching and Chern–Weil identities, this gives quantitative restrictions on negative pinching in these families [Steps 2–3].

- A claimed independent pure \(W^+\) lower bound
  \[
  \int |W^+|^2\ge \frac{4\pi^2}{3}(a^+)^2
  \]
  was withdrawn. The derivation incorrectly dropped a negative gradient term in LeBrun’s Weitzenböck estimate and treated \(F_A^+\) as generally harmonic. The usable evidence is the published mixed scalar–Weyl inequality, not this stronger Weyl-only claim. This correction invalidated the earlier overstatement that all known no-Einstein families had been eliminated by a uniform gap [Step 3].

### Ishida–LeBrun critical family and near-saturation profile

- The main four-dimensional negative-branch test interface is the Ishida–LeBrun Theorem 7 family
  \[
  M=\left(\#_{j=1}^m X_j\right)\# N,
  \qquad
  A=\sum_j c_1^2(X_j),
  \qquad
  D=4m-(2\chi+3\tau)(N),
  \]
  for \(m=2\) or \(3\). The theorem excludes Einstein metrics when \(D\ge A/3\). At the boundary \(D=A/3\), strictness in the exact Einstein equality argument does not by itself produce a positive infimum of the Ricci-pinching defect over all metrics, so this boundary remains the main known no-Einstein/topological obstruction interface for possible \(\delta\to0\) negative pinching [Step 3].

- For a hypothetical fixed critical Ishida–LeBrun manifold with metrics satisfying
  \[
  \delta_i=\|g_i^{-1}(\operatorname{Ric}_{g_i}+g_i)\|_\infty\to0,
  \]
  normalized Chern–Weil quantities \(S_i,W_i,R_i,I_i\) were defined and gave
  \[
  I_i-R_i=\frac{2A}{3},\qquad R_i=O(A\delta_i^2).
  \]
  Thus \(R_i/A\to0\) and \(I_i/A\to2/3\). The calibrated energy profile recorded was
  \[

### Weyl profile, bubbles, and quantitative equality defects

- From the genuine scalar–Weyl inequality and uniform scalar convergence \(s_i\to -4\), the completed-square identity gave

Therefore positive-volume regions of a hypothetical critical sequence cannot converge to ordinary negative Kähler–Einstein bulk geometry [Step 4].

Because four-dimensional Weyl energy is scale invariant, any smooth noncollapsed shrinking-scale blow-up of a hypothetical fixed-topology sequence must be Ricci-flat and \(W^+=0\), hence locally hyperkähler in the relevant orientation. This allows anti-self-dual hyperkähler bubbles such as Eguchi–Hanson but rules out arbitrary Ricci-flat bubbles in that orientation. For varying topology \(A_i\to\infty\), only normalized smallness is available unless \(A_i\delta_i^2\to0\), so finite absolute \(W^+\)-energy bubbles are not excluded by this argument alone [Step 4].

The defect decomposition controls amplitude, approximate harmonicity, and eigenline alignment, but not near-parallelness of the forms [Steps 4, 9].

- A convention ambiguity in the Weitzenböck formula for two-forms was resolved by testing candidate curvature endomorphisms against constant-holomorphic-sectional-curvature Kähler–Einstein metrics with \(\operatorname{Ric}=-g\), \(S^4\), and K3 checks. The convention retained is
